Okhema is a far more welcoming place than Castrum Kremnos. Mydei notes this immediately upon entering the city. The day he arrives is rainy and gray, but the city is still golden, and the streets are still full, and the people still smile. It’s fascinating, heartening, and disconcerting all at once.

So he enters this smiling city with a purpose, and hours later, he sells himself to it as a bargaining chip.

Lady Aglaea outfits him with his own guest chambers. He’s given a soft bed, a warm bath, and a breathtaking view of the city. The sheets are crisp and smell like cherry laurel, and Mydei hates this cage of a room like he hates little else. He feels like a thistle in a garden of flowers, and a handful of days after his arrival, he’s already set to leave.

After breakfast, he packs his scant amount of things and makes a final stop to speak to Lady Aglaea before his departure. He finds her at the Hero’s Bath, standing before the golden water that cascades from above. Her back is turned to him, so he can’t see her face, but her posture is upright and strong. Aglaea the Goldweaver is not a monarch, but she holds herself like a queen. Bearer of the Romance coreflame, Mydei doesn’t doubt that she’s one of the most powerful people in Amphoreus.

One of her threads sits on his finger, beneath his gauntlet. It warms when he’s reminded of it, and he wonders—not for the first time—how exactly it binds him.

“Crown Prince Mydeimos,” Aglaea greets, though the water is loud enough to cover his footsteps and he has yet to speak. Her back stays turned as he approaches, but her power of perception means she likely doesn’t need to look at someone to know their every move. “To what do I owe the pleasure?”

Her voice is smooth and impartial, and Mydei is wary of her in a way he is rarely wary of anyone else. She makes conversation into a game of strategy. Mydei was raised a warrior, not a diplomat.

“I must return to Castrum Kremnos to share the news,” he answers, crossing his arms over his chest. Hesitating briefly, he adds, “Many will seek asylum. The longer I stay, the more lives are lost.”

Aglaea’s shoulders rise with her breath. “Yes,” she says, and finally turns, her eyes leveling with his. “Do you know why the water in the Hero’s bath shines with gold?” she asks, gesturing behind her with one open palm.

The string on his hand again makes itself known. Mydei tenses. “No,” he says, and she waves him forward. With a few reluctant steps, he’s faced with the pool, glittering in uneven patterns as the stream from above disturbs it.

“It’s a blessing from Phagousa,” Aglaea explains. “The Hero’s bath is steeped with their lifeblood to cleanse the black tide from the Chrysos Heirs’ bodies.” She bends to dip her fingers into the water, and when she straightens up, the water that clings to her holds a faint shimmer. “Parts of Castrum Kremnos have already succumbed to the tide, haven’t they?”

Mydei stays carefully silent.

“You came alone,” Aglaea continues, “without anyone to wait on or advise you. You don’t want to send a messenger with the news and instead wish to go in person. Your father, according to rumor, is dead.”

The hair on the back of Mydei’s neck stands on end. Nothing she says to him is a secret, and yet. “What are you getting at, Goldweaver?”

“You spent a long time away from home, Undying prince.” She smiles slightly and lowers her hand. “Do you truly believe you can prevent Castrum Kremnos’ fall?”

She is a terrifyingly perceptive creature. “Whether or not the city falls,” Mydei says, “my people will not.”

Based on her expression, this gives away more than enough. “Okhema is a refuge with open doors,” is all she says. He already asked for this before any other negotiations were made. Safe haven for the people whose homes have been turned to rubble. Sunlight, for those trapped in the dark. Mydei’s hand, this scant amount of freedom lost, is hardly a price at all in the wake of that.

He bows his head in respect and says, “You have my thanks.”

“Would you join us in the rebuilding of the world?” Aglaea asks.

“Nikador’s coreflame already belongs to your cause.” The last pieces of his crumbling god. Mydei has nothing left to give.

“Yes,” Aglaea agrees. “But who better to bear it by our side than you?”

It’s a horrible feeling that the words give him. Ink on his tongue, staining his teeth. “No,” Mydei says with a low laugh. “Your perfect vessel will bear it. You have no need for me.”

Slowly, she nods, but her smile is a small, knowing thing as she turns back to the water. “Phainon has been waiting a long time to fulfill his destiny,” she says, and leaves it at that. She has more to say, this much is obvious, but she won’t say it. Mydei remains quiet.

“Will you meet him before you go?” Aglaea asks lightly, and Mydei remembers a challenge of a smile. Blue eyes and soaked white hair. A sun on the side of a pale throat and the tip of a dagger to his belly.

“I can,” Mydei says, instead of I have, because he thinks better of lying to a woman like this, and he doesn’t think the kind of meeting they had is one for the history books. The string on his finger heats, and Aglaea isn’t looking at him, but he feels as though she sees right through him.

△

Phainon—dressed to be out in public—wears a white coat and a blue and gold half cape. His hair sticks up in a handful of places when dry, and he obscures the sun on his neck with a high collar and a choker fitted tight to skin. He looks every bit the hero he’s said to be, and Mydei does his very best to pretend they have never spoken.

Aglaea introduces them, playing the role a parent might in a marriage between people who have those. Mydei makes all the proper pleasantries, and Phainon plays along. When they bow to each other to complete the act, he quirks one eyebrow, lips curling up, and Mydei looks away.

“You’re pretending you don’t know me,” Phainon notes later when they’re seated beside each other at the dinner Aglaea had prepared for this. The room is packed full of Okhema’s most important people, and he leans in close enough that Mydei can smell the olive oil and pine resin scent of him. He’s terribly indiscreet, and Mydei does not look at him.

“Yes,” he agrees, keeping his voice low. “Unless you would rather everyone here know we accosted each other in the baths?” Across the table, the Holy Maidens of Janusopolis pluck grapes from a bunch as they talk to a girl with pink hair and a delicate crown. She wears a dress adorned with flowers and a tired expression, and she gives the people around her a wide berth. The Maiden of War, he thinks, but he’s forgotten her name. She meets his eyes when she notices him looking, and there’s an odd flash in her expression.

Beside him, Phainon interrupts his train of thought. “You’re just afraid they’ll find out you lost,” he whispers, far too cocky, goading.

Mydei inhales and flicks his gaze to him. “I had you by the throat,” he hisses.

The smile it earns him is far too pleased. “And I had you,” Phainon says. He cocks his head a little. “So I suppose we can call it a stalemate.”

The way he carries himself—he is a fledgling hero still waiting for a chance to fulfill his destiny. Mydei holds his ice blue gaze and says with surety, “You wouldn’t hold a candle to me in a real battle.”

Phainon squints. “You speak rather confidently for someone who’s never seen me in a ‘real battle.’”

“Is that an invitation?”

"Do you want it to be?"

Mydei studies him. The honest challenge in his eyes, the fluff of his hair that makes him look like some over eager dog. In Castrum Kremnos, a test of strength is standard before a betrothal. The groom to be will challenge the father of the bride, and the outcome determines whether or not he earns her hand. Neither of them has a father to speak of, and neither of them is much of a bride. "Perhaps," he says. "I'd like to know whether or not I can regard you as an equal."

Somehow this makes Phainon laugh, taking the insult with far too much ease. "They say you have the bloodlust of an entire army," he says. "Is someone’s fighting prowess directly proportional to the respect you give them?" He's too close. Olive oil and pine resin. Mydei narrows his eyes.

"Respect," he says, "is earned, not given."

"Respect," Phainon counters, "is given so it can be earned."

A brief pause. Mydei considers the earnest way he says this. Phainon, he thinks, must be merciful on the battlefield. A virtue, or a vice that could get him killed. "You're fascinating, Deliverer."

"What did I say about calling me that?" Phainon asks, voice low, leaning in a little more.

"Beat me," Mydei challenges him, grinning, "and maybe I'll stop."

"Is the food to your tastes, Your Highness?" Aglaea interrupts, looking between them with an unreadable expression. Mydei can never tell what she's thinking. Perhaps she finds their behavior improper or wants to prevent a conflict. The Maiden of War is watching again. Mydei meets her eyes and dips his head slowly.

"Yes," he says, and turns back to Aglaea. Beside him, Phainon has returned to his own space and is picking at his plate, chastened. An over eager dog with his ears drooping. Mydei doesn't know what to make of the switch. "My compliments to your cooks."

△

"This is for you." Phainon catches him before he can slip away at the end of the night. He presents Mydei with a small box under the watchful eye of Aglaea on the other side of the room. Mydei feels her gaze on him like a tangible thing. The sensation is like a pair of too tight boots. The hair on the back of his neck prickles.

Slightly wary, he takes the box and asks, "What is it?"

Phainon blinks. "A gift," he says, like it's obvious. "For you."

"I see." Mydei lowers his gaze to the box. Courting gifts are not customary in Castrum Kremnos. He does not relish the thought that he'll have to give one in return. "Thank you."

Again, Phainon blinks. He glances at Aglaea, almost anxious. "Aren't you going to open it?"

Managing not to sigh, Mydei does. He lifts the lid and peels back the paper on the inside. The box holds bottles of rust solvent and armor polish, no doubt expensive, and entirely, unexpectedly practical. “Oh,” he says, inspecting one of the bottles.

Phainon shifts, watching carefully for his reaction. “You didn’t strike me as someone who likes flowers or jewelry,” he explains. After a brief pause, “Feel free to correct me if I’m wrong.”

“No,” Mydei says, gaze lifting to him as he puts the bottle back. “You’re correct; I appreciate things I can actually use. Thank you.”

Phainon lifts a hand to rub his neck, fingers hooking beneath his choker. He’s relieved, obviously. He wears every emotion openly—that or he’s an exceptional pretender. Mydei still can’t make sense of him, can’t decide what he is and what he isn’t. He thinks of a fight in the bath and a challenge at the dinner table. And then he thinks of the man kneeling in the rain and finds him completely at odds with the one in front of him. Their marriage is a massive inconvenience at best. At worst, it will upend Phainon’s life and rob him of a chance at real, earnest love. He doesn’t want this, Mydei knows that, and yet here he is.

And yet here he is, smiling somewhat nervously, saying, “You’re very welcome,” and giving Lady Aglaea the smallest glance. Perhaps that’s it, her orders, her instruction, her idea of a courting gift.

Something like guilt churns in Mydei’s stomach as he slips the box in one of his trouser pockets.

“Lord Phainon,” he says, stiffly formal for fear that their banter earlier may have gotten Phainon in trouble. For fear that this may too. “Could I speak to you alone for a moment?”

Something strange crosses Phainon’s expression, his smile faltering. “Yes,” he says, glancing again at Aglaea. “Of course, um.” He gestures rigidly and leads the way out and down the hall to one of Marmoreal Palace’s cold bath chambers. The pool is empty, closed to the public this late, and dappled with light. Phainon stops them here, turning to face Mydei, cast in blue. “Is something wrong—?”

“Is she forcing you?” Mydei asks.

“What?”

“Lady Aglaea. Has she forced you into this?”

“I—” Phainon’s eyebrows furrow. “Huh?”

Mydei makes a frustrated sound. “You knelt in the rain for hours,” he says. “I know you don’t want this, and now you’re giving me courting gifts after dinner while she watches like a hawk. What changed?”

The confusion on Phainon’s face shifts into a frown. His gaze floats around Mydei’s face for a moment before it slips off him like water. “I apologize for that,” he says softly. When Mydei grunts, he adds, “Kneeling out there. Making a spectacle out of it. I was…” He sniffs, the tail end of a cold sounding with it. “Upset, at first. I didn’t think you would see it, I was just…”

Mydei sighs. “I need to know if you’re unwilling,” he says. “I can’t exchange your wishes for the fate of my people, but perhaps—”

“I’m not,” Phainon says. Again, “I’m not. Unwilling, that is. I was upset at first, but anyone would be. I’m not going to abandon an entire people just because I hoped I’d get the chance to marry for love.” He purses his lips and laughs a little. It’s bittersweet, that laugh. Mydei has never dreamed of marrying for love, but he gets it. The discomfort of being bound like this. Phainon will have to open his home, and Mydei will have to accept it as a cage.

“Aglaea is only advising me on how to conduct the courtship,” Phainon continues. “She gave me plenty of outs; I swear to you I wouldn’t be here if I was truly unwilling. That night in the rain was a tantrum, and I’m frankly mortified that you saw it. I’d ask you to forget about it, if possible.”

Mydei studies him for untruth. He doesn’t have the power of perception like Aglaea does, but Phainon has his heart on his sleeve. He meets Mydei’s gaze again, and he must mean this. And so, Mydei laughs. “Forget Okhema’s perfect vessel in the rain like a wet dog? Not a chance.”

“I’m going to excuse that,” Phainon says, raising his eyebrows and rocking on his heels, “because it’s nice to know that the person I’m bound to for the rest of my life cares, at least a little bit, about my wishes.”

Mydei folds his arms and stares at him, unimpressed.

“I meant it,” Phainon tells him, grinning. “I like you, Mydei. We could build quite the partnership out of this, as equals.”

“You’re far too certain that you’re my match.”

“And you’re far too stubborn in denying it.”

△

The return to Castrum Kremnos is anything but grand. Mydei is sure to keep it that way. He dresses to cover up the markings on his torso and slips through the city gates without procession or fanfare.

The streets are crowded with people, cacophonous with raised voices and chaos, and there are droplets of blood spilled on the ground in his path. This section of the city is one of many that haven’t yet fallen to rubble and eternal night. Many have been forced to relocate, but there’s little space and fewer resources to share. Castrum Kremnos has no shortage of fighters and few, if any, peacemakers.

He makes it to the palace and removes the cloak he’d been wearing. A shocked servant stumbles over himself to bow. “Your Highness,” he gets out, tripping over his tongue. “We. You—”

“Send for Krateros,” Mydei tells him. Faced with high walls and the sharp smell of crushed indigo stones, he finds himself bending under the weight of his exhaustion. This place is no home, but it’s the closest he has, and when the servant bows again and leaves, he finds his way to his chambers.

They’re kept carefully clean in his absence. Have been, even since before his original return, kept carefully by a handful of his mother’s trusted servants. Free from dust, the bed made with fresh sheets, clothing hanging neatly in the closet, armor and weaponry lining the walls, with a spot to sit and polish.

There’s a window stretching from floor to ceiling on one wall, the drapes pulled open to light the room. Mydei comes to it and is faced with the view of his ruined city. Much of it looks the same as it always has—neighborhoods lined with densely packed houses, grand architecture tipped with gold, wide market streets filled with people. Castrum Kremnos has never been happy the way Okhema seems to be, but Mydei’s memories have always painted it as strong and prosperous. There’s one that sticks out. Candied pomegranate and a rough hand in his hair belonging to a scarred, smiling woman.

He sighs. At the far edges of his city there are buildings reduced to dust, homes shrouded in darkness, roads patrolled by titankin. Day by day, they take more and more from his people.

From the pocket of his trousers, he tosses the gift from Phainon on top of one of his trunks. It lands without breaking and he backs into the bed to sit on crimson sheets, spine bowing forward, elbows resting on his knees. He wrestles the pauldron off his left shoulder and removes his gauntlets, letting them crash to the ground. He lets out a long, heavy exhale. It’s a bitter kind of nostalgia he’s overcome with. This place hasn’t been his home in a long time, and yet. His sleeve slips off and pools with the rest of the fabric at his waist and he just… breathes for a moment. Tries, shutting his eyes and rubbing his temples.

He’s interrupted by a knock on the door, quick and loud and frantic. “Your Highness Mydeimos,” comes Krateros’ urgent voice. Mydei huffs the closest to a laugh he can muster and opens his eyes to the hard floor and his own palms. His body aches as he stands. “You will open the door this instant or so help me, I will—”

Mydei pulls the door open. Krateros cuts off, mouth open, and then his expression shifts to something seething. “Where have you been? It’s been days, and we’ve been left without a leader! What was so important that you had to disappear without a moment’s notice? We are at war, in case you haven’t—”

“I was busy securing options,” Mydei says, biting the inside of his cheek and moving out of the doorway so Krateros can come inside.

“Options?” Krateros echoes, incredulous. He shuts the door behind himself, looking Mydei over. “Nikador’s Strife, you stink like cherry laurel, where were you?”

After an inhale, turning his back and retreating further into the room, Mydei answers, “Okhema.”

Krateros follows, still standing as Mydei settles into one of the armchairs amidst his armor collection. It smells like oil and polish over here, ever familiar but not quite comforting.  “You…” Krateros trails off, suddenly contemplative. 

Mydei hesitates, frowning, and then clears his throat to continue, settling into the chair with his legs wide and his cheek on his fist. “They’re willing to lend aid,” he says, “and their gates are open to our refugees.”

“Okhema,” Krateros says under his breath. He sits, finally, folding his hands in his lap and nodding slowly. “You’re thinking like a leader, Mydeimos, so when will you take the throne and make yourself one?”

“We’ve already discussed this,” Mydei says, straightening up.

“You know better than anyone that nothing good comes from trying to prevent a prophecy.”

Mydei stares coldly at him. Remembers, against his will, the rush of frigid water filling immortal lungs. The way it feels to die, over and over again. “The prophecy says I will guide Castrum Kremnos to its fall,” he growls.

“And yet you still lead them,” Krateros says. “A king in everything but name.”

“I tire of this.”

A sigh. “Fine then,” Krateros says, waving a hand. “Okhema then. What of their terms?”

“They ask for Nikador’s coreflame,” Mydei tells him.

“The authority of Strife is no small price to pay,” Krateros notes. He purses his lips and shakes his head, and Mydei remembers the last thing he has left of his mother. You can trust Krateros. He’s my chosen guardian.

“I have no want for it,” Mydei replies as evenly as he can. “They will take it for their flame-chase journey to rid the world of the black tide.”

“And you believe in them?”

“Krateros,” Mydei says. “It’s as simple as this: I do not care.”

Krateros studies him with a frown but does not press. “The coreflame, then,” he sighs. “Is that all they ask?”

And this part, Mydei thinks, will not go over well. “A marriage between their perfect vessel and myself to solidify our nations as allies,” he answers.

Krateros’ eyes flash. “What?”

“Peace, Krateros,” Mydei says. “I believe we may be an even match.” He thinks of the stalemate in the baths. Phainon’s eager expression when it comes to testing that theory properly. Even if they’re not, it’s clear that Phainon is a fine warrior. He carries himself like it, confident in his own ability, and anything he lacks, there’s still time to learn. Regardless of whether or not he’s actually Mydei’s match, he’ll be a strong ally. 

Mydei knew he would never marry for love. This is the best he can hope for. “I’m fine with it.”

“If you take the throne—”

“I won’t take the throne,” Mydei cuts him off. “You have no need to worry about me elevating an Okheman to king.”

Krateros leans forward on his elbows, holding Mydei’s gaze. He takes a deep, punctuated breath and shuts his eyes. “You’re free to do as you please,” he says, “but I wish you wouldn’t take on everything alone.”

“I trust you to watch the city,” Mydei says. “Saving the people is my responsibility.”

△

Days later, Mydei returns to the palace bloodstained and battered after an assault on the battlefield that has become Castrum Kremnos’ outer edges. His soldiers were heartened to see him on the front lines again after his absence. The battle went well, every titankin in sight crushed, but that piece of the city is only a small part of a very large problem. But Mydei can’t take on Nikador alone, and it feels good to do something.

When he pushes through the doors, hair messed, the hems of his robes tattered, gauntlets stained in dried blood, there’s a servant waiting for him. She clears her throat and bends at the waist. “Your Royal Highness,” she says stiffly.

“Rise,” Mydei tells her, and when she straightens, she holds out an envelope to him. It’s crisp, creamy white paper, and it bears Okhema’s seal.

“A letter has arrived from Okhema,” she says, “addressed to you.”

Mydei plucks it from her hands and turns it over. T o Be Delivered to Crown Prince Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos is written in careful penmanship, and it’s sealed with gold wax stamped with Kephale’s visage. Mydei has already left crusted blood on the paper just by taking it.

“Thank you,” he says, dismissing the servant, and trudges to his rooms for a bath.

Castrum Kremnos doesn’t have them like Okhema does. He has his own tub and a tap with hot, running water, but nothing blessed by Phagousa themself. As it fills up, Mydei pulls off his armor piece by piece, setting it on the table amidst its stand to be cleaned later. He does this himself as he does most things. His experience with luxury had been short lived, and now he’s unaccustomed to—and uncomfortable with—the thought of having servants for everything.

Washing his hands in a small basin and drying them, Mydei takes the letter again and uses the dagger he keeps hidden at his waist to open it. Inside are two sheets of smooth paper. It’s a letter from Phainon, though it’s only been a handful of days since Mydei returned to Castrum Kremnos. His handwriting is different from that on the envelope. Denser and somewhat loopy, his letters bleeding into each other. Mydei sits on the side of the bathtub and unfolds it to read.

Mydei,

I hope that isn’t an overly familiar way to address you in a letter, considering you told me to call you that yourself. Although, I suppose courtship is overly familiar by nature. If you’d rather use full titles and formality in our correspondence, feel free to say so.

I’m writing to you because you disappeared far sooner than expected and I thought you might want the news. The reception to our engagement has been nothing but positive since Aglaea announced it. The people are curious about you; you should have heard some of the things said at the procession. They have you painted as a beautiful, delicate maiden rather than one of Amphoreus’ strongest warriors. Only a handful have anything to say about the fact that you’re Kremnoan, which leads me to be optimistic about the future of our alliance. Hopefully Okhema can be the safe haven that your people need.

Briefly, Mydei pauses to check the temperature of the water. He dips his fingers in it and finds it near to scalding, just how he likes it. In goes a handful of salts, and as he stirs the water, he notes the soft glow of the string on his pinky finger. It only ever makes itself known when he wills it to or when he thinks of Phainon. It’s an unsettling, disconcerting thing, a thread from the Demigod of Romance.

“ Think of it as nothing more than a matchmaker’s whims,” Aglaea had told him as she tied it to him. “ You have my word that it can’t be used to harm or surveil you in any way.”

“Then why tie it at all?”

“If one day it turns gold, you will find it important,” is all Aglaea provided as an answer.

Now, it’s a soft, translucent silver, hardly there but for a soft warmth it radiates. It’ll fade if Phainon dies or is in particularly perilous danger, which, if nothing else, would be useful to know if need arises. Until then, Mydei supposes he can do nothing but wait to see if it’ll turn gold. He wipes his hand dry on his pants and returns to the letter.

When you return, we’ll have a short celebration here. Aglaea wants to set the wedding for the third day of the harvest month—rather soon, I’m aware, but sooner may be better with the fate of your people in mind. If you have a need for me in Kremnos, whether for some tradition preceding a marriage or anything else, don’t hesitate to send word. Until then, Aglaea and I are preparing everything here.

Unfortunately yours,

Phainon

Mydei turns off the tap. The water ripples, then stills. He flicks his gaze to the last line of the letter.

P.S. Hopefully my courtship hasn’t been terribly underwhelming. Aglaea advised me to send romantic poetry, so I’ve tried my hand. Do tell me if it’s to your liking.

Warily, Mydei turns to the second page in the envelope, shifting it in front of the first as he shuffles half out of his clothes to prepare for the bath.

Beautiful maiden or Undying warrior

I have yet to see

With you parted from me

I wait for your return so we can decide

A powerful soldier on the battlefield

Or a delicate bride

I am not one to gloat

But it will not be me again

With your knife at my throat

△

Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,

It pleases me to hear that your people are open to welcoming me and mine. I have released a decree sanctioning migration to Okhema for those who have lost their homes to Nikador and the titankin. Most are resistant at the moment, as mine are a stubborn people, but you may be able to expect an influx of refugees soon.

I approve of the wedding being at the start of the harvest month if that means Castrum Kremnos can be aided sooner. My army has kept the titankin at bay these past weeks, but Nikador themself has yet to show their face, and I anticipate a great deal of destruction when they grow restless. If wedding you sooner can put a stop to that, I’m willing to oblige.

I advise you to stay where you are for the time being. Bloodshed is custom to legitimize a wedding in Castrum Kremnos. Should you show your face, my people will demand you defeat my honor guard as well as any challenger that chooses to step forward to prove that you are worthy of my hand. There will be no celebrations or joyous processions.

I will return soon,

Crown Prince Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos

P.S. Poetry is not a talent of yours. I ask that you refrain in the future.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

I've been out of town and haven't played 3.1 yet so if anything seems weird with new lore, that's why.

Mydei,

As you’ve said nothing regarding how I can address you, I’m going to continue like this, even if you’ve chosen to be stiffly formal in your reply.

Okhema has made preparations for refugees already. With the Black Tide getting worse and worse, we’re prepared to provide sanctuary for as many as we possibly can. May Kephale’s light shine on anyone who lost their homes to Nikador’s insanity.

With the wedding rapidly approaching, I’d like the chance to meet your people as you’ve met mine. Aglaea and I both worry about the reception of our marriage in Castrum Kremnos if I’m to be completely absent during the duration of our courtship. I’m not against a contest between myself and any challengers if that’s what it takes to gain approval. Is there a preferable time for such a thing?

I await your reply,

Phainon

△

Nikador's blade stands above Castrum Kremnos like an executioner's axe. This is Phainon's first thought upon approaching the city on foot. Kremnos is a proud city, with resplendent gold towers and lit braziers lining the long path up to the gates. Behind these walls, Phainon knows there are homes wreathed in darkness and reduced to rubble, but at least from the outside, Castrum Kremnos stands strong.

These, he thinks as he arrives, are angry, fighting people. Each person he passes is solemn-faced and armed to the teeth, and they watch him in his blue and white coat like he doesn’t belong here. He knows he looks like an outsider. Everything from his hair to his clothing stands out. Regardless, he stands tall.

"Halt, traveler," says a woman in military dress at the gate. She wears her hair in a braid over her shoulder and wields a spear, which she tips diagonally to block his path. Her eyes—medium green—are cold. "State your name and purpose."

Phainon looks past her at the gate, and then around at the warriors adjusting armor and sharpening weapons. Their eyes land on him in turn. He's heard, in passing, that there have been groups challenging Nikador and their titankin. Men and women turning a disaster into a contest of strength. A chance to become heroes and save their homeland. So far, none have succeeded. He wonders how many lives have been lost. How many have fallen to Strife. How many will yet.

Now, he straightens up and pushes away the discomfort of uncertainty. "I am Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," he introduces himself. A murmur runs through the crowd. He lets silence stretch. He knows little of Castrum Kremnos, but when he thinks of Mydei, he guesses these people are best met with confidence and strength. “I come on account of my betrothal to your crown prince.”

"Prince consort to be," the woman in front says. She studies him, gaze falling to the sun on his throat, then back to his eyes. Finding no fear there, she dips into a small, reluctant bow. "You come out of respect for our rites?"

Bloodshed, as Mydei warned. Phainon knows little of Castrum Kremnos, but they value strength above all. Mydei warned him away, but they'll never accept Phainon if he doesn't meet them halfway. To form this bond, Kremnos needs to accept Phainon just as much as Okhema needs to accept Mydei. It would certainly have helped if Mydei had responded to his letter. He’ll have to ask after him once he enters the city. "I do," Phainon says.

Another ripple sweeps through the crowd. The ice in this woman's gaze eases. Slowly, she nods. "Can you prove to be his equal?" she asks. Medals adorn a cape at her shoulder, crimson and gold, Kremnos' colors. She must rank highly to wear them, to speak to him without care of insult.

Phainon keeps his back straight. "I can," he asserts.

After a moment, she gestures for the gates to be opened. “Very well,” she says, shifting her spear out of his path. “Welcome to Castrum Kremnos.”

△

Instead of being led to the palace for a chance to rest from the journey and speak to his husband to be, Phainon is brought to the very center of the city. A wide clearing is forcibly carved out by a group of soldiers, fringed by crowds and market stalls. The air is warm, and Phainon is expected to fight without repose. A hundred eyes watch as he peels off his coat, bundling it protectively around the courting gift tucked into one of the pockets.

“Will you fight unarmed, or would you prefer to duel with weapons?” The woman from the gates asks. Erynis, she introduces herself, a retired sergeant turned guard and recruitment officer. She prepared an assortment of weaponry. Spears, javelins, xiphos and longswords. Phainon has his greatsword, a dagger at his waist, and his own two hands.

“I will do whatever is custom among your people.”

At this, she laughs. “Custom would be a fight to the death, or near to it,” she says. “But we can not leave you for dead, would-be hero, or we would start a war.”

Phainon holds his ground, and his temper. Respect, he remembers Mydei saying, must be earned here. “Nor will I kill today.”

“‘Valorous death before glorious return…’” She scoffs. “Very well. Unarmed it is. Ptolemy is your first challenger.” She gestures at a tall man with cropped brown hair. His arms are folded across a broad chest, expression impassive, draped in a tan chiton tied with crimson. “Do you accept?”

Phainon removes his dagger and leaves it with his coat. “I do,” he says, shrugging his shoulders to warm them up. He worries, briefly, just what exactly he’s getting himself into.

“I hope you’re as strong as they say you are,” Ptolemy says, considering him as they step up to one another. Around them, the bystanders begin to chant something in the Kremnoan language. A cheer or a battle cry. Their tongue is sharp and clipped, and it sends Phainon’s blood rushing through him. “They call you a perfect vessel with a destiny of deliverance. Is it true?”

His hands flex, ankles rolling in his boots. He tests the ground beneath him, feeling the support of hard, textured stone. It’s hardly a good place for a casual spar, but this, he thinks, is anything but that. He takes a deep breath of the city—catching the scent of blood, indigo, and refuse—and says, “no man can claim to know the future in whole. I do not know my own destiny.”

“I see,” Ptolemy says. “You are flawed, then.”

Phainon smiles and shifts into a fighting stance. “What man is not?”

“This is true,” Ptolemy agrees, and throws a punch.

Phainon ducks under it, slipping smoothly into his combat training. The next he stops with a forearm, ducking in to aim a jab at Ptolemy’s ribs. He’s blocked with ease, so he aims a sharp kick to Ptolemy’s other side, this one connecting with a painful sound. Briefly, they part.

“You’re swifter than I expected,” Ptolemy notes, smoothing a hand over the injured spot before he raises his hands again.

Phainon shoves his hair back and falls into step as they circle each other. “It would be an insult and a lie to say your strength is a surprise.”

Ptolemy chuckles, closing back in. “After I win,” he says. “I will treat you to kykeon.”

“Arrogance gets good men killed,” Phainon warns, and strikes first. He aims for the throat, then swings with his knee when Ptolemy goes to block. The impact earns him a hiss, and then Ptolemy catches his leg and tries to use his momentum to throw him down. Phainon wrenches free and doesn’t waste a second, aiming a kick and grabbing Ptolemy’s wrist to guide him forward when he lunges. He doesn't stumble, just catches himself and elbows Phainon in the chest. The pain is sharp for a moment, but Phainon doesn’t have time to focus on it as Ptolemy aims a hit at his face.

He throws himself to the side, gaining space, finding his gaze sweeping unfamiliar faces in the crowd. They’re loud, these spectators. Cheering and taunting and watching him, assessing him. Deciding if he’s worth it. Phainon throws his next punches in quick succession, clipping Ptolemy in the jaw, then the clavicle. The impact of flesh rings out. The adrenaline floods him, blood roaring in his ears.

Ptolemy charges, and Phainon doesn’t manage to dodge. It only takes moments before he’s caught and taken to the ground, and then they’re trying to fight each other off. Phainon takes an arm to the throat before he manages to throw Ptolemy off, grunting as they roll. Then, with a carefully timed knee to the stomach, he manages to pin one arm behind Ptolemy’s back, wrenching it back until he’s forced to surrender.

Next, he fights a man named Georgious, then Herklas, then Leonidas. Phainon starts to tire, and then to ache as he collects hit after hit. First it’s his chest, then his ribs, his jaw, his tongue when he bites it taking a punch. Still, Phainon fights each challenger in turn, and when he comes out triumphant for the fourth time, the crowd affords him a cheer.

They don’t care who wins, Phainon notices. They only care for the spectacle or the thrill of the fight, but he knows it makes him less of an outsider, into someone they can root for. The way to this city’s heart is through its blood. Phainon sits on a stone half wall for a short rest when a hand holds out a chalice of red liquid to him.

“You’re bruised terribly,” an older man says. He’s outfitted in brown and red, as most of them are, built strongly with chestnut and silvering hair. He wears scars like medals and seems to be blind in one eye. He notices the trepidation in Phainon’s face as he stares at the cup, because he chuckles as says, “It’s pomegranate juice.”

“Oh,” Phainon says, and accepts it. His jaw protests as he speaks, likely bruised. He’d taken a hard hit from Leonidas, growing sloppy in his fatigue. Now, he’s allowed a rest, but the challenges will resume in time. “Thank you.” He spares a glance around the crowd and finds, still, nothing.

“You’re welcome,” the man says. “Where are your servants?”

“I came alone.”

He hums, considering this, and then turns to lean on the wall at Phainon’s side. “You’re like him then. Too independent and impulsive for your own good.”

Careful, Phainon studies him. The weather in his face. The slight, tired fondness. He stares into the pomegranate juice. “You know him well, then?”

“Mydeimos?” A chuckle. “Better than most.”

“And you are?”

“Krateros,” the man answers. “His teacher. Guardian, perhaps. Or perhaps not; he wouldn’t like me to call it that.” He gestures at the cup expectantly, so Phainon raises it, carefully scenting it before he takes a sip. It’s a bit sour, but mostly sweet, stinging the sore on his tongue. Krateros smiles. “He’ll be livid when he finds out you’re here.”

“I wrote.” Phainon pushes up his sleeves and again searches for strawberry blond hair or a red painted chest. Those colors don’t stand out in this crowd, but even after a careful search, Phainon comes up empty. “Where is he?”

“In the bath,” Krateros answers. “Probably will be for a while.”

Phainon hums, prodding around his jaw. It’s hot, swollen, and sore to the touch.

“You’ll want something cold for that.”

“Yes,” Phainon agrees. “But I still have business here.”

Krateros straightens up and smooths out his clothes. “You’ll be here for a hundred days and nights if you try to take on every challenger that wants you to prove you’ve earned his hand. My advice: fight someone more important.” And then he strolls away, leaving Phainon to lick his wounds. Phainon stares after him, then down at his wobbling reflection in the juice. He sets the chalice aside.

“Wait,” he calls, standing and jogging after Krateros, who halts and turns with something almost like a smile in his expression. “Someone more important,” Phainon says, gaze flicking between his eyes. “His teacher. You.”

“You exaggerate my importance,” Krateros says, falsely modest.

“Will you do it?”

“Should I consider that a challenge?”

Phainon takes a breath. “Yes,” he says.

Krateros guffaws. “Then I accept,” he proclaims.

Erynis steps between them. “A challenge has been issued,” she announces to the watching crowd. “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae to Krateros of the Golden Brigade elite.”

Murmurs. This, more than anything so far, has the crowd excited. He looks at Krateros—half a head shorter but no less muscled, carrying himself with the confidence of a long practiced warrior—and feels a flutter of nerves. Still, he stands his ground. Krateros unclips his sash and tosses it, a flash of red, and the crowd cheers. Phainon follows him into the middle of the clearing, and then they start chanting, louder than before, that same Kremnoan battle cry.

“‘Courage, honor, reason, tenacity, sacrifice,’” Krateros translates. “They speak of Nikador’s virtues.”

Lips pursed, Phainon nods. Nikador. Still their god and their idol, even as they descend into madness and turn homes to dust. A hundred voices speak in time as a bead of sweat drips down the back of his neck. This, he thinks, is the one that matters, the one that will secure his place as someone worthy of their crown prince's hand. Phainon takes a deep, deep breath.

"A friendly match, " Krateros says.

"I hope that doesn't mean you'll take it easy on me," Phainon says, shifting on his feet. Slow, they walk a circle together. The crowd backs up a handful of steps, still chanting. The sun beats down, and Phainon's jaw still aches.

"I'm an old man past his prime," Krateros says.

"They seem to think you're one of their best," Phainon tells him, gesturing vaguely.

"They respect me," Krateros agrees, settling into a fighting stance. "But perhaps they're rooting for you as well." Erynis stands between them, lifting a hand for the crowd to quiet. They do, silence stretching, every eye trained to the two of them. "Mydeimos could use a strong partner at his side. They want that from you. Don't assume they're thinking the worst."

"I don't come from here," Phainon points out.

"Kremnos doesn't care for foreigners, true," Krateros concedes, "but strength recognizes strength. Prove your worth and they will sing your praises to the sky."

Castrum Kremnos has a reputation for bloodlust, barbarism, and a lack of care for human life. Krateros speaks of them as if they just want someone to root for. As if the hardness and anger in them comes purely from care. Parents toward their children, friends and lovers toward each other. At the heart of it, perhaps these people just want someone to show them that their fight to survive is worth it after all the pain. Phainon exhales. "If possible," he says, "I will be what these people need."

"Earnest lad," Krateros says, nodding. "Show me what you can do."

The first strike is his, a quick lunge that ends with his' fist in Phainon's side. It's unexpected; Phainon hisses through his teeth as he jumps back and raises his guard. Krateros presses his advantage, one arm swinging into a hook that Phainon blocks with his forearm. They trade hits back and forth, each swapping between offence and defense.

There’s cheering when Krateros lands a hit. More when Phainon does. As the fight stretches, it seems the audience hasn’t taken sides. That, or they’re caught up in the thrill of a good battle.

Phainon slips into Krateros’ space just swift enough to catch him off guard, snatching a wrist in one hand and using the other to push the back of his head down. His knee comes up for a strike just as Krateros uses the momentum to headbutt him in the stomach. They both groan and tumble, rolling as each tries to pin the other down and fails. Krateros gets his wrist free and manages to get a forearm around Phainon’s neck before he’s thrown off. Phainon tries to wrench Krateros’ arms behind his back before he’s twisted and forced to let go or be crushed into the stone.

They catch their breath briefly. Phainon wets his lips before he takes another shot, punching and kicking and scrambling in the dust. He takes an elbow to the face that splits his top lip and has his nose unbroken but bleeding, and he’s fairly certain his shirt tears, but he fights with everything he has, with everything he knows he owes these people, and at the end of it, he comes out on top, pinning Krateros with his body weight and pulling one arm and shoulder back to immobilize him.

A deep voice speaks from within the crowd. “You have some nerve coming here, Deliverer.”

Beneath him, Krateros mutters something in the Kremnoan language. “I yield,” he wheezes, so Phainon releases him. They’re both covered in dust and sweat, and when Phainon rises, he offers the other man a hand. He takes it, and they turn, not quite chastened, toward where the sea of people parts for a man patterned in red. Blood drips down Phainon’s chin and stains his clothing. He’s certain he makes quite an image.

“Son of Gorgo,” Krateros greets him, lowering his head as he bows deeply. Around them, the circle of Kremnoans bends too.

Phainon wipes his mouth with the back of his hand, likely only making a mess of himself, and says, “I’ve come to respect the rites of your people.”

“You’ve come to make a fool of yourself,” Mydei corrects him, coming closer. He wears his robe open on one side, displaying his marked chest and smooth contours of muscle. “And you, teacher, are no better. I have sanctioned no contests between the people and my betrothed.”

The crowd is eerily silent, every face tipped down. The command Mydei holds, even without a formal seat on the throne, is palpable.

“I challenged him,” Phainon says, pulling one sleeve down to hold it to his nose. He swallows the blood in his mouth, the metallic taste clinging to his tongue.

Mydei crosses his arms. “I’m sure,” he says, eyes narrowing. He lifts a hand toward the crowd and orders, “Disperse.”

A moment passes, then two, and then the people reluctantly obey.

“You’re bleeding,” Mydei says, and turns his back. “Let’s go.” He leaves without waiting for a response. Phainon curses and tries to wipe the blood on his pants so it wont get on his coat as he gathers it off the floor, hiding his dagger back at his waist and throwing his greatsword onto his back.

“Kephale’s light,” he pants, jogging to catch up, a fresh line of blood slipping down his chin as he has to remove his hand from his face. “You act like it’ll kill you to wait a little.”

“I’m not the one gushing blood out the nose, now am I?”

Phainon slows when he comes close enough to catch Mydei by the elbow, which he does with his cleanest hand. “Wait, Mydei.”

Mydei stops. An amber gaze hands on Phainon’s hand—the one with the translucent string, now manifest.

“Are you truly upset?” Phainon asks.

After a moment, Mydei looks back at his eyes. “Why are you here?”

“You never wrote back,” Phainon says, licking the blood from his lips just for more to replace it. “I intended to come speak to you, but was swept up in this. Regardless, it doesn’t make sense to ignore your traditions, not if anyone here is going to take this— me —seriously. I—” Again, he tries to clean up the blood as it dribbles into his mouth, but his sleeve is already soaked.

“Strife,” Mydei curses, he makes a deeply unhappy noise in his throat and digs in his pocket. “Would you just—” He pulls out a handkerchief—the third Phainon has had to borrow in the span of a few weeks—and shoves it into Phainon’s hand.

It’s creamy white and embroidered with the Lance of Fury, and Phainon can only stare for a moment.

“You’re getting blood everywhere,” Mydei admonishes. His gauntleted hand grips Phainon’s wrist, pushing his hand up to his face. “Use it, damn you.”

His gauntlet is warm with body heat. Phainon presses the handkerchief to his nose and lets out a laugh. "Thank you," he says, "sorry." As the adrenaline slows down, all of his aches return with a vengeance. His jaw throbs, and he can feel his heartbeat in his nose. His clothes are a terrible mess, and this, the absurdity of it all, has him grinning hard enough for a fresh stab of agony to run through the tear in his lip.

"I can't decide if you're foolishly brave or bravely foolish," Mydei says, and it sounds halfway like a praise and halfway like an insult. He releases Phainon and turns again, storming in the direction of the palace. Eyes follow them the entire way, but no one dares to speak or interrupt them.

"A fool feels no fear," Phainon says, nearly stumbling to catch up on weary legs, "and thus can't show courage."

"That had best not be the beginning of another poem," Mydei says. His expression is as hard as his voice, but there's something about him that gives Phainon the impression that he isn't as gruff as he seems. It makes him laugh again, cut short for the pain.

"No," he says, "certainly not. That's just... something someone I once knew used to say."

Finally, Mydei slows to a reasonable pace. "A fool feels fear," he says, "they just fear the wrong things."

They're about the same height, Phainon notices. Neither has to look up or down to meet the other’s eyes. He pulls the handkerchief back to find that the bleeding has stopped. He uses a clean edge and wipes up what he can as they walk. "Maybe," he considers, trying to sniff and finding his nostrils horribly clogged. "So what does that make me?"

"That depends on what you're afraid of."

They pause briefly at the doors of the palace as they open. Mydei steps aside for him to enter first, an odd gesture based on what little Phainon knows about him. But there it is again, the sense that he's not quite what he makes himself out to be. Something a little warmer. The bloodlust of an army but the compassion of a man.

"A lot of things," Phainon says. "Whether or not they're the right ones, I don't know."

Mydei nods and resumes leading the way. "It takes courage to admit fear," he says as they walk down a hallway with high ceilings and warm lighting.

"A compliment?" Phainon asks. "From you?" Mydei gives him a dry look. Phainon laughs, lip stinging. He tongues at the cut and dabs it lightly with the handkerchief, turning the fabric over and eyeing all the bloodstains. "I'll wash this," he says, a bit awkwardly as he tucks it away in his pocket. "The blood should come out."

"Keep it," Mydei tells him, not bothering to look. He stops at the doorway and pulls it open, again stepping aside for Phainon to go first.

"A token of your love?"

Another dry, unimpressed look. "Yes," Mydei says, and follows him in.

This room is something like an infirmary, though it's much smaller and more private than the ones Phainon is used to. This is quiet, with a single padded bench and a counter with a wash basin and boxes of supplies. Phainon sits on the bench, draping his coat over the far edge as Mydei wets a cloth.

“Patching me up, husband-to-be?” Phainon asks as he comes closer, excess water dripping from his fingers as he brandishes the cloth like a weapon. Mydei grimaces as he makes himself still and pliant, the perfect patient, and then the cloth connects with his face, frigid and wet and jarring.

“Do it yourself,” Mydei says disdainfully, turning his back. “I’ll get a change of clothes.”

Phainon catches the cloth from where it fell to his lap, eyeing the blood spilled down his front. “Thank you,” he says, the corners of his mouth twitching. Mydei shuts the door behind him.

When he’s gone, Phainon lets loose a deep sigh and undoes his shirt, letting it fall to the floor. His eyes fall shut. He breathes, once, twice. Forces himself to straighten up.

There isn’t a mirror here that he can see, so he picks a spot and starts cleaning himself up from there. His chest, throat, chin. He’s careful as he wipes down his face, attempting again to breathe through his nose. The clot stays firmly in place, so he blows lightly, then a little stronger, clearing up an airway. He takes three triumphant breaths, and then starts bleeding again.

“Titans above,” he curses, pressing the cloth to his nose. It stops quicker the second time around, for which he’s grateful. Mydei comes back just as he’s cleaning up the last of it, mouth breathing for fear of setting it off again. He tosses a tunic at Phainon, blood red with a deep vee in the front. “Your colors,” Phainon observes.

“You’re in my homeland. My colors are to be expected.”

“I know,” Phainon concedes, pulling it on. “I know, I just don’t look very good in red.” Mydei turns and looks him up and down, gaze holding weight like hands, though he doesn’t speak. He lingers somewhere around Phainon’s throat and then turns, wetting a fresh cloth before he steps forward.

“You missed a spot.”

Phainon holds a hand out. “Where?” he asks. “I’ll get it.”

Mydei says nothing, just sighs and steps closer. He reaches for Phainon’s neck, but his hand is stopped along the way by Phainon’s around his wrist. Surprise flashes briefly in his expression, but he doesn’t pull away.

“What are you doing?” Phainon asks, voice low. His pulse jumps. He’s still in fighting mode, though he doesn’t need to be.

“Helping,” Mydei says, drawing back. “Unless you’d rather I didn’t.”

Phainon clears his throat, embarrassed, letting go. “It’s here, then?” he asks, tipping his head back. Mydei looks at him for a moment before he accepts this for the permission that it is. With a kind of care that doesn’t seem common from him, he slips one armored finger beneath the choker around Phainon’s neck.

“Here,” he says, keeping the sharp parts of his gauntlet from touching skin. With his other hand, he wipes blood from the space beneath the leather, then the choker itself. He’s exceedingly careful, and when Phainon swallows, his adam's apple brushes armored fingers. It tickles, and he’s torn between a nervous laugh and a full body shudder.

“Why did you come, Deliverer?” Mydei asks, wiping a final spot above Phainon’s clavicle before he steps back. The damp spots left by the cloth chill in the air, and Phainon fights the urge to rub at them.

“I already told you,” he says. “I didn’t mean to get caught up in that.”

Mydei looks unimpressed. “And yet.” 

Phainon sighs. “I’ll admit, I wanted to prove my worth to them,” he starts. “If we’re to be wed, it should be by the standards of both our nations, not just mine.”

“There’s no glory to be found in an accolade only obtainable through bloodshed,” Mydei tells him. “I am not a bride to be won. The only person you must prove your worth to is me.”

“But your traditions—”

“Will be honored,” Mydei interrupts him. “The people are overeager. Gorgo fought Eurypon and no one else. Hold your own against me, and that will be enough.” His expression offers little, but Phainon gets the sense that Mydei means this very deeply. Compassion, more than bloodlust. Curious.

“Why didn’t you write back?” Phainon asks.

“I’ve been on the front lines,” Mydei says, raising an eyebrow. “You’d have received a reply sooner or later, if you’d been patient enough to wait.”

“Has my coming here upset you?”

“No,” Mydei says, but he collects the rags and turns toward the counter so Phainon can’t see his face.

“And yet,” Phainon echoes. The silence stretches between them. “Were you…” He hesitates. “...Worried?”

“About the man who turned a knife on me in the bath?” Mydei scoffs. “Hardly. It’s simply…” More silence. Mydei’s shoulders tense before he sets himself to digging through a container of medicines.

“Simply…?” Phainon prompts. After a moment, he stands, coming to Mydei’s side. All he catches is the hint of a red ear before a jar of ointment is shoved into his chest. He startles, catching it.

“Humiliating,” Mydei answers, turning on him. “You embarrass me in front of my people, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

He stares. The red in Mydei’s face. The scowl. The way his eyes flick from one place to another but don’t ever meet Phainon’s. He’s…

“Oh,” Phainon says. “I’m sorry.” A laugh startles out of him. “Seriously, I—”

“Cease,” Mydei orders, scowling harder. Phainon does not. Mydei grits his teeth and gestures at the jar in Phainon’s hand. “Put that on your lip. Or don’t. I’m leaving.”

“Wait!” Phainon laughs. He presses his lips together to stop it, but a smile still creeps around the edges, even through the pain. “Wait,” he says again. “I’m sorry, I really am.”

“Somehow I doubt that.”

Finally, Phainon is able to smooth his face into something sincere. “I mean it,” he promises, turning to face Mydei fully. “I’m sorry.”

“Fine,” Mydei says.

“Fine,” Phainon echoes. They look at each other, Mydei still frowning, and there’s a sudden knot in Phainon’s stomach. This is unprecedented between them. He’s afraid he’s made a horrible mess of things. Swallowing, Phainon admits, “I fear that you must dislike me.”

A pause.

“Then I think you’re a fool,” Mydei answers.

“I—” Phainon pauses. “Oh.”

Chapter Notes

throwing canon to the wind from here on out. also,,, sorry for breaking the exactly 5k streak :(

A servant gets guest quarters ready for Phainon. He cleans up alright, despite the bruise blooming on his jaw and the cut on his lip. Red, as he told Mydei, does not look good on him, clashing with the color of his hair and his eyes. But he tucks the red shirt into his trousers, open part way down his chest and outlining the width of his shoulders, and it doesn't look terrible on him either. Mydei notes this but takes care not to linger on the thought.

Later, when the quarters are ready, Mydei offers to walk Phainon, though he wants to do anything but that. He could have a servant do it, but a part of him cringes at the thought of Phainon interacting with his people more than he has. Irrational, he knows. Phainon will have to speak to many Kremnoans during his stay, more once they're married, but right now Mydei just wants him tucked away to deal with later.

"Ever the gentleman," Phainon says, folding his coat over his arm. Mydei scoffs and opens the door, holding it open for Phainon to walk through first. As Phainon passes him, he raises a brow, pointed, and Mydei realizes what he's done. Heat rises to his face. He clears his throat and starts leading the way.

The palace has wide hallways and tall ceilings, lit by fire and smelling faintly metallic. It isn't beautiful in the way Okhema is, isn't warm and welcoming. Mydei wonders what Phainon must make of it. He doesn't comment much, not on the place itself, not on the people, not on anything at all. From someone as seemingly open as Phainon, it makes Mydei itch. They walk in silence uncharacteristic for them, and things keep replaying in Mydei's head.

Oh, in Phainon's voice. Over and over. The look on his face. Mydei isn't sure if he got it, and he doesn't know if he wants him to. The sight of him, holding his own against Krateros, brow furrowed, blood smeared across his face. For a too long moment, he's imprinted on the backs of Mydei's eyelids.

"You'll want to see the state of the city," Mydei notes.

"Yes," Phainon says. "Whenever it’s convenient. The battlefield too."

"Tomorrow," Mydei says, and leaves it at that. They pause at the door to the housing wing of the palace, and this time, Mydei goes first. Behind him, Phainon huffs a laugh.

So when will we have that spar?" he asks, catching up. Their shoulders brush, fabric against skin. Goose flesh prickles up Mydei's arm. "Sounds like tomorrow will be too busy."

His jaw is purple and he can hardly smile for the way his lip is cut. Mydei shoots him a look. "How many of my men did you just fight?" he asks. "And you're already eager for another spar?"

“Against you?" Phainon grins, blood welling on his mouth before he licks it away. "Yes."

"It's the adrenaline talking," Mydei tells him, coming to a stop at the prepared guest room. He pushes the door open and stands aside for Phainon to enter. "Your body isn't immortal; you'll be aching soon enough."

"I heal fast," Phainon says, peeking inside. He surveys the room: the seating area, the wide window along one wall, the bed made with cream colored sheets and red blankets. He takes a breath, smelling the faint odor of indigo that lingers everywhere in Castrum Kremnos, and turns back to Mydei. “Besides, if a warrior can’t fight sore, perhaps he shouldn’t be on the battlefield at all.”

“A fool,” Mydei mutters. Phainon studies him.

“I’m not a hundred percent sure what you meant by it when you said that earlier,” he says, soft and contemplating, and this strange, uncomfortable jolt thrills through Mydei. Silence stretches, then he steps back, out of the entryway so the door is free to shut between them. For now, Phainon holds it in place.

“It’s nothing to concern yourself with,” Mydei says. “Goodnight, Deliverer.”

△

The next day, Phainon’s bruise has worsened significantly in color. Still, he’s in bright spirits. The have breakfast, during which Phainon teases Mydei unnecessarily for taking milk in his pomegranate juice, and then Mydei takes him to the highest part of one of the palace towers, a room with broad windows that overlook the entire city.

“We can walk the streets,” Mydei says, standing next to Phainon in front of the glass. “But this is the best place to see it all.”

“Titans above,” Phainon breathes. He’s looking, most certainly, at the places shrouded in eternal night, at the way the destruction is visible at the edges of the city even from so far away.

“We’ve lost six percent of the city,” Mydei says, voice a knife’s edge, “Projected to become seven percent in the next week. The attacks are worsening in size and frequency. The people are angry and scared, and I struggle to console them.”

For a long moment, Phainon is silent, just staring at the city. The untouched sections are grand and laudable—the indigo quarries and the main streets, the markets and gilded buildings. This is a city worthy of pride, and there is something in Mydei that trembles like a child at the thought that he might be the thing that lets it fall to ruin.

“Mydei,” Phainon finally says. He turns, solemn-faced, and asks, “How did King Eurypon die?”

The whisper of silence. “He had gone mad,” Mydei answers. There is a saying among his people. The kingslayer be king. “I ended his life with my own hand.” Prophecy come true. Patricide succeeding patricide. A mother’s voice: he will be the one to end the cycle. Blood on his hands. A spear in a concave chest. The feeling of failure, even after a necessary job done right. The son of Gorgo will be crowned in blood.

Slowly, Phainon nods. He doesn’t ask questions, whether out of respect or horror, Mydei doesn’t know. “I’ll see the battlefield now,” is all he says, “if you’d be so kind as to take me.”

“Very well,” Mydei says, trying to shake the curdling feeling that sticks in his chest.

△

Along the way, Mydei shows Phainon the markets, the quarries, the neighborhoods. He buys candied pomegranate to eat as they walk. They get gawked at, more than a little bit, but it seems that both of them are adept at not caring about this sort of thing. Slowly, the streets grow less and less populated, the sky darker and darker. There’s something strangely cold about these parts of Castrum Kremnos. Eerily silent, but for the sounds of their footsteps.

“You’ll hear Nikador’s war cries the further in you go,” Mydei says. “It’s best we steer clear to avoid getting caught in their bloodlust.”

“They fight?”

“No,” Mydei answers, stepping over a cracked, fallen pillar. “But their voice makes it difficult to control oneself.” He stops, the remains of a temple toppled before him. In front of him, there’s a distinct line in the dust where the world goes from light to dark. “Here,” he says, grabbing Phainon by the elbow. Together, they take a handful of steps forward, crossing into the darkness. “Listen.”

Faintly, a chant rings in his ears. Even so quietly, it stirs something in his blood. A desire for action, and itch to fight. This feeling—this thrill—has been both a help to him and a horror in battles these last several weeks. It’s so easy to tear things limb from limb under its influence. It makes him worry that there could come a point when killing titankin isn't enough.

“This feeling,” Phainon breathes. 

“Dangerous,” Mydei tells him. “The soldiers lose themselves. At times, I nearly do too.” Wasting no time, they draw back into the light, Nikador’s voice fading out. Mydei takes a breath to settle his spirit.

“Do they fight each other?”

“Not yet,” Mydei answers. “I hope it never comes to that.”

△

The rest of the day is spent with diplomatic blather. Mydei’s councilmen, joined by Krateros, sweep the two of them up for a discussion. A clear cut outline of Okhema’s plans to aid them, details on the wedding, and an overly thorough briefing on, well, everything about Castrum Kremnos’ situation later, Mydei is finally free to retire for the night, exhausted in this heavy, bone deep kind of way.

He’s stopped caring so much what Phainon does. He’s free to embarrass himself as much as he likes, considering he’s already, unfortunately, won a good portion of Kremnos over. Mydei may have to face some humiliation upon becoming his spouse, but he’s decided enduring that is preferable to policing his every move. So as soon as he finds an opening, he stands and unceremoniously leaves the meeting room. No one so much as calls after him, until, moments later, the sound of footsteps chases him down the hall.

“You’re just leaving?” Phainon asks, slowing to a walk at his side. He walks too closely, too familiarly, as he always does. Mydei can almost taste the olive oil and pine resin scent of him. It must cling to his coat, because he’d smelled of nothing but sweat when he’d been dressed in Kremnos’ reds the day before.

“We had nothing left to discuss,” Mydei says tersely. It makes Phainon frown, a small, petulant thing.

“And you didn’t even consider walking your dear husband-to-be to his quarters?”

This earns him an eyebrow raise. “Is your sense of direction so terrible that you need me to?”

Phainon huffs, partway in jest. “It wouldn’t kill you to be kinder,” he points out.

“There is no word for kindness in the Kremnoan language.”

“Funny,” Phainon says, letting their shoulders brush before Mydei takes a pointed step to the left. “You know what they say about your people?” Phainon continues. “That you have no word for love in your language either, but that can hardly be true.” Mydei remains silent. They pause at a doorway, and as they wait for it to open, Phainon turns to him. “Look, would you come with me? I won’t take more than a minute or two of your time.”

Mydei narrows his eyes. “What need do you have of it?”

“Have I upset you?” Phainon asks, very earnestly, and it’s— Mydei grits his teeth, nauseous at the thought of making him worry he’s done something wrong. Moreso, at the thought of offering a reassuring word.

“Fine,” he says, and waits—before he realizes what he’s doing—for Phainon to pass through the doorway first. “Your chambers are this way,” he adds, catching up and gesturing to the left.

Phainon chuckles lightly. “Yes, I know,” he says. “I can find my way perfectly well; I just… have something for you that I forgot yesterday, and I thought now would be a good time. Unless you’d really rather retire already. I won’t blame you if you do.”

“Let’s get this over with,” is all Mydei offers as a reply.

“Don’t sound too excited now,” Phainon laughs.

When they reach his door, Phainon pushes it open and pauses. “Would you like to come in?” he offers. There’s a table and chairs, as well as a balcony looking out at the city, but he doesn’t have a proper sitting chamber, only the one room and attached bath. Mydei wasn’t raised in the court but even he knows better than to accept.

“That wouldn’t be appropriate,” he says, and holds his ground in the hallway. He watches Phainon’s lip quirk, the horrible, soft thing it does to his face before he steps the rest of the way inside and lets the door shut briefly between them.

He’s only gone for a matter of moments before he returns, stepping back into the hallway with something wrapped in shiny blue cloth and tied with gold thread. It’s small, about the length of his palm and half as wide, and he holds it out with both hands. "This is for you," he says, smoothing a fold in the fabric.

"Another courting gift," Mydei observes, though he’d figured it couldn’t be anything else when Phainon said he had something for him. Something complicated twists in his stomach—discomfort at this or the obligation to give something back. He reaches out and accepts the bundle, loosening the strings with an armored finger. "You'll have to wait as I prepare something suitable to give back."

"What?" Phainon blinks. "Oh, no, you don't have to. It’s— Gifts are Okheman tradition, I don’t expect you to participate. Court me the Kremnoan way.”

“I hardly think Lady Aglaea and the Council of Elders would take kindly to me dueling half your city,” Mydei says dryly. The knot comes undone, so he pulls the strings free. Phainon laughs, a little awkwardly, folding his arms and watching as Mydei unwraps the gift.

Inside the silky fabric is a comb, ivory carved in the shape of the Lance of Fury, neatly and expertly done. It’s a beautiful gift, expensive too, and there’s an odd sensation that goes from Mydei’s spine to the tips of his fingers as he lays eyes on it, because this gift, though coming from an Okheman, is deeply Kremnoan.

Phainon watches as he turns it over. The detailing is fine and delicate, identical on both sides. "I had it made by one of the best carvers in Okhema," Phainon says. "Hopefully it isn't— Well, considering the situation, maybe the Lance of Fury was a bit— And I'm sure you already have a comb, but—"

"Sometimes I wonder," Mydei interrupts him, tracing each even prong, "whether you're clueless about Kremnoan tradition, or if you know more than you let on."

"Clueless," Phainon answers, embarrassingly breathy. "I attempted to research, but there are very few translations from the Kremnoan language into the common one, and Ohkema's histories are biased against your people. It's... well. As I mentioned earlier, they say there isn't even a word for love in your language, which can hardly be true, you’re people aren’t—"

"It is," Mydei says. At Phainon's blank expression, he adds, "True. We don't have a word for love. Our courting rituals are based on proving strength more than affection."

"Oh," Phainon says. He backs himself into the door, leaning against it, seeming to sense a conversation. So much for only taking a minute or two of Mydei’s time. Firelight from the sconces on the walls dances on his face, and the ceiling is far too tall for just the two of them. "I hope... a comb doesn't signify anything offensive, does it?"

Laughable, the earnest concern on his face. "Offensive, no," Mydei answers. A smile pulls at his mouth, despite the exhaustion of the day and the ache beginning to pound at his temples. "Just terribly presumptuous."

Phainon cocks his head, looking no less concerned. "Pardon?" he says. "Presumptuous?"

“You'll notice that many of my best officers have long hair," Mydei says. Slowly, Phainon nods. "It's a hindrance in a fight, so only the best warriors are allowed to wear long hair to battle. To a Kremnoan, hair is a status symbol and very personal. Only close family and partners are allowed to touch it, and traditionally, in gifting a comb, you ask for permission.”

He sees Phainon’s attention turn toward his hair, the reddened ends of it, the braid behind his right ear. He brings a hand to his mouth and looks, somewhat sheepish, at the comb still in Mydei’s hands. It’s a beautiful thing, really. The closest he could possibly come to a traditional Kremnoan courting gift, and yet he stumbled upon it entirely by accident. That titans-damned string on Mydei’s finger thrums with warmth.

“That’s…” He watches Phainon fumble for the right words. “That wasn’t my intention,” he says, “I apologize if I’ve made you uncomfortable. I should have gone more in depth in my research.”

“Hardly,” Mydei says. “I know just as little of Okhema’s traditions. Even less of… Aedes Elysiae’s.”

“Then you’re not offended?”

“No,” Mydei assures him, and watches as something almost like a smile drift onto his face.

“Then I must say that that’s a terribly romantic tradition,” Phainon says, smiling fully into his fist as he watches Mydei handle the comb delicately, turning it over once more before he rewraps it in the blue cloth to protect it until he finds a suitable place for it.

“I remind you we have no word for romance,” Mydei corrects him.

“And yet,” Phainon says, lowering his hand and pushing himself away from the door to stand up straight. “Is there anything else I should know about your traditions before we wed?”

Mydei purses his lips into a thin line. They will have an Okheman wedding, he knows. Something with a grand ceremony and feasts and dancing. Kremnoan weddings come with little fanfare, but, perhaps…

He swallows, this odd nervousness filling his belly. Another thing he doesn’t have a Kremnoan word for. The warmth around his finger threatens to distract him. He clears his throat. “You’ll have to learn to braid, if you don’t know how already,” he says.

Phainon’s eyes are ice blue but horribly warm as his expression changes. “Braid?”

“Yes.” Mydei watches the shadows the sconces paint on the walls rather than look at him. “It’s a tradition,” he says, flicking the braid behind his ear. There’s an odd inhale. He glances at Phainon, finding him looking mildly constipated. Mydei frowns. “What?”

“Nothing,” Phainon says weirdly. “Nothing at all.” He swallows. “I’ll learn to braid before the wedding.”

“...Very well.” Mydei pockets the wrapped comb and crosses his arms. Stiffly, “Thank you for the gift. I will… take my leave.”

“Of course,” Phainon says, exhaling. “Then… Goodnight, Mydei.”

“Goodnight,” Mydei echoes. He turns and takes a handful of steps before something possesses him to pause. When he does, he catches Phainon with his eyes squeezed shut and a palm to his forehead in shame. Curiously, it makes the corners of his mouth tick up.
