It's no surprise that Castrum Kremnos has a proper arena. It's a massive, circular thing, with terraced seating for an audience thousands strong. The entire thing is paved in stone, railings along the steps, the ground worn and dusty. Grand braziers are lit in a half circle around the seating, and Phainon stands at the bottom, watching the seats fill up with so many people it feels like they blot out the sun. He smells dirt and sweat, hears the chorus of hundreds of voices, and feels, for the first real time, nauseous with anticipation for a fight.

To have something to do with himself, he goes through a thorough warm up. Static and dynamic stretches, sword forms. He shrugs out of his coat when he gets too hot. A deep breath, and the din quiets. On the other side of the arena, Mydei steps out, his strides long and purposeful. He stops in the center, all these eyes on him but his attention on no one but Phainon. "Are you ready, Deliverer?" he asks, a gust whipping the fabric of his robe around his armored legs. Dust stirs at his feet.

Phainon steps up, his sword steady and solid in his hands. A breath in, then out. "I've been ready for weeks, Your Highness," he says, standing tall, forcing himself to smile.

"Kremnos!" Mydei raises his voice, strong and commanding. His next words are in the Kremnoan language, clipped and rough on his tongue as he turns in a slow circle to address each side of the audience in turn. Quieter, turning to Phainon, he translates, "You witness a contest," he says, "between myself and a would be suitor."

"Would be," Phainon laughs, "as if this isn't mostly your doing."

Mydei's eyes narrow as he raises his voice again, addressing the crowd but holding Phainon’s gaze. "He hawks himself as one of Okhema's greatest warriors," he continues, "and has come to prove his might."

A chant or a cheer resounds from the crowd. Five words, spoken in time, each punctuated with a hard stomp on the stone. Courage, honor, reason, tenacity, sacrifice. Nikador's virtues. The silence echoes when they finish. Phainon gets chills.

"No pressure," he mutters to himself. Mydei smiles a terrible, feral smile. He delivers a final line in Kremnoan, raising his fist, and there's another cheer. When he lowers it, all goes silent, hundreds of eyes trained to them, hundreds of breaths held. No more than a handful of moments pass, and then Mydei lunges at him. He's swift, unarmed but for his gauntlets, but every bit of him is filled with lethal power. Phainon blocks him with the flat of his sword, the force making him lose ground. He presses back, side-stepping to Mydei's flank and shifting his grip on the hilt of his sword to swing it where he sees an opening—a flash of rib, a red mark that serves as a target. He feels more than he sees the way Mydei shoves the blade away with his forearm, growling as he aims another blow, uncaring of the way he's lacerated himself with Phainon's blade, golden blood crystallizing in an instant, the wound healed. Phainon skips back.

"Well that," he says, switching back into a standard grip, falling into stance, "is rather unfair, isn't it?"

Mydei doesn't bother to respond, advancing again, twisting around the next swing of Phainon's sword, knee lifting, trying to land a kick to Phainon's open side before he shifts to avoid it. Somehow, the move walks him straight into Mydei's opposite fist, which collides with the space between his chest and armpit. His sword swings, catching Mydei in the side, cutting flesh with frightening ease before it crystallizes and gets stuck. Wrenching it out earns him a grunt, and they both stumble back, Mydei running a hand over the rapidly healing wound, Phainon caught somewhere between awe and horror.

He doesn't cut like that during a spar, not ever, but Mydei will push himself into Phainon's blade if it means gaining the upper hand. He's reckless, entirely unconcerned with injury.

"Doesn't it hurt?" Phainon asks, hands sweating on his sword.

There's no answer. Mydei ducks back into his space, throwing a punch that Phainon narrowly dodges, bringing his sword up, only for Mydei to catch it, letting the tip tear into the inside of his elbow as he uses his momentum to ram his knee into Phainon's side. It connects, sure to bruise, Phainon hissing through his teeth, distracted by the gold of blood and the red of crystal. It's... he loves the thrill of a fight, the sweat, the adrenaline, the physicality of it, but this does nothing but scare him. He gets the sense that Mydei would let Phainon run him through a hundred times, live that agony over and over, and not give it a second thought if it means winning.

Phainon grapples for the space to breathe, spinning his blade to hit Mydei in the chest with the pommel, stepping on his foot, if only to make him back up a step. Then Phainon drops his sword, shifting into a hand-to-hand stance instead. Mydei follows the motion with his eyes, skin sealing back up, unscarred and intact, and says, "Are you going to pick that back up?"

"No," Phainon answers, going so far as to kick it out of the way. "I don't particularly enjoy stabbing you."

"My flesh is immortal,” Mydei reminds him.

"Yes," Phainon agrees, "but I'm not convinced you don't feel pain."

He watches Mydei's eyes narrow, the corners of his mouth tipping down. And then his fist is directed straight for Phainon's face, fast enough that he barely sees it, barely manages to slip away from it. A breeze brushes his cheek, brought by the force of Mydei's hand. His eyes go wide, and it's only by pure reflex that he manages to block Mydei's next blow with his wrist, then the three that come after that in quick succession. Next is a kick, but he manages to catch Mydei by the leg and unbalance him, landing a hit to his gut, another to his cheek. And then Mydei is grabbing him around the waist and butting hard into his already bruised jaw. Together, they topple, Phainon biting his tongue, pain in his entire face as they grapple.

They roll in the dirt, a tangle of limbs, each struggling to gain the upper hand. Phainon claws Mydei in the face rather than be pinned, accidentally shoving a finger up a nostril before turning them over, scraping his knees, pulling hair before he’s elbowed in the throat and jabbed in the ribs where it already hurts.

The pain nearly blinds him. He coughs up spit and blood from his bitten tongue, vision blurry as he’s rolled over again, feeling the dig of stone against his back, grit under his palms, ears roaring. Mydei tries to punch him straight in the face, but by some miracle, he avoids it. His senses struggle to return to him, but as they do, he bucks wildly, flinging a handful of dirt into Mydei’s face, shoving his foot into Mydei’s stomach, giving him the leverage to shove him off and maneuver him into a chokehold. He gets to bask in having the upper hand for no longer than ten seconds before he’s thrown—with no small amount of strength—over Mydei’s shoulder.

It ends like this: Phainon on his back, Mydei astride him. He hits his head on the way down, stunning and dizzying him, knocking the breath from his lungs and leaving spots dancing in his vision. Everything aches, from his bruised jaw to his beaten sides to his forearms where they’d caught a few too many blows. The blood roars in his ears, and blurring in and out of focus, there’s Mydei, one hand pinning Phainon’s wrists to his chest with enough force to make it hard to breathe, the other resting with one armored finger in the bowl of Phainon’s throat.

“Yield,” he orders, because the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos does not ask nicely for anything. His weight pins Phainon firmly to the ground, knees spread at either of his sides. It hurts. Titans above, it hurts. Body heat comes with the pressure along Phainon’s hips. For a moment, Mydei comes into focus, that copper-tipped braid of his hanging between them as he bows over Phainon, the rest of his hair mussed, robe threatening to slip off his other shoulder if not for the pauldron keeping it in place. His chest heaves, he’s covered in sweat, grit sticking to his clothes and his skin, and he’s grinning.

Heat, horrible heat makes its way south.

Phainon shuts his eyes, vision imprinted with red and gold, still dancing with black. Pulse pounding in the veins of his exposed throat, he parts his lips. “Titans,” is what comes out, hoarse and breathy and entirely inappropriate for an arena with the entirety of Castrum Kremnos watching. He swallows, Adam’s apple bobbing, feeling the tip of one of Mydei’s fingers slip under his choker, pulling it tighter.

Phainon tries to catch his breath, blinking the last of the spots from his vision to find Mydei still there, impossibly solid and impossibly strong, enough to match him blow for blow, to beat him, by even the tiniest margin. Scant few have pushed Phainon even half this hard. They’ll need a rematch, he decides then and there, because he’d pushed Mydei too, and that grin holds the accomplishment of a battle hard fought. They’re evenly matched, Phainon thinks. Perfectly, wonderfully matched, and next time the victor will be him.

“Kephale above,” he tries again, breathy, still a little dazed, “you’re beautiful.”

“Yield,” Mydei only repeats, finger digging right into Phainon’s pulse point. His gaze holds steady, eyes narrow, that smile smoothing out. So much fight tucked into one man. Phainon is helpless, lit like a match.

Loud, so the rest of the world, forgotten outside this tiny bubble of just the two of them, can hear, he shuts his eyes again in surrender and says, “I yield.”

The arena erupts with cheers.

△

The door to Phainon’s guest room is sharp in places where Mydei has him against it. A ridge between his shoulder blades, another at the small of his back. The palm of one hand pushes into it to steady himself as they’re pressed chest to chest, hip to hip, a mouth on his throat, teeth sharp as a blade, tongue between the straps of his choker, tracing the sun there.

There’s one hand curled in Phainon’s hair, another on the outside of his hip. Mydei’s touch—his mouth—works anything but softly, and he is impossibly solid, like he had been, impossibly warm. Phainon has fingers splayed on his ribs—taut, molten skin, not a hint of softness, still covered in grit—and loses each thought as it comes, strings in the wind. “This,” he pants, even as he lets his head be wrenched back, neck bared, “is a catastrophically bad idea.”

The smear of lips along the place where his neck and shoulder meet. The prick of a tooth. Mydei pauses, the sensation of his breath sending sparks up Phainon’s spine. “Second thoughts, Deliverer?” he asks, close enough that Phainon can feel it. The heat of him, the realness. He’s rigid between them, against the inside of Phainon’s hip. One armored thigh sits between Phainon’s, the promise of pressure, the question of it.

“I just…” The end or beginning of a red marking beneath his fingertips. It’s perfect and surreal and entirely inappropriate. He’s too hot in his coat, still sweat soaked and covered in dirt from their spar. He presses himself into the hard metal of Mydei’s thigh and finds this frighteningly reckless. An exhalation, a sensation like pleasure-pain, the crack of his head against the door and the smooth, forge-hot flesh beneath his palm. “...Worry that this won’t end well.”

Mydei presses his thigh back into Phainon, grinding himself against the inside of Phainon’s hip, tangling his hair. “What does it matter?” he asks, his voice a little bit rough, deep in a way that does wretched things to Phainon’s wavering will. “We’re to be wed regardless.”

“Yes,” Phainon says, breathless, and through it all, something anxious still bubbles up in his chest. Too much, he thinks. They’ll make a mess of things, and drag Mydei’s people with them. “But this is… abrupt, isn’t it?” It’s good but it’s too much, too fast. Phainon hadn’t considered Mydei this way until that last moment during their spar. He doesn’t love him, doesn’t—

Mydei’s hum vibrates right into skin, and then he takes a deep breath, breathing Phainon in, or just—breathing. And then his hand slips out of Phainon’s hair and fixes the open collar of his coat. Briefly, he rocks forward, pressing them together, chasing Phainon’s thoughts away like butterflies, giving him that same dazed, white-out feeling from when he’d hit the floor in the arena. The hand on Phainon’s hip slides up his waist, side, chest, and then there’s a firm hand on his sternum, pinning him in place as Mydei steps back, away, leaving nothing but a flood of cold air in his wake.

“You’ll say yes or we won’t do this at all,” he says, and Phainon can do nothing but stare at his spread fingers, the red of his mouth, the heaviness of his eyes. He can smell the sweat, the want, and a part of him regrets terribly, wants him back, but he’s hyped up on the adrenaline of a good fight, and for once he knows better than his impulses.

“That’s…” Phainon wets his lips and tries to forget the feeling, the heat, the insistent throb between his legs. “Yes, that’s… A good policy.”

Mydei huffs a laugh, breath lifting the longer hair in his face, lips quirking up. “Yes,” he agrees, and pushes off Phainon’s chest to stand up straight, then brushes him out of the way of the door. “Goodnight, Phainon.” And then he’s gone, and his voice is echoing in Phainon’s ears. Phainon, Phainon, Phainon, over and over.

△

Aglaea will smell it on him. The way his thoughts race. The part guilt part incredulity part Phainon, Phainon, Phainon thrumming through him like blood. The memory of a body against his own. A mouth. An armored thigh.

Phainon arrives in Okhema an utter mess.

“You reek of bloodshed,” Aglaea tells him. She circles him when he comes to report to her, taking her time, her threads vibrating in the air. Their resonance is frightening. Phainon is much too high strung.

“Bruises, all over. Just what exactly did you do during your visitation in Castrum Kremnos?”

Bruises. Can she see the one on his neck? It’s a tiny thing, mixed in with the one on his face and his black and blue ribs. Barely noticeable at all, really, and Phainon heals fast. Two days and it’ll be nothing more than a whisper. He can feel the sweat drip down his back.

“I was proving my worth to the people,” he answers.

“By fighting them?” Aglaea scoffs. “What folly.” Her strings silence. “Rest, Phainon, you can report to me later.

“I…” His body aches. His mind is still racing. His head bows. “Very well.”

So he rests. A long soak in the Hero’s bath, a full meal. He rubs ointment on his bruises and changes into fresh clothes, sending his old ones to be laundered. By the time he’s dressed and sated, the sky is dark. His sleep is anything but dreamless. In the morning, he pens a letter.

Mydei,

I’m to be fitted for my wedding robes tomorrow. They’re going to be red, did you know? Red is a wedding color in Okhema. I thought you might find that funny. Red like the blood of mortals or the symbol of strength for your people. Here it represents transition and the warding of evil. As you’ve seen, red does not look good on me. Please make due with this ugly bride.

As I left for Okhema from your city, there was a man that tried to speak with me. I don’t speak the Kremnoan language, and he knew little of the common one, but he called me “king” and tried to gift me a garnet set in a gold ring. I wonder if this means your people have accepted me. I hope mine will welcome you with arms just as open.

There’s a bruise on my neck. Did you leave it intentionally? I don’t like that you’ve succeeded in making me think of you. I—

He stops there and sighs, dropping his pen, rubbing his temple. With his other hand, he crumples the letter up.

Later, he gives Aglaea the full report he owes her. He tells her of his reception, the state of the city, Nikador’s war cries on the battlefield. He tells her about the fighting, the arena, battling Mydei. She listens intently, stopping him now and then to ask questions, nodding and bringing a hand to her mouth in thought.

Finally, she says, “And when will Mydeimos return?”

“Two weeks from now,” Phainon answers.

△

“Lady Tribios, would you teach me to braid?”

Bright eyes look back. “Trianne does ours. Do you want to learn?”

“Yes, please.”

His fingers are clumsy. He practices with lengths of rope that remind him of fishing nets and twined flower stems. Later, he tries on a child’s silken hair. She laughs when it comes out uneven and permits him to try again and again until the plait is neat and smooth.

△

Three weeks until the wedding, celebrations in Okhema begin. Banners of white and gold are strung through the city, fresh flowers tied to every post. There are preparations for feasts and festivals and the formal ceremony once Mydei arrives. Phainon is congratulated in the streets. He catches whispers about the beauty he’s to be wed to, and feels sick with laughter and something like guilt.

He knows these people don't know Mydei. If they did, they'd find him beautiful in a way poets don't write about and people don't brag about on the streets. His beauty is in his strength, his will, his impossible compassion. These people imagine him as beautiful in the way thin stemmed flowers are beautiful, but he isn't, not at all. They'll be surprised by the hardness of his gaze and the downturn of his mouth. Phainon looks forward to it.

He pens another letter, and this time he sends it.

Mydei,

Did you never speak to any of my people during your stay in Okhema? The rumors get worse and worse in your absence. I heard a group of women calling you "fair-skinned and delicate of face" when out today. We'll need a rematch when you return, if only so I can see the expressions of shock on their faces when presented with the truth of your immortal body.

We've begun to mobilize forces for the reclamation of Nikador's coreflame already. Many of the Chrysos Heirs are eager for a chance to prove themselves and continue the flame chase. Morale is high, and with their might combined with that of your soldiers, I'm optimistic of the outcome.

Regarding the wedding, the city has been decorated in anticipation of your return. Be prepared for dramatics when you arrive; your walk to Marmoreal Palace will be something, to put it plainly. Dress nicely and prepare to be gawked at. Later, there will be three days of celebrations surrounding the wedding. The day before, day of, and day after. Do you dance? Expect dancing.

Your would-be suitor, one of Okhema's finest warriors,

Phainon

P.S. Aglaea would like me to remind you that your wedding robes need to be altered.

P.P.S. Another poem, because I know how much you loved the last one.

If poor sportsmanship is an ailment then I am well

Bruises will heal, time will tell

But defeat slightly injures my pride

Strong soldier, my delicate bride

This travesty nothing can soothe

I'm left with something to prove

That clash of fists was just the prequel

Mydeimos, I swear, I am your equal

△

Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,

During my initial visit I was careful to avoid the attention of your people. I had little desire to be seen in a difficult spot, and unlike some of us I am not overly obsessed with winning over every soul on Amphoreus. It's as simple as this: so long as they are willing to aid my people, I care not what Okhemans think of me. So yes, aside from Lade Aglaea and yourself, I spoke to very few of your people. As for the things they're currently saying about me, I find it insulting that you take their compliments in jest.

We've lost another percentage of the city since you left. Please remind Lady Aglaea in my stead that I have no intention of inheriting the authority of Strife.

I'm prepared for whatever your city tries to throw at me. What kind of fool doesn't know how to dance? I'm certain I'll be fine.

The victor of our every contest,

Crown Prince Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos

P.S. Your insistence upon making everything rhyme is greatly hindering your poetic ability. Again, I ask that you refrain from subjecting me to these in the future. If you want a rematch, ask normally.

△

Two weeks until the wedding, Phainon’s bruises are healed. His ribs don’t ache when he breathes, jaw when he speaks. His throat is unmarked but for the sun there. Still, when he checks in the mirror, head tilted, choker removed, he’s still plagued with the thought of where that healed bruise came from.

He’s less stuck on it now. It, the raw physicality. The body heat, the damp of Mydei’s tongue, the pleasure-pain. Now, he’s only afraid of the implications. The mess it might make. They’re to be wed, sure, but Phainon wants to make the best of things. He’s afraid that sex will muddy the waters, that attraction will squash whatever comfortable dynamic they’ve managed to cultivate.

Yet Mydei already knows. He felt the way Phainon has ended up wanting him. He wants Phainon too.

Titans above. The string on Phainon’s finger proves to be a nuisance at times like these. He forces himself to stop thinking about it.

He wears his wedding robe for Aglaea to pin and alter. She’s making it personally, as the Dressmaster of Okhema. It’s a beautiful thing of red, white, and gold, colors of transition and triumph. Aglaea adjusts the fit of the fabric around his shoulders, folding the hems of the sleeves and pinning them around his wrists. She pulls the waist a bit tighter, adjusts the collar so it mimics that of the coat he favors.

When she’s satisfied with the alterations she’s made, she steps back and circles him one last time, very slowly. Her garmentmaker brings a full length mirror, placing it in front of Phainon. His breath stills as he studies himself.

The fit is perfect. He looks regal and resplendent enough to marry a crown prince, even in red. Aglaea has somehow managed to keep it from clashing with his complexion with just the right shade or the right placement of the color. Phainon looks… like someone he never really imagined himself being. “You do beautiful work,” he says.

Aglaea smiles slightly and steps up to his side. She smooths the fabric around his chest. “What do you think of a half sun here?” she asks. “Embroidered in gold.”

“Like a new dawn,” Phainon says. He looks at himself a little longer. The groom in the mirror, marrying not for love but for life. He wonders if he’s ruined things. Maybe Mydei doesn’t care at all. “Why not? It’s lovely, Aglaea. Thank you.”

“You seem unhappy.”

“That obvious, huh?” He sighs. “It’s just… real now, in a way it hasn’t been, but I’ll get over it.”

Transition, triumph. Phainon isn’t afraid of this. He just thinks back to life in a small town and can’t help but wish—just every now and then—that things were simpler.

“Do you dislike him?” No strings hum. Aglaea asks him as person to person.

Somehow, this makes Phainon laugh. “No,” he says. “No, not at all. That’s the strange part. I just…”

Aglaea picks an invisible piece of lint off his shoulder. “You just…?”

Phainon stares himself in the face. “I don’t know.”

△

At sunset, a week before the wedding, Mydei comes back. Phainon makes the trip to meet him at the gates dressed in his finest blue and white.

Mydei comes in red, as expected, dressed neater but no less boldly than Phainon is used to. The top half of his hair is pulled back, the bottom down, that thin braid still behind one ear. His eyes are low lidded and impassive as he watches Phainon approach, his mouth a smooth line, the markings on his body standing out even in the dying daylight.

He’s beautiful, in all honesty. Beautiful in a way the poets don’t write about, but attraction is dangerous, and Phainon has already made that choice for them both.

He slips, gracefully, into a formal bow. There’s a crowd gathered to watch them meet, to see the soon to be husband of their city’s perfect vessel. How Phainon hates that title. He rises steadily and holds out an arm for Mydei to take.

He does, gloved instead of gauntleted today, though he still wears armor on his legs. His fingers curl around Phainon’s forearm, watching him carefully with one red lined eye as they begin to walk.

The path to Marmoreal Palace is lit with votives, some on the ground, some held in the hands of people who line the street to watch. The way is clear in front of them, warm with the tail end of golden hour and the flicker of candlelight. Phainon leads the way, one slow step at a time. He can feel Mydei’s gaze on him. They make eye contact for a brief moment before it sends something uncomfortable stinging through him.

“You warned me of dramatics,” Mydei says, voice low, rough as it always is. “Is this it?”

This hairstyle exposes his temples. The tips of his ears. Each group they pass sparks a wave of whispers. A young girl tosses a handful of crocuses at their feet.

“Every able person in Okhema has come just to see you walk,” Phainon murmurs. “There are thousands of eyes on you. Is that not dramatic enough?”

Their shoulders brush with every step, body heat bleeding through fabric. Mydei runs warm, impossibly warm. Phainon remembers that, knows the feeling of touching him like touching flame.

“I suppose I was expecting singing and dancing and flower petals thrown in my face, with how you made it sound,” Mydei says. The sun starts to dim, the myriad of colors in the sky fading to blue. Now, the candles stand out. Hundreds of them, thousands, all to light their way.

Phainon smiles, laughs a little, soft for fear of the eyes on them. Too soft, because as a wave of whispers runs through the crowd, he catches a voice saying something like, maybe they really are in love.

“I think they like you,” Phainon murmurs. Mydei isn’t the sweet-faced, delicate bride they’ve somehow come to expect, but no one wears displeasure directly, and all are riveted as they watch. It seems they still find him beautiful.

There’s a sea of nymphs in Phainon’s stomach. His heart climbs up his throat.

“Where’d you get that from?” Mydei asks, conscious to keep his voice low and his eyes forward. “They’re all just gawking.”

He’s quite handsome, isn’t he?

“They’re complimenting you,” Phainon says. The path slopes into a soft turn as they continue, the sky growing darker. It’s a long walk from the gates to the center of the city. More children toss flowers, and Mydei is careful to step over them instead of on them, his expression kind of soft.

“I suppose they are,” Mydei concedes. A girl whispers, too loud, aren’t they lovely? “Why do they throw flowers?”

“They’re well-wishes,” Phainon answers. “Crocuses are for new beginnings, cyclamen are for love, colchicum for fidelity. They’re blessing the marriage.”

Mydei’s hand shifts a little lower, warm fingers circling Phainon’s wrist. “Your traditions are terribly sentimental.”

“Romantic,” Phainon corrects. “Just call them romantic.”

“There’s no such word in the Kremnoan language.”

A soft laugh. They spend much of the rest of the walk in silence, watching as the sky darkens the rest of the way, the street lit by softly flickering candlelight. When their path comes to an end, he walks Mydei inside. At the door to his guest quarters, their arms slip free from each other.

“Rest well, Mydei,” Phainon says, feeling achy and strange, unable to help studying him. “It’ll be a lot from here on out.”

The eye contact they make is strange and intense. “You as well.” After a moment, Mydei slips something from his pocket and holds it out. A pouch of coarse, burgundy fabric. It crinkles when Phainon takes it.

“What is this?” he asks.

And Mydei answers, “something small. Excuse my lack of creativity, but I didn’t think you’d be the type to care for flowers or jewels either.”

Phainon laughs, more air than sound, and opens it. Inside is a handful of hard candies in waxed paper. He takes one out, unwrapping it and finding it blood red and a bit transparent.

“Pomegranate,” Mydei tells him, “since you seemed to like it back in Kremnos.”

“I did,” Phainon says, trying the candy. It’s sweet and tart, and he likes this too. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome,” Mydei says, and sets a hand on the door. “Goodnight, Deliverer.”

Heart still in his throat, looking at him, tucking the candy in his cheek, Phainon says back, “Goodnight.”
