Chapter Notes

boss makes a dollar, I make a dime, I post fanfiction on company time

Mydei gets his wedding robes fitted first thing the next morning. He'd already been measured and prodded before he left, so they already fit, but Aglaea still pins tiny half inch alterations here and there as if it makes any kind of difference. Mydei stays still and silent through the entire process, patience thin but knowing better than to pick a fight.

He observes himself in the full length mirror held by Aglaea's garmentmaker. The robes are red, gold and white. Wedding colors in Okhema, as Phainon said. It's a palette that suits him, not too far off from his usual clothes. The sleeves are full length and he's given one glove, the hand with Aglaea's string bare. The top opens at the chest, dipping low enough to show some of the markings on his chest. It's comfortable, the fabric soft and designed in a way that doesn't impede his movement. He'll be able to dance in this, as promised.

Aglaea quits fiddling with the fabric at his waist and steps back. "There isn't much time left until the wedding," she says, "but if there's anything small you would like added to the ensemble, I will do my best."

The draping fabric of the robes is split at the legs, revealing red trousers and gold-trimmed boots. He feels bare without armor, but he doubts full plate on his legs would be appropriate at a wedding. The clothing is as nice as he could have imagined it, all things considered. Perhaps he should care more, considering this is what he's to wear at his wedding, but he finds himself largely impartial.

"This is fine as it is," he says, crossing his arms and noticing the way nothing pulls at his shoulders. They're comfortable and fit well, and that's really all he can ask for. "Thank you, Lady Aglaea."

"You're far less picky than most of my customers," Aglaea muses. She paces around him, standing next to her garmentmaker and considering him up and down. A hand comes to her mouth in thought. "More gold, perhaps..."

"Don't trouble yourself," Mydei says.

Aglaea smiles slightly. "You're quite resistant to being waited on for a crown prince."

"I simply tire of this."

A soft hum. Aglaea waves her garmentmaker away. "Be careful not to pull out any of the pins as you take those off. I won't make any significant changes if you're satisfied as is."

"I am," Mydei says. Aglaea steps out to give him privacy as he strips out of the wedding robes and pulls his own back on, armor and all. He folds the clothing neatly over his arm and returns it to her outside, careful with the pins. "Thank you," he says again.

She studies him for a too long moment after she accepts the bundle of fabric. "Thank you," she says back. "You're a very cooperative customer. Are you certain there's nothing I can improve for you?"

No," Mydei tells her. Her expression is so calm. She unsettles him still. "But... there is something I'd like to ask."

She doesn't look at him, just smooths the cloth in her hands, adjusting a fold, a pin. "Most things I can answer."

He takes a breath. "Many of my people will want to attend the wedding. There's a small Kremnoan tradition I'd like to include if possible."

Now, she looks at him. "That, I can arrange." A small, knowing smile. "So long as it doesn't involve another vicious spar between the grooms."

△

On his way back to his rooms, Mydei nearly bumps into someone in the hallway. She's short and slight, a blur of whites and purples as she stumbles out of his way with far more force than anyone ought to. They don't touch. She clutches her hand to her chest with wide eyes before she gives a short bow.

"My apologies, Lord Mydeimos," she says. The Maiden of War, destined for the coreflame of Thanatos. Mydei still forgets her name, but remembers the feeling of her gaze following him.

"Servant of Death," he greets, nodding to her. Slowly, she lowers her hand, smoothing her skirt and clasping both in front of her.

“Castorice, Your Highness.”

“Castorice,” Mydei repeats.

She nods back, then shifts on her feet. She parts her lips, then closes them, glancing down the hallway like she means to leave. And then she hesitates, finally setting on saying, “How are you enjoying Okhema, Your Highness?”

“It’s… bright,” Mydei answers. Castorice doesn’t seem to know how to reply to this. She opens her mouth again, closes it. Mydei waits for her to find the words for a moment longer, then says, “I’ve noticed your gaze. Do you have something you want to say to me?”

Her eyes widen, if only slightly. “I apologize if I’ve caused you discomfort—”

Mydie raises a hand. “Speak plainly,” he tells her, and then attempts to soften his voice. “I only wish to know what you want to say.”

“I…” She pauses. “You carry the scent of the River of Souls.”

Years later, she can sense that. Perhaps it’s his curse of immortality that she smells, or perhaps she’s really that keen. “Yes,” Mydei agrees. “I drifted there for nine years before I dragged myself out with this immortal shell.”

“I… see.”

Left to die by his father’s hands. Mydei remembers the feeling of a caved-in chest. The scent of blood in the air. The son of Gorgo will be crowned in blood. This girl doesn’t know him, not really, but that’s okay. “If you seek Thanatos,” he says, “I’m afraid I am of no help. I saw no sight of them.”

“I understand,” she says, and bows again, one long tail of hair slipping over her shoulder. She stands far, but she smells like hyacinth. Her hands, clasped in front of her, curl so tightly it must be painful. “Thank you.”

△

All too early in the morning, there's a knock on the door. Mydei is awake, though he's still unarmored and half-dressed, caught in the middle of redoing his braid. He waits until he's finished, fastening off the end before he stands and goes to the door. Phainon is on the other side, hands clasped in front of him, messy haired and a little bit flustered. He's begun to turn away, but turns back when he hears the door open.

"Hello," he says, and his eyes dip to Mydei's bare chest before they snap right back up. "I hope I didn't wake you." He's dressed head to toe in his usual coat, a flush beneath the collar.

"No," Mydei tells him. For some reason, Phainon laughs a little, flashing the points of his teeth. One finger hooks in his choker. Mydei remembers what it tastes like. Salt and leather. The scent of pine resin.

"Good," Phainon says. His gaze goes somewhere over Mydei's shoulder, then to his face, then the floor. "Great. Would you like to get breakfast?"

"You'll have to wait," says Mydei.

"That's fine." Phainon nods. "Take as long as you need."

Mydei holds his gaze for a moment, then steps out of the doorway and shuts it between them. Phainon waits outside as he pulls the rest of his clothes on and armors himself, as he lines his eye in red and puts his earring in. There's a strange feeling that it gives him, thinking of Phainon leaning against the wall, hands clasped, soft haired and warm bodied and far firmer than he looks. Mydei is unused to being denied a person he knows wants him too.

When Mydei steps into the hallway, Phainon straightens up and smooths out his clothes. He smiles, and something about him looks like he's been in the wind, young like fresh grass. He holds out an arm, then seems to think better of it, fingers flexing and dropping back to his side. "Shall we go?"

Mydei takes a breath and shuts the door behind him.

They leave Marmoral Palace instead of heading to the dining chamber like Mydei expected. Phainon leads him onto the streets of this golden, sunny city. It seems to get brighter every time Mydei sees it. More banners, more flowers tied to posts, ribbons hung between buildings in shades of red, white, and gold. A city in celebration. He thinks of Castrum Kremnos: homes turned to dust, sky overcome with darkness, people left bleeding on the streets. For years after Mydei dragged himself out of the River of Souls, he would feel the sickening rocking of waves when he closed his eyes at night. The feeling he gets now is similar to that.

“Where are we going?” he asks.

“I thought you might like to try more authentic Okheman food,” Phainon explains. “There’s a stall not too far from here.”

“Street food,” Mydei notes.

Phainon looks at him. “Yes,” he says. “Is that a problem?”

Mydei grew up closer to a common soldier than a king. “No.”

“Perfect,” Phainon says, and leads them around a corner. Mydei watches his back and thinks, for the first real time in a month, that this is the man he’s going to be married to in less than a week.

He’s strong enough, certainly. Had Phainon not put down his sword when they fought, Mydei isn’t certain he would have been the victor. The next time they fight, he may very well lose. He thinks of the stories he’d been told of Gorgo and Eurypon. The way they fought time and time again, never ending up with a clear victor. There is no word for “lover” in the Kremnoan language, but there is one for “equal.” That stupid poem comes to Mydei’s mind, unbidden. Mydeimos, I swear, I am your equal.

Just like the comb, Phainon probably hasn’t the slightest clue about the significance of such a statement. Dense as a rock, but Mydei remembers the feeling of him, skin under his lips soft as—

“Snowy!” One of the Holy Maidens of Janusopolis skips up to them. She’s easily half Mydei’s height, with red hair and chopped bangs swept out of the way of her eyes.

“Lady Tribbie,” Phainon laughs. His hand reaches back, catching Mydei’s forearm and squeezing, whether consciously or not. “Mydei and I were just going to get some koulouri. Are you hungry?”

She blinks, then turns her attention to Mydei, noting their positioning. Phainon’s warm, staying palm. “We spent a long time searching for you, De,” she says. “It’s nice to see you in Okhema.”

Searching for him. “‘De?’” Mydei repeats.

She perks up and says, “A nickname! Snowy is Snowy, Agy is Agy, and you’re De!”

He frowns, imagining Lady Aglaea answering to “Agy.” And aside from the shade of his hair, there is little snow-like about Phainon. “I… see,” is all Mydei can muster.

Phainon squeezes once more and lets go, fingers skimming skin as his hand drops. He laughs, a little awkward. “Are you hungry, Lady Tribbie?” he asks. “Can we get you something to eat?”

“We ate,” she answers, “and now we have business with Agy and Cas, otherwise we would love to stay.”

“Of course,” Phainon tells her. “Have fun then, Lady Tribbie. We’ll see you later.”

She smiles and lingers a little, looking between them. “Congratulations,” she finally says, then starts to turn away. “See you later, Snowy, De!” She skips away in a matter of moments. Mydei watches her go, still frowning.

“She’s…” He’s uncertain how to finish that sentence.

Phainon sighs. “Child-like?” he offers, rolling his shoulders as they begin to walk again. Slowly, Mydei nods in confirmation. Childlike, though he knows Lady Tribios is older than all the rest of them. “She ages in reverse,” Phainon continues. “It’s part of her… blessing, from Janus. She split herself into a thousand pieces, but each one lives on borrowed time.”

“Just call it a curse.”

Phainon looks at him. “No,” he says, and shakes his head. “She’s a blessing to all of us.”

They walk the rest of the way in silence.

The stall Phainon takes them to is run by a woman with graying hair and smile lines on her face. She serves them koulouri far bigger than anyone ought to eat at once, covered in sesame seeds and smelling warm and bready. The way she smiles is proud and bittersweet.

“You’ve grown up, Lord Phainon,” she says, and she refuses when he tries to pay. “Congratulations. Mnestia’s blessings upon your marriage.”

“Do you know her?” Mydei asks as they find a spot to sit, pretending not to notice the eyes that follow them.

“She’s been running that stall since I was more boy than man,” Phainon says. “Maybe longer than I’ve been in Okhema.” He lifts his koulouri, the ring of it as big as his head. “She makes good food, though.”

Mydei takes a bite of his and finds that he can’t refute that. His eyes close at the flavor before he catches himself and opens them again. The corners of Phainon’s lips curl when he does, but it’s small, subdued. Mydei would have expected some kind of teasing. When there’s none, Mydei studies him.

“Your hometown,” he says. “Aedes Elysiae. What’s it like?”

“Small,” Phainon answers. “Destroyed, now, and taken by the black tide. That’s why I’m here now, like everyone else.”

“Like everyone else?”

Phainon takes a bite and chews slowly. Swallowing, he explains, “Most Okhemans aren’t really from here, what with the black tide. Most of the Chrysos Heirs aren’t… The Ladies Tribios come from Janusopolis, Castorice comes from Aidonia, I’m from Aedes Elysiae…”

“And the actual Okhemans, how do they feel?”

“They’re welcoming people,” Phainon says, turning his gaze back to the woman running the cart. She passes pastries wrapped in paper to a couple of parents and their children, patting the mother’s hand as she does. One of those girls, with mousy brown hair and the straps of a hand-me-down dress trying to fall off her shoulder, had tossed flowers when he arrived. Mydei turns his gaze up, toward the blazing sun and the streamers strung over every inch of the city, all for them, and gets something different than that cold water feeling.

“I’m sure some aren’t happy,” Phainon continues. “But most of them…” Flowers and well wishes and strange but kind rumors floating through crowds. Not once has Mydei witnessed a fight in the streets. These people don’t flaunt bloodshed, don’t dismiss the value of life, even those of strangers. They don’t throw their children in the River of Souls, and they don’t drive spears through their fathers’ chests.

The koulouri is the slightest bit sweet. Laughter comes from across the plaza. A boy gapes at them and hides behind his mother when he’s caught staring.

“Are you worried about the Kremnoans? I know Okhema and Castrum Kremnos haven’t exactly had the best relationship in the past, but they’re welcome—you’re welcome—just like anybody else.”

Mydei has seen children cry when asked to swallow medicine. This is the feeling he gets now. A bittersweet taste in his mouth and a helplessness toward what he must do to save himself. His people. Like a dog in a cage, he makes the choice to lay down and accept it.

“This,” he says, squinting at the sky, “is a terribly bright city.”

Phainon laughs. “Isn’t it? We’re so close to Kephale. It takes some getting used to.”

“Yes,” Mydei says, and leaves it at that.

△

The day before the wedding comes with two separate feasts, one for Phainon, another for Mydei. They’re kept apart as per Okheman tradition. Mydei’s dressed in a robe other than the one Aglaea made for him, though the colors are the same. Red and white tied at the waist with a gold belt.

Guests are free to visit each feast as they please, stopping by either or both for bites from tables stocked generously with breads, meats, cheeses, fruits. There’s wine that Mydei indulges in perhaps more than he’s meant to, but he needs something to keep him from going insane from the small talk he’s forced to engage in with more strangers than he can count. Each one is kind, welcoming, and congratulatory, but Mydei has never been much of a people person.

After perhaps four hours of this, there’s a headache pounding behind Mydei’s temples, and Lady Aglaea deigns to visit.

“In a half hour the feast will come to a close,” she says. “You will be expected to thank the guests, and then you will be led outside for the festival.”

He’s already been given the rundown a half dozen times. Energy leaving him like the little honey pastries on the dessert table, Mydei can only nod. Aglaea studies him.

“Is there anything you’d like to ask of me?” she asks. “Now would be the time.”

“No,” Mydei says, sounding just as tired as he feels. “Only that you keep your word once all of this is seen through.”

“We may make the charge as soon as three days from now, if you wish,” Aglaea tells him. Solemnly, Mydei nods. Thin, golden threads hum between them. “You’re ready, then?”

“Yes.”

“Marriage, in Okhema, is a sacred thing.”

Mydei inhales, nostrils flaring. “And in Castrum Kremnos it’s not?”

There’s a sharp, resonant sound like one of the strings has been plucked. “I mean to ask if any part of you is uncertain,” Aglaea says, cold as ice, “not to insult you.”

“A bit late for doubts,” Mydei says. Aglaea’s expression does not change, more stern than favorable. He sighs. “As far as prospects go, your Deliverer is far from the worst.” The string around his finger heats. Aglaea’s voice dips low.

“You will treat him well,” she murmurs, as soft as the touch of a blade on skin. It’s the most hostile she’s been to him, and Mydei does not appreciate anything she’s insinuating. In his lap, his hand curls into a fist.

“I would not take him as my—” The word he almost uses is a Kremnoan one. The one they have for lack of “lover” or “spouse.” “Husband,” Mydei finishes, “had I any intention of neglecting or mistreating him. One would think, in offering me his hand, you would be sure of this as well.”

Aglaea’s gaze falls to the thread on his finger, his hands bare and unarmored in the outfit he’d been dressed in for today. The silvery, translucent thing goes hot once more, and then her gaze goes back to his face. “You do not love him,” she says.

“There is no word for love in the Kremnoan language.”

Something changes as she examines his expression. She goes from hostile to calm, unbothered as the surface of a still pool. “Yet surely you feel,” is all she says, and then she stands, smoothing out her skirts. “Mnestia’s blessings upon you.”

△

Thanking the guests apparently means standing in the doorway and shaking the hands of each one as they leave to join the festival. His headache intensifies the longer he’s asked to smile.

On their way out, each guest lights a candle for him, until there’s a pathway leading him out of Marmoreal Palace that resembles the one that led him to it days earlier. A symbol of passage. As the last guest clears out, a servant comes by and lights the unlit candles.

He’s made to wait, and he does so with his eyes shut, basking in the small bit of silence he’s been allowed. One deep breath, two, three. When he opens his eyes, it’s to the warm flickering of candlelight lining either side of the hall, curving around the corner and out of sight. It smells, as much of Okhema does, of cherry laurel. After a handful of moments, Mydei is waved forward, so he sets off on the path. One step at a time. One foot after the other.

As he goes further, he starts to hear the din of the celebrations outside. People talking, laughing, music playing. It reminds him of the moments before stepping into the arena. The roar of the crowd as they wait. The heat of the braziers, the feeling of the ground under his feet. But there’s no fight at the end of this path for Mydei, and somehow that's so much worse.

The doors to Marmoreal Palace are wide open, the candles continuing through the doorway and leading outside to where there are hundreds of faces. Cheering erupts as he rounds the corner, and he squints as he steps into the light. Again, flowers are tossed at his feet. Brightly colored, sweet smelling things. He's careful to step over them.

The path turns into a loop that curves back into Marmoreal Palace. Mydei stops at the bottom and watches Phainon come out, stumbling a little as he trips over the seam between the door and the ground outside. The cheers are deafening, even as he straightens up and laughs a little, rubbing his neck. Mydei is too far to hear him, but somehow knows exactly what that laugh must sound like.

Moments pass in a flurry of cheers and flowers, the scent of cherry laurel and candles and people staining his nose. There's a strange sensation in Mydei's stomach. It's light and fluttering, like sickness but soft, and he doesn’t know what to do with it. Phainon joins him at the end of the path, dressed in white and gold with red accents here and there. His robe opens up at his chest, the collar folding down to show his neck devoid of its usual choker. His throat is smooth and bare, the sun displayed starkly on his skin, and a breeze fluffs up his hair and makes him look... bright, maybe. Enough to have to squint at. Enough for Mydei to feel a little bit nauseous.

"You walk slow, Deliverer," he says as Phainon comes to a stop. It earns a laugh, and then they're facing each other, more flowers thrown at their feet.

Phainon's eyes are anything but icy. "Who's to say you didn't start before me?" he asks, lips curled up. "Or maybe my path was longer." It takes a handful of moments, but the cheering dies out.

Somewhere in the crowd, music starts. Phainon holds out a hand. "Are you ready?"

Mydei takes it and steps closer to him, setting his other hand on Phainon's shoulder, feeling the heat of the one Phainon puts on his waist. It's the closest to each other they've been since the day of the spar, since...

The scent of pine resin. Phainon's eyes flick between his, tongue peeking through a half smile to wet his lips.

"Ready for what?" Mydei asks. Their hands adjust, palms sliding together. They stand for just a moment, waiting for the music to pick up. It does with a soft arpeggio on a lyre, and then Phainon leads him into the dance. All eyes are on them. "This dance?"

"I forget you mentioned having skill in this area," Phainon says, taking a step forward in time with Mydei taking one back. "Watch your feet," he adds, flower stems snagging on their shoes. Another step back, his palm slips an inch up Mydei's back, steering them away from the candles. Their eyes meet. Too close. "Coordination on the battlefield often spells out coordination on the dance floor too. I should have figured."

"Is that two compliments in one?" Mydei asks dryly.

"You'll find I'm far more generous with those than some of us," Phainon tells him. That smile. "They've dressed you quite nicely today.” His hand on the center of Mydei's back. "Can I twirl you?"

Mydei's eyes narrow, but he doesn't object as Phainon spins him and draws him back, catching his waist again. A soft "ooh" comes from the crowd. Phainon looks far too pleased with himself.

"You walk on thin ice," Mydei warns as Phainon's hand slides to his hip. He's far too comfortable, casual.

"It's a good thing I don't mind the cold."

Cocky. Where did that come from? "I should know, having seen you in the rain."

Phainon's face goes from smug to incredulous. "You—” He spins Mydei again like he means this as a punishment. "Will you ever let that go? I was reasonably upset, and— How did you even see that anyway?"

"The window to the guest chambers Lady Aglaea assigned me looks directly out on the plaza,” Mydei says, and flicks him in the chest. His palm flattens and slides from chest to neck, skimming skin, cupping the sun. “You practically put yourself on display.”

He can feel Phainon’s startled breath. Again, they turn to avoid the candles. “Did I?” Vibration against his palm. Phainon’s neck is warmer than the rest of him. His pulse thunders. Mydei puts them a half step closer, enough that they almost brush with the next step they take together. The hand on his waist flexes.

“You are terribly easy to turn the tables on,” Mydei murmurs. He trails his hand over Phainon’s shoulder, rests it on his upper arm. Keeps their eyes fixed on each other.

A blue gaze flicks to a red mouth. “I—”

“Thin ice,” Mydei reminds him. “You made that choice, not I.”

The song comes to an end. They part amidst crushed flowers under their feet. Phainon bows first, deeply at the waist, then Mydei back. A hundred faces watch, but they’re nothing more than the sound of sandals on stone and whispers of breath. This time, when the next song starts, Mydei holds out a hand. The string, thin, translucent silver, gold at a trick of the light, dangles between them. Phainon’s palm slips back into his, his other hand on Mydei’s shoulder, Mydei’s on his waist.

Their second dance is Mydei’s to lead. He does as Phainon did, guiding with soft pressure and clear, telegraphed steps. They twist through the carnage of flowers, eyes on each other. He spins Phainon close to the edge of the crowd, the candles flickering as his robes swish by them. Someone gasps softly.

Phainon comes back in close, catching himself on Mydei’s chest, looking thoughtful. “I didn’t say no,” he murmurs, and nearly steps on Mydei’s foot. He chews on his lip as he corrects himself, then swallows and adds, “I said not yet.”

The music builds into something that feels like a crescendo. Mydei spins Phainon into a shallow dip and says, “What are you afraid of, Deliverer?”

Their faces are close. Eyes wide with surprise, Phainon clings to him as they snap back up. He spares a laugh for the crowd, falling back into step. To Mydei, he whispers, “Risking the alliance. Your people. The coreflame.”

They almost trip over crushed flowers. Neither is looking at the ground. Mydei can smell the sweet scent from their bruised petals with each step they take.

“And what makes you think any of those things are at risk?”

“You can’t be with someone like that and not change things,” Phainon answers. “I don’t want—”

Punishment: Mydei twirls him twice in a row. He comes back a bit flustered, lips parted. “Fool,” Mydei admonishes. Softer, firmer, “Husband-to-be.”

“‘Fools fear the wrong things,’” Phainon breathes.

“Yes.”

“I said I was afraid you disliked me, and you called me a fool. I understand now.”

“I don’t love you.”

Phainon gives a wry smile and plays with the folds at Mydei’s collar. His fingertips trace a bit of skin, by accident or on purpose. He feels like the stars that come when you hit your head hard. “No,” he says, “there’s no Kremnoan word for that anyway.”

Mydei squeezes his waist, slides his hand around his hip. “Someone’s finally catching on.”

“What happens if one day you do, and I don’t?” Phainon wonders. “Or if I do and you don’t? Can you honestly tell me nothing’s at risk then?”

It’s a terrible time for a conversation like this, hushed low so the crowd can’t hear them. What does it look like they’re saying? Sweet nothings? Provocations? They must make such a strange pair.

“Would you drive my people out of your city over such a thing? Would you rescind your aid against Nikador?” Mydei gives him a look. “Perhaps you overestimate your own importance; would Lady Aglaea even let you do such a thing?”

“Thin. Ice,” Phainon says, enunciating each word clearly. Mydei watches the way his tongue flicks his teeth. The sharp points of his canines. He grins back, and, sensing the end of the song, dips him again, holding him there, flushed and glaring.

“I have no interest in coercing you,” Mydei tells him as the final notes ring out. “Figure these things out yourself, and in the meantime, refrain from attempting to seduce me.”

If not for the setting, Mydei is sure that would have earned him a punch in the face. Phainon fumes for no longer than three seconds before they’re straightening up and bowing to each other once again. The applause that comes is uproarious.

“Thank you for joining us in celebration!” Phainon shouts as the crowd quiets. He stands at Mydei’s side, warm where they brush shoulders, grinning like this is the happiest day of his life. Perhaps a better pretender than Mydei initially thought. “Any who are able and willing are welcome to join us in song and dance.”

On cue, the people in front bend for the candles, each taking one and shuffling to the back of the crowd for the next person. Somehow, together they manage to widen the circle into a ring big enough to hold hundreds. The next song begins, and they’re swept up in a wave of bodies, each one in tune to the rhythm, crushing the last of the flowers into the street. When Mydei turns, Phainon is no longer at his side, swept along or slipped away, out of sight.

Someone taps him on the shoulder, smiling and asking for a dance, and he realizes this is going to be a terribly long night.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
Phainon does not run from the party so much as he… takes a break from it, making his way through clumps of smiling people calling his name and offering small talk. He smiles at each one and exchanges handfuls of words before he claims a need for the restroom and wades a little further through the sea of faces. Each beat of his heart is an audible thing. When he makes it back inside, he's too warm and out of breath, stumbling into a quiet corner of Marmoreal Palace and taking a seat.

One breath in, big enough to make his lungs ache. One out, slow through his teeth like the sound of an ocean wave. The smell of grass, a soft voice telling him to breathe. You'll be a hero someday, I'm sure of that. Remember it. His heart calms. He rubs his fingers into his temple. Sighs. Curls in on himself at a sudden shock of embarrassment. Knocking his head into his knees, he mutters to himself, "Kephale above. What is wrong with me?"

Phainon is not often bold—not without a bit of wine in him—but something must have possessed him in the moments before this.

"That was quite the spectacle," comes a voice. Phainon bangs his head on his knees once more before he looks up. Aglaea stands there, an almost smile on her face

"Lady Aglaea,” he greets, standing up and smoothing out his robes. The heat in his face never has a chance to cool before it's coming back full force. "I was just, well…”

"I'm not here to drag you back to the festivities," she says, and finds a railing on the wall to half sit on. "I saw how they swarmed you as soon as you were free."

"Yes, it's... a lot," Phainon agrees tentatively. He folds his arms, then wonders if he looks like he's curling in on himself and drops them. Aglaea's gaze follows the movement, but she does not send out her strings to read him.

"How do you fare?" Aglaea asks him. Person to person again. Just asking. Strangely, this arranged marriage thing has humanized her.

Phainon blinks. Gingerly leans against the railing too. "Well," he answers. "I... Well, I suppose. Or, as well as I can."

Slowly, she nods, studying him, scrutinizing. “Are you prepared for tomorrow?”

“For the ceremony?” Phainon asks. “Or for the fact that I’m going to be a married man?”

“Both,” Aglaea says, “either.”

“How prepared can I really be?” He laughs, tries to. “I have to just… face this head on. But I’m alright, Lady Aglaea. I’m not… Mydei’s a good man. I’m…” Happy is not the right word. Relieved, perhaps. Glad, fortunate, satisfied. “...Content, that it’s him.”

Aglaea is quiet for a moment. “The people are enamored.” She holds a hand out for his, which he tentatively offers. The one with the string; it appears in her cool palms, glowing faintly with a soft, warm light. She looks at it for a long while, expression unreadable but a little bit soft. “They believe you’re in love.”

“I’m…”

“Contentment,” she interrupts, “is far more than many in your situation could hope for.”

Phainon hesitates. “Yes…” he tries. Their eyes meet, green gold to blue, sobriety to confusion.

“I will not tie you where you are unhappy,” Aglaea says, squeezing his hand in both of hers. “This is the last time I may ask. Are you certain?”

A breath. He thinks of sparring in the baths and taking turns leading a dance. He thinks of the way they bicker but don’t quite fight, the way they both take the care to listen. The strange thing that sits between them now, the ease of companionship, the heat of attraction. He finds that, perhaps, he isn’t just resigned to or accepting of a marriage to Mydei, but a small part of him, a small, irresponsible, brash, reckless, and impulsive part of him actually wants it.

Phainon tends to move fast when it comes to action, slow when it comes to people. He hasn’t known Mydei long, but maybe if they’d known each other outside of this, been given months and years instead of a handful of weeks for a courtship, maybe…

Figure these things out yourself. Phainon exhales. Maybe he needs to be braver. Maybe he needs to trust that not every good thing eventually goes up in flames. And even if it does, maybe those risks are worth taking. “I am certain.”

Aglaea searches him for truth or falsehood. And then she nods and steps back, her hands slipping from his, her mouth curled into another one of those almost smiles. “Very well,” she says. “Mnestia’s blessings.”

When she leaves, he takes a look at his hand, the heat and the glow coming from the thread tied to his pinky finger. It’s different than before. Still translucent silver, but if Phainon really looks, he can see flecks of gold.

△

He spends most of the rest of the night dancing. He’s swept around by friends acquaintances, and strangers. Here and there, he’ll catch a glimpse of Mydei through the crowd, sometimes looking back, sometimes not. It’s a while before they end up in each other’s hands again. The final dance of the night. Every person in the crowd finds a partner. By Okheman tradition, Mydei is Phainon’s.

No words are exchanged between them. Mydei simply holds his gaze, the orange of his eyes intense as flame, and takes his hands. He lets Phainon lead, pulling his hand to his waist. They wait for the music to start. Phainon’s fingers flex against the heat of a body, the hardness of muscle. Mydei’s attention lands on his throat as he swallows.

And then they dance. One step after the next, in sync with the crowd. This time, the eyes are not on them, or at least not quite so many. And yet not a bit of the pressure is off.

“This is the last chance we’ll have to speak until the wedding,” Phainon points out. “Have you nothing to say?”

“I don’t think I’m the one that needs to,” Mydei tells him. “There’s nothing I have to say that can’t be said just as well after the wedding as before it.”

Phainon looks at him. Searches him for doubt, or the same realization he’d had moments before. But he finds neither of those things, just the conviction that’s always there. “We’ll be married this time tomorrow,” Phainon reminds him. “No thoughts about that? No concerns?”

“Any worries of yours are things that we do not share.” The steps of the dance call for a twirl. When Mydei comes back, they are closer than before. Nearly enough to share air. “I am sure of this in a way I am sure of few things.”

“For your people,” Phainon says, and finds his gaze affixed to a red mouth.

“Yes,” Mydei agrees.

“But how do you…” feel? Phainon thinks. Mydei would marry a stranger to save his people. He would give up everything he has. But how do you feel? You would marry anyone, but what do you think of me? This is not the time or place to ask such a thing. Perhaps that isn’t the kind of thing that should ever be asked at all. Phainon turns Mydei with gentle pressure, letting his hand slip around his back, resting at the center of it. Beneath his palm, there’s slight, sudden tension. Mydei takes a breath, relaxes again, and Phainon is at a loss. “Are you not afraid of the things you’ll have to give up?”

“There is no word for fear in the Kremnoan language,” Mydei tells him. “I am not afraid. It’s as simple as that.”

A handful of moments pass without conversation. Just the music, the swish of fabrics, the feeling of the ground underneath their feet. When they turn, Castorice is at the edge of the crowd, though she isn’t dancing. She smiles at him when he catches her eye. Nearby, there’s Aglaea and Tribios. The rest of the Chrysos heirs; Hyacine and Cipher and Professor Anaxagoras, all gathered just for this. Because Phainon is getting married, and that’s—

“You are a better match than I was hoping for,” Mydei says, voice low over the music. “Is that what you need to hear?”

“I…”

“Though you aren’t quite my match in strength, I will not be tormented by a marriage to you.”

The music comes to an end. They’re meant to part and bow to one another, but Phainon just stays, still holding him, still looking. Should he be flattered, he wonders, or is it fair to be a little bit offended?

“Does that help?” Mydei asks him. “When it comes to figuring things out?”

Now, Phainon steps back. As he bows, his hair falling into his face, he laughs a little. “What a convoluted way to say you like me,” he says, straightening up. “Why can’t you ever just say it outright?”

“You strike me as someone with a very large head, and little sense to fill it.”

“I think I could say the same,” Phainon retorts, almost losing the words in the chatter of the crowd. “You just wait until that rematch, Mydeimos. We’re equals, at minimum. I may even be a bit stronger.”

△

In the morning, Phainon bathes in water blessed by Phagousa and Mnestia both. It is perhaps the most luxurious bath he’s ever taken. Hot and swirling with gold, the tub deep enough to drown in. He’s given sweet smelling oils, a stirgil to clean himself, and soft towels to dry with. After he’s sufficiently raw and pink from cleansing, hair still damp, dressed in a silken white robe, he’s attended to by a handful of servants. They powder, perfume, and prepare him, and when he looks in the mirror he’s a bit startled by his own face.

They’ve done something to smooth out his complexion, and his eyebrows have been shaped and filled in above eyes lined with gold and lips stained a half shade pinker than they normally are. His hair is softer and shinier than he’s ever seen it, styled slicked back on one side, combed neatly on the other. He looks… handsome, he supposes. Like a groom on his wedding day. His stomach roils.

“A bit like magic, isn’t it?” the servant standing at his shoulder asks him.

“Yes,” Phainon says, and it sounds like he’s underwater. “You’ve done an excellent job with this. Thank you.”

“Just doing my job, Lord Phainon. Congratulations on your marriage.”

“Yes,” Phainon repeats, still staring himself down. “Thank you.” That gold around his eyes, the way it makes the sun on his throat stand out. He’s afraid, suddenly, of what they must’ve done to Mydei. 

They dress him next, helping him into the freshly altered and perfectly tailored wedding robes Aglaea made him. Red, white, gold. A high collar, a newly embroidered sun, graceful fabric draping to the backs of his knees. Maybe he looks like someone who’s ready for this.

He stands as final adjustments are made to his clothes and hair. And then all the hands retreat. He’s left alone in the mirror. A groom, a man, a hero, a Chrysos Heir, a prince consort. Someone who is entirely unprepared for the future, any bit of it. One breath in. Another out.

“Are you ready, Lord Phainon?”

He can’t count how many times he’s been asked that question. The answer will never be anything but no, not even a little bit. He smiles and says, “as I’ll ever be.”

△

The wedding stage is decorated with swathes of white and gold fabric and long chains of flowers. Candles light where Phainon and Mydei are meant to walk onto the upraised platform in front of all of the city of Okhema and anyone else who came to attend.

The ceremony is held at Kephale’s feet. It’s so bright Phainon has to squint. His stomach still churns. As the music plays and he begins walking up the steps of the stage to the altar in the center, he feels a nervous kind of nauseous, or a nauseous kind of nervous. He wonders, briefly, if this is what all grooms feel on their big day. Dressed and made up as nice as they’ve been in their life. A thousand eyes on them. Soft music and the sounds of hundreds of people trying to keep quiet. The wood of the steps creaks softly.

Mydei is just as resplendent as he feared. There’s far more red on him than on Phainon. Full sleeves and a low dip in the chest. Some of his markings are on display, disappearing into fabric, and somehow it feels far less appropriate like this than it does when he has his entire chest out. One of his hands is gloved, one of Phainon’s too. The ones with the strings are bare on both of them.

When they come to a stop, face to face, Mydei holds his gaze. They’ve made him up too, with his lower eyelids lined in red and a thin dash of gold, his brows filled in, his mouth stained a slight, subtle red like the touch of wine or pomegranate juice. They’ve done nothing at all to soften the intensity of him. Phainon feels far too warm standing here bearing his attention under a sun practically within reach.

Mydei’s hair is undone, unstyled and unbraided. Phainon knows for a fact that not a single attendant would have been allowed to touch it. Mydei would have combed it himself, unravelling the braid with his fingers until the strands hold nothing more than a faint wave in its place.

A breath. A heartbeat pounding in his ears.

Aglaea officiates, as the bearer of the Romance coreflame. She guides them in prayer to Mnestia to bless the marriage. They take turns lighting candles twined with ribbon and olive branch. Phainon’s hands shake as he lights his. Mydei is steady as ever. When he steps back, twin flames stand between them, flickering lightly.

Again they pray, this time to Nikador’s virtues, as is custom in Castrum Kremnos. Phainon is careful not to stumble over the words, though his tongue is unused to the sharp sounds of the Kremnoan language.

After, Aglaea presents them with two thin gold hair cuffs. Mydei is calm and unreadable as he lifts one between his bare fingers. His nails are trimmed square and clean. He takes a step closer. His gaze against Mydei’s, Phainon bows his head.

Mydei picks a section on the non slicked side of his hair. Phainon can’t feel how much he takes, or see what it must look like, but he feels the way he divides the hair into three. The slight tickle as he braids it. Steady as ever. Careful not to pull.

Whether consciously or not, Phainon finds his breath held as he waits, nymphs in his stomach.

Mydei’s hands fall to his sides when he finishes the braid. It’s a small thing, likely no bigger than the width of one of Phainon’s fingers and only as long as his hair is. The gold cuff has been warmed by Mydei’s palm. It brushes Phainon’s cheek.

His turn, now. He accepts the other cuff from Aglaea. Tries not to be blinded by the sun as he raises his head. A small glance, a thousand faces tipped in his direction. One more right here, amber eyes trained to him, softened but anything but soft.

He thinks about gifting Mydei that comb. The accidental intention behind it. Phainon may not be the first to braid Mydei’s hair for him. He spent a long time away from home; maybe he doesn’t see quite as much significance in this as he claims his people do. Maybe this is just another ritual like the prayers and the candles, but Phainon still imagines the way this might feel for him too. The nerves, the slight, almost wistful feeling of it. Again, his hands shake. He finds that he isn’t as practiced at braiding with the cuff in hand as Mydei is. He can’t quite decide how to hold it.

Mydei’s hair is one step back from soft. Phainon finds the pieces that still hold the impression of a braid behind Mydei’s ear. The back of his hand brushes a warm throat. As he sections the hair into three he can feel the slight brush of breath. Strands slipping through his fingers. He could be sick with feeling.

He’s careful. One section over the next, pinky and ring fingers of one hand tucking the cuff to his palm. Mydei is silent. His attention says enough. When Phainon secures the braid and steps back, his chest caves with a breath. Their eyes meet as Aglaea resumes the ceremony.

A third time, they pray. This one is to Kephale to bless them with the light of a new dawn. Phainon knows this one by heart, by soul. He turns his face to the sun on Kephale’s back, eyelids red against the light of it, and tries his best to trust in this.

They turn, side by side instead of face to face. Phainon takes Mydei’s ungloved hand, or maybe Mydei takes his. They clasp, strings entwined, silver flecked with gold on both ends, and hold their joined hands out. Aglaea ties them together with a long white ribbon. She ties it thrice, once beneath the elbow, once at the forearm, and once at the wrist.

A goblet is offered to Phainon. He takes it, drinks deeply of the ambrosia inside and passes it to Mydei without so much as a brush of their hands. He drinks too, presents Aglaea with the empty goblet. She takes it and sets it back on the altar, and then her cold fingers are folding over theirs. She murmurs a prayer over their tied hands and says, “Mnestia’s blessings.” She lets them go and steps back. “With this, you are bound.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.html:
“We’re legitimately tied together for the rest of the night?” Phainon’s fingers are too warm around his. Between them, they’re starting to grow slick with sweat. Letting go doesn’t help much, aside from making this look terribly awkward, since they’re tied up to the elbow. Mydei can’t be further than half a pace from Phainon at any time without the ribbons digging painfully into them both. Of all of the traditions Mydei has been made to put up with over the course of the last month, none can begin to contest this one as the worst.

“Yes,” Phainon answers. “Romantic, isn’t it?”

He’s closer than Mydei would like him. Much closer, gold lining his eyes, Mydei’s braid in his hair. It doesn’t help that he’s basically dressed in Castrum Kremnos’ colors. It’s… distasteful, the pleasure Mydei gets from this.

“Romantic,” Mydei echoes, dropping Phainon’s hand and pulling them both so he can dry his palm on his leg. “What if I need to relieve myself?”

Phainon’s lips part. Soft red, his tongue peeks out to wet them before Mydei can stop looking. “I… avert my eyes and try not to listen?”

Mydei scoffs. “HKS.”

Phainon frowns. “Hai— What did you just call me?”

“HKS,” Mydei repeats. He turns to face forward, uncomfortable with the wanting, almost possessive feeling in his chest. Husband, he thinks. Equal. Mine until the black tide takes us all. His braid in Mydei’s hair. Mydei’s in his. Nikador’s strife. “It’s a Kremnoan word.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow. Mydei is looking at him again. Too close, tied together. He doesn’t smell like pine, just like powder and something unpleasantly floral. Mydei too. “It sounds like an insult.”

“Yes,” Mydei agrees. “That’s because it is.”

An incredulous laugh bursts from Phainon. He starts them walking, the pull on Mydei’s arm forcing him to move too. “You sure do know how to charm a man, husband of mine.”

An odd sensation climbs his neck. Phainon pulls them along, out from behind the stage so they have no choice but to join the festivities. More song and dance, more feasting, more small talk. All while tied to this much too friendly man Mydei is now married to. He can already feel the headache building in his temples. Phainon’s fingers curl back around his, if only because it feels more natural than whatever they were doing before. Mydei glances between their hands and the hint of a smile on his face.

Are you happy? He wonders. The vision of a boy in the rain. He can’t be, can he? What does he have to be happy for?

Am I happy? A stranger question still. Mydei is bound by duty and nothing else. Attraction isn’t strong enough to make a miracle of this.

In moments, they’re swarmed. Mydei can barely hear his own breath amidst all the congratulations and greetings and Phainon talking to a dozen people he seems to know like his best friends. He laughs that laugh that Mydei has memorized. It plays on repeat in his head. Over and over. Equal, are you happy? Softly, Phainon squeezes his hand. It isn’t a no, at the very least.

△

Nightfall comes with a torchlit procession back to Okhema, to what will become Mydei’s new home and his… for lack of a better term, bridal bed. There are no candles this time; attendees hold brightly blazing torches as they march alongside them. Mydei and Phainon, still bound together and sweating profusely at the palms because of it, walk in front.

It’s anything but quiet, the air filled with conversation and laughter. The sound of joy, of people coming together. Mydei breathes in sweat and smoke. It’s been a long, long day.

“One more day,” Phainon says, turning to him, “and then we’re free of this.” He’s shiny with sweat and oils, powder worn off. His eyeliner is smudged, a bit of gold smeared on one temple, and his lips are chapped and red from the way he keeps chewing on them. In this moment, at least, he does look happy. “And the day after doesn’t involve nearly as much partying.”

“Big commotion, just for us,” Mydei notes. It’s a strange thing, being beloved by people he doesn’t even know. They love Phainon, and in turn, love him. It almost makes him feel guilty. If not for his need of aid, he wouldn’t be here at all.

Phainon laughs. “It’s like this any time anyone even a little bit important gets married here,” he says. “Maybe not quite on this scale, but Okhema loves its parties.”

Soft, high laughter. Behind them, the Maiden of War laughs at something one of the ladies Tribios says. Lady Aglaea looks on with a smile. Back to Phainon, torchlight and shadow dancing on his face. “Are you having fun, at least?” he asks.

Mydei has a lot to worry about. The fate of an entire city on his back. Still, he looks at Phainon and considers. “Yes,” he decides. “I suppose I am.”

“I’m glad.” Phainon smiles a little wider. They keep walking, shoulders brushing every few steps. “And then after all this, we’ll march to Kremnos.”

“Are you coming with us?”

Phainon blinks. “Am I? I thought that was a given.”

In Kremnos, equals never leave each other alone on the battlefield. Mydei purses his lips. “I made aid negotiations with Lady Aglaea, not you.”

Somehow, this gets a laugh. “So you think I’d marry you to help your people, but draw the line at actually fighting for them? No, Mydeimos, I’ll be right there next to you, watching your back. With the love your people have given me… I could hardly forsake them now.”

Him, in Kremnos red. Bloodstains on his cuffs. Gold on his cheek. Guarding Mydei’s back. Even the littlest things he does spark unwarranted heat. Mydei untangles their hands to wipe his palm again, loathing the warmth of Phainon’s forearm against his. How he can’t wait to untie this damned ribbon. “There is no word for love in the Kremnoan language,” Mydei reminds him.

“Sure,” Phainon agrees. “So what do you call it, then? Because I know you feel the emotion.”

“That…” A trap Mydei set for himself. “That is none of your concern.”

“One of these days I’ll have to find a Kremnoan dictionary,” Phainon muses. Their shoulders brush. He takes the opportunity to wipe his palm too. Mydei’s knuckles skim his leg. All they’ve done today is touch. His skin is beginning to prickle.

It’s another twenty or so minutes before they reach Marmoreal Palace. At Phainon’s—Mydei’s now too—quarters, the people halt, turning from a parade into a clump. Together, they pray to the Titans to bless the newlyweds, and then they throw rice. Handfuls and handfuls of rice. Mydei squeezes his eyes shut and only manages not to slip away or fight someone because he’d been warned.

Thunderous cheering. Mydei opens his eyes to a thousand smiling faces and tries to shake the rice from his robes. Phainon’s hand folds back around his and pulls him inside.

When the door shuts, he sighs, and then goes silent. Rice skitters to the floor with each tiny movement they make. It’ll be a pain to clean, Mydei can already tell. He starts picking at the ribbon binding them, undoing the first tie, then the second, third. Phainon doesn’t speak. There’s an odd tension about him. Mydei opens his mouth to say something as the ribbon drifts to the floor between them. Then, a fist hits him straight in the face.

He stumbles back, reeling, but next is a hard kick to his side that he doesn’t manage to dodge. Another punch that he just ducks under, the pain in his jaw from the first not even finished blooming. “What are you—!” Another hit. He blocks it with his forearm. One to his ribs, connecting hard. He grits his teeth and steadies his weight, guard raised, sweeping one foot out in an attempt to trip Phainon.

He’s too steady, now that he has momentum. He hits hard and fast, forcing Mydei on the defensive. “Rematch,” he pants in a moment between blows. He backs Mydei far too close to the wall for comfort; Mydei growls and refocuses, hitting back, clipping Phainon’s shoulder as he regains ground.

Things only devolve from there. Phainon kicks and Mydei catches his boot, slamming into the door and yanking him forward. They slip on rice, tumbling to the ground with a hard thump, breath hissing through teeth, limbs colliding. Mydei gets Phainon pinned—sees his gritted teeth, the feral look in his eyes—and raises his fist. He’s shoved off by a foot to the ribs and rolled, grunting as his back hits the ground, shoving Phainon’s face away as a knee digs into his gut, trying to kick, catching a handful of fabric between his fingers and pulling—

Something rips. Phainon stumbles forward, catching himself on one forearm. Mydei tries to take advantage to switch their positions again, but when he moves his head he finds his hair caught beneath Phainon’s arm and grunts, trying to change tactics too late before knees lock around his and a strong arm pins his to his chest.

There’s rice sticking to Phainon’s cheek. When he grins, catching his breath, a couple of grains fall. One hits Mydei in the chin. “Yield,” Phainon says. The silence between them is deafening. Slowly, Mydei tests the strength of the hold Phainon has on him, flexing his legs, pushing against Phainon’s hand. Phainon only tightens his grip in response, his other hand joining the first to hold Mydei’s arms down.

There’s a fresh bruise blooming beneath his eye where Mydei must have clipped him in their scuffle on the ground. His makeup is still smudged all over. He’s still covered in rice, smelling more like sweat this late into the night than anything else. He’s molten everywhere they touch. There’s a tear in the front of his robe, bisecting that carefully embroidered sun. Lady Aglaea will not be pleased.

“Yield,” Phainon insists, staring him down. He looks like an ocean at midnight. The taste of blood and dirt on Mydei’s tongue. 

Again, he tries to shift, finds that he cannot move. “Did you not spare a thought for the fact that your entire city is listening right outside that door?”

“I don’t think they think we’re fighting,” Phainon says. His smile slips into something more serious, something Mydei can feel between his teeth. Heat, from his body and something else. Palpable want. Phainon slips a hand into his robes and produces a dagger, that same one from before in the baths, and presses the dull edge to the base of Mydei’s throat. He doesn’t ask again, only raises his eyebrows expectantly. Mydei can’t stop looking at his mouth. The red of it, the way it would look smeared with the gold of his blood.

Kremnos red and gold. Equal, he thinks with a hot kind of passion. All the blood in his lower half. “I yield,” he says, tipping his head back.

Nikador’s strife, if Castrum Kremnos could see him now. How far he’s fallen, to have his throat bared for the first man to match his strength. It wasn’t even a fair fight.

Phainon tucks the knife away and releases Mydei, climbing off of him, wiping the rice from his cheek.

He sits. Mydei breathes, willing his blood to cool and his heart to calm. Slowly, he pushes himself up, brushing off his now rumpled robes, scattering rice to the floor. Phainon picks at the tear in his own clothing, holding the pieces together with his lips pursed. A soft laugh. "Lady Aglaea isn’t going to be happy."

Mydei's fault, but still. "You made the choice to fight."

Phainon shakes out his hair, messing up the slicked side, making himself look like some kind of dog in the wind. "You know," he says, "I finally found a source on Kremnoan courting tradition.”

Mydei barks a laugh, still battling his own blood, dragging his legs into a seated position. The tension in his trousers is terribly conspicuous, but he hardly cares. Phainon already knows; they've been here once before. Post fight, sweat slick, adrenaline pumping. He’s felt Phainon’s want against him. "Then you know," he says, "what happens after the battle on a Kremnoan wedding night."

Phainon doesn’t have the decency to blush. “Yes,” he agrees. “I imagine that part of tradition is the same from culture to culture.” He stretches closer on his knees and one hand, the other reaching out. “You have rice in your hair,” he says. “May I?”

Mydei studies him and wonders if he’s really this clueless. To read up on Kremnoan tradition and ask to touch Mydei’s hair anyway. Did he forget, or does he mean it?

Slowly, like walking himself to the edge of a cliff, Mydei tips his head in the direction of Phainon’s hand. Fingers slip through his hair, lightly ruffling it to shake the rice out, then smoothing it back down. It tickles the slightest bit, sending a chill down the back of Mydei’s neck, trying to halt the breath in his throat. Mydei is still so terribly unused to being denied what he knows another wants too. It wrings him out like a rag left to dry.

“You read up on my culture,” he says, “and still choose to partake. I wonder, are you cruel or foolish?”

A soft laugh. Phainon falls back onto his shins. “Foolish, I think,” he admits. “I’m afraid of things I shouldn’t be, but I want to…” Words seem to fail him. He wets his lips, parts them, swallows. Mydei can still feel the phantom of his hand in his hair.

“Take a risk,” Mydei finishes for him.

“Maybe,” he confesses.

“And what of the people?”

A chuckle, more air than sound, more nerves than amusement. “Not out there listening still, I hope, but if they are, I’ll handle that embarrassment tomorrow.”

Mydei shakes his head. “You know what I meant.”

Phainon sighs. “I’m not worried anymore, if that's what you’re asking,” he says, trying to sound firmer than he really is. “You were right. I trust us.”

“What do you want, then?”

“I…” Mydei waits as Phainon struggles for the words. Long enough that his blood cools, heart calms. Slowly, he stands and dusts himself off. He undoes the ties on his outer robes and strips out of them, wrestling with the straps on his glove and pushing up the sleeves of his linen undershirt. He holds out a hand, raises an eyebrow when Phainon only stares.

“Were you planning on staying there?” he asks.

“What are you doing?”

“Resting,” Mydei answers, and waves his hand. “It’s been a long night, and I would like to recuperate.”

Phainon exhales but clasps his hand. Mydei pulls him up, and then he’s struggling out of his ruined robes too, tossing them to the ground, leaving him in a white under robe. “I suppose I could be amenable to that,” he says, and sighs. “You’re too patient with me.”

“Hardly,” Mydei says. “We have a lifetime.”

△

It's with a laugh that Mydei notices their wedding bed. It's made neatly with creamy white sheets, the bedspread scattered with flower petals, money, and a handful of jewels. Candles line the bedside tables, and there's a pungent, too sweet smell in the air. "What is this?" he asks.

Phainon steps in beside him, scratching the back of his neck. His fingers slip around his throat, looking for a choker that isn't there, and he lets out an awkward chuckle. "Ah, I believe the Ladies Tribios and Castorice are responsible. It's tradition for friends and family to decorate the wedding bed in Okhema."

Metal coins and pointy jewels. Again, Mydei can't help a laugh, rough and wheezing, as he picks up a particularly angular gemstone. "Practical," he says. "Quite comfortable to consummate a marriage on."

At this, Phainon laughs too. Together, they gather up the hard things in the bed, piling a small wealth of them on the nightstands, and then Mydei collapses amidst soft sheets and flower petals. He sighs, hands folding over his stomach, eyes slipping shut. The bed dips as Phainon settles in beside him. Mydei peeks at him, white hair spread on his pillow, staring at the ceiling. When he feels Mydei's gaze, he looks back.

"You know," he says, kind of quietly, "I usually sleep on that side."

Slowly, Mydei blinks. "We can fight for it next time."

Airy laughter. "I won today," Phainon reminds him. "This is my bed."

"Mine now too," Mydei says, quirking an eyebrow, "husband."

Phainon's eyes narrow. It's beautiful on him, like blood on snow. "I'm going to wash," he says, and slips out of bed, petals stuck to his back. Mydei watches his back as he goes, the width of his shoulders, the way he thins at the waist. And then he shuts his eyes again, breathing in that too sweet air. Just a couple of days from now, he'll be back in Castrum Kremnos, back on the battlefield. All of this will come to fruition.

When Phainon comes back, the smudged makeup is washed clean from his face. The ends of his hair are damp, his feet are bare, and he's kept Mydei's braid in. "Your turn," he says, falling with a huff into the bed. "Down the hall to your left." Mydei sinks his teeth into the insides of his cheeks and stands. As soon as he's gone, Phainon takes his spot on the bed, petals slipping over the edge.

As Mydei leaves the bedroom, he studies this home that's now meant to be halfway his. Cool stone floors, an abundance of windows and warm lighting from wall sconces. Pictures on the walls of Phainon and the other Chrysos Heirs and people who must be his friends. His smile, his laughter caught in time. Everything is clean in a way that feels recent and rarely maintained. It’s a homey, lived in place.

Mydei washes his face, water slipping down his forearms to soak the edges of his sleeves. He runs his wet fingers through his hair, finding a stray petal, a grain of rice. His eyes are tired when he meets them in the mirror. He feels too much strange emotion. His own want like a pit in his stomach, an ache in his teeth, beneath his fingernails. He heaves a sigh and pulls off his shoes to wash his feet before he pads back to the bedroom.

One of Phainon's eyes cracks open from where he's laying in Mydei's spot. The corner of his mouth twitches at the look Mydei gives him, and then he rolls onto his side, turning his back to Mydei. "Goodnight," he says.

"HKS," Mydei murmurs. Briefly, he debates shoving Phainon out of bed. Fighting him for it. But he's tired and achy, and he knows that if they do, if he has to see the intensity in Phainon's eyes again, or worse, the laughter, he'll only drive himself insane. He doesn't really care about what side he sleeps on anyway. "Goodnight."

"You said that's an insult," Phainon says to his back when he lays down. He reaches out, one finger snagging in the fabric of Mydei's undershirt. He tugs lightly, the tickle of fabric sending a shiver down Mydei's spine. "But you almost sound affectionate when you say it." His knuckles skim the center of Mydei's back, flooding him with sensation all the way to the base of his neck.

What did I say, Mydei thinks. What did I tell you?

He rolls over, catches Phainon's hand as it tries to retreat. "Does silence offend you?" he asks. "Or do you simply enjoy playing with fire?"

"I..." Honest, oblivious bewilderment. The beginnings of that bruise blooming beneath Phainon's eye. He isn't even aware of his own effect. Maybe Mydei really is too patient with him.

"You already know," Mydei says, "that I want you with a vengeance.”

Phainon’s lips part. Somehow, he doesn’t blush furiously or run into the next room. He just… studies Mydei, then turns his trapped hand palm up. “That’s the first time you’ve really said it.”

“I’ve said it a dozen different ways by now.”

“Maybe,” Phainon admits. He shifts, cheek on the pillow. “But I’m a fool, remember?”

“So what?”

Their palms brush. Phainon slips his hand up Mydei’s forearm, tracing a marking there with his fingertips, eyes following it. He looks like he’s wanted to do that; many of Mydei’s lovers do. And then his gaze snaps back up. “Maybe it means I need things spelled out for me,” he starts, pausing, eyes half lidded with a lazy challenge. “Just what exactly do you feel for me, Mydeimos? If not love, then what?”

“Lust,” Mydei answers, pillowing his head on his arm. With the free one he catches Phainon’s again, pulling it to his chest, flat against the space where his undershirt splits deeply so it wouldn’t show beneath his wedding robes. There, his heart beats. Phainon’s breath hitches. “Rivalry. Frustration. Annoyance, bemusement, friendship. A modicum of respect.”

Phainon’s mouth twitches. He lifts an eyebrow, but his words are too shaky to give any effect to his attempt at a smirk. “Only a modicum?”

Mydei sighs. The word he barks next is a Kremnoan one.

“What?” Phainon asks helplessly.

“Equal,” Mydei translates. The significance of such a thing is lost on Phainon, he knows. “Mine.”

“Your equal,” Phainon echoes, and as it dawns, a shiver runs through him. His fingers spread, pressed flat over the beat of Mydei’s heart like he can feel it beneath bare skin. “Oh. You really… Oh.”

“You fight like a dog,” Mydei tells him. Dirty, he means, with tricks and vigor, but Phainon takes this as a compliment.

“Thank you.”

Mydei makes a frustrated sound. “It’s not—”

“I’m your equal,” Phainon breathes, pushing himself up, pushing Mydei flat with that hand on his chest, staring down at him. Radiant in that way he’s been since the wedding without the makeup, without the robes that make him look more like a prince than Mydei does. He looks like victory. “You can’t take it back.”

“You—”

Phainon kisses him, one hand on his chest, the other in the pillows. 

He does it too fast and with too much pressure, clipping Mydei's lip with his teeth before he softens it, hand slipping between the folds of Mydei's shirt along his collarbone to grip his shoulder. His breath puffs in Mydei's face, and he seems to regret this as soon as he does it, swiftly pulling back with wide eyes and a parted mouth.

"I should have asked if that was okay before I did it," he says. "I apologize—"

It's with a hiss that Mydei grabs him by the shirtfront and pulls him back in, Phainon falling onto his forearms, mouth stiff and surprised before he begins to relax. He is, by all accounts, a terrible kisser, slow to react and too tentative, unwilling to fix his bad angles. Mydei slips a hand around the back of his neck, squeezing tight, moving him into a better position. His heart thunders beneath Mydei's thumb, and he makes this little sound in the back of his throat, and he— his eyes are open.

Mydei shoves him back with hands on his chest and laughs, rough and startled out of him. Phainon laughs too, and then he realizes that perhaps he should be angry, folding his legs beneath him and sputtering something out. "Are you laughing at me?" he asks, and when Mydei doesn't stop, "You really are! What a horrible, unkind husband I have. I can't believe—!"

"I'm giving you a chance to redeem yourself," Mydei says, sitting up and pulling him in again with both hands on his collar.

His mouth is still open, lips parted and wet to match Mydei's half smile. This one is better after a brief adjustment. Phainon unfreezes, remembers to kiss him back, to touch him. One hand props himself up on the bed beside Mydei’s hip, the other slips around his waist, up his chest to grip his shoulder. It’s push and pull, heat, tongue and teeth.

The fabric of Phainon’s under robe is silken. His body is hot when Mydei grabs his waist instead, drinks the sound that spills from his mouth, squeezes, pulls. Rigid muscle and soft flesh— Phainon is balance and contradiction, good and bad at this both. Mydei checks and his eyes are closed. He tastes like the charcoal he must have used to clean his teeth, feels like conquest.

His hand slips over the nape of Mydei’s neck, into his hair, nails skimming along his scalp, fingers tangling in the strands. He presses closer, kneeling, practically stretching into Mydei’s lap, firm between his hands. They part, breathe. Phainon’s teeth sink into Mydei’s bottom lip, just the right amount of pressure, a natural or not as inexperienced as he seems to be. Mydei groans into him, presses into him with greedy, long waiting fingers.

“Are you going to stop me again, Deliverer?” he wonders, mouth smearing along his cheek, grabbing him by the nape of his neck as he sucks at the point of his jaw. He feels Phainon’s breath hitch as much as he hears it, brings a mark to bloom beneath his teeth. Phainon heals fast, but not so fast that no one will see it, and who else will they conclude it belongs to but the new husband after their wedding night, after—

“I want to take a risk,” Phainon pants, “I want—” He cuts off as Mydei pushes him into the sheets, hair spread on the pillows, mouth red and spit slick. He stares, the light reflecting off his eyes, and finishes, “this.”

Mydei kisses him again, shoving a thigh between his, pressing hot and hard against him, moving to mouth at his neck, the sun devoid of its choker, the thump of a heartbeat.

“‘I want you with a vengeance,’” Phainon gasps. “It— It’s enough for me, in essence.”

Mydei pauses. “What?” he says into skin. Phainon swallows, and he can feel it right against him.

“Husband, soldier, king.” Fingers on his shoulders, gripping tight. “I’ll trust us with everything.”

Poetry. Mydei exhales, presses his brow into Phainon’s throat.

“Don’t love me, but see me as an equal.” Phainon wraps Mydei’s braid around his thumb and keeps going, “Because all is fair in this and war. And something about you is more than lethal. I’m with you until the end of… Nikador?”

Mydei sighs and pushes himself up, finding Phainon quite proud of himself. “Again with rhyming,” he mutters. “Did you write that yourself?”

“Yes,” Phainon says, lips twitching into a smile. “Just now.” Phagousa’s ocean in his eyes.

“Just like a dog awaiting praise,” Mydei notes. “Were you expecting me to enjoy that?”

“Well… Did you?” Phainon’s terrible poetry. The way he’s far too proud of it. “I don’t think that one was half bad, considering I came up with it on the spot. With a bit of time to workshop—”

“Just shut up,” Mydei tells him, one hand balling in the front of Phainon’s shirt, pressing into him with half his body weight as he kisses him again. An inhale. One hand slips around Mydei’s waist, Phainon settling in, parting his lips, tugging Mydei’s braid between two fingers. It’s maddening, the way he does that so easily, nothing to it at all, even though he knows, and he’s read up on Kremnoan tradition. When Mydei tries to swat him away, their hands only end up tangled, pressed into the sheets.

“Sorry,” Phainon says as they part for air. “I should’ve asked if that was okay too.” His chin tips up and Mydei catches his mouth, kisses him and kisses him, mapping the shapes of his teeth and his tongue. A wet sound as they separate. Phainon’s hips tilt up. He groans properly when Mydei rocks down against him, head falling back to expose his throat. The sun there, Mydei’s burgeoning red mark. “How I’m glad you’re not in armor this time.”

Mydei barks a laugh. Phainon’s hands slip inside his shirt, hot on his low back, encouraging as he grinds hard into Phainon’s thigh. 

“Is this much alright?” Mydei pants.

Planting a foot on the bed, Phainon rolls them over, pushing Mydei into the sheets to sit astride him, one hand on his abdomen, staring at the place where they meet, where Mydei’s shirt rides up above his naval. Curiously, he pushes it further, palm flat, dragging up until he reaches the center of Mydei’s chest. His fingers drift back down, tracing the markings on Mydei’s ribs as he rocks them together with slow, maddening pressure. Mydei can only lay there and watch, his hands on Phainon’s thighs before a blue gaze flicks back up to meet his eyes. A breath. The almost pleasure of this not enough friction. 

“Did you want to go further?” Phainon asks.

The heat of him, his weight pressing Mydei down. The way this memory is sure to play over and over in Mydei’s head as soon as it’s over. The way the last time has haunted him ever since. Phainon under Mydei, above him, inside him, around him. Mydei knows lust. Whatever this is, it’s bone deep. Equal, he thinks, spelling out his own mistake. Strife. “I wasn’t the one who wanted to stop before.”

A parted mouth. A hand that slides slowly to his waistband. “Well, then,” Phainon starts, wetting his lips as he undoes the button. He doesn’t show the anxiety Mydei expected of him, just slight hesitance before he settles on his choice. Determined as he is once he decides something needs to be done. Flawless, as he is. Amphoreus’ perfect vessel. He cups Mydei in his palm, firm and brave, and says, “It’s our wedding night after all.”
