They march. Mydei, Phainon, Castorice, Krateros, and the soldiers. The breeze carries the scent of people sweating under the sun. It takes them an hour to get to the battlefield, to the place where the streets divide, one side touched by sun, the other by eternal night. They halt before the divide, before the sound of Nikador's cries will become audible, before the end of this war begins.

Mydei turns to face the men. He looks at Phainon, just briefly, and the resolve in his expression is almost tangible. Phainon nods. He nods back and levels his gaze on the crowd, posture changing. His feet plant, spine straightening, head tall. Nymphs in Phainon's stomach. His palms sweat.

"Soldiers," Mydei says, voice raised. He repeats it in Kremnoan, delivering this speech in two languages. One for his people, one for Phainon's. His language is sharp and passionate, and with each phrase, he gets a shout from the Kremnoans, metal clattering as they slam swords and shields together. The sight of it, the sound, the glint of armor in the sun and the rows of determined faces. Phainon gets chills. Mydei switches languages.

"Okhemans, this may not be your homeland, but this battle is a part of your purpose." He turns, meeting the eyes of the soldiers in the front, each one in turn. "Today we fight for a purpose," he shouts. He turns to Phainon, lifting a brow in question. Phainon grins back.

"Today," he says, reaching for Mydei's wrist. "Together with the Kremnoans, we claim Nikador's coreflame!"

Mydei, "Today we save lives!"

Phainon wrenches their hands into the air, toward the sky. "Today we further the flame chase and lead us closer to the new era!"

Cheers, metal on metal. They're ready, all of them. Phainon breathes out a laugh, lets Mydei's wrist go. It's Castorice who silences them, lifting her hands. They're disciplined enough to listen. He knows she'd been worried. When she gives them the signal to put in their earplugs, they listen to that too. He watches her shoulders relax, smiles when she meets his eyes.

"Think you can kill more titankin than me?" he asks Mydei, pulling his earplugs from a pocket in his pants, wedged a bit awkwardly under his armor.

Mydei's lips quirk. "By a landslide," he says, and puts one earplug in. Phainon grins back.

"You're on," Phainon says. "Tally it up. Make sure you count correctly."

That earns him a scowl, and then they cross into the eternal night. With his ears plugged up, all Phainon can hear is his heart beating in his chest. Mydei and Castorice at his sides, the soldiers behind them. They're walking for no longer than ten minutes before they find the titankin, gathering into ranks. Their army holds. Ten bated breaths. They turn to each other and nod, and then Mydei gives the signal to charge. Phainon grips his sword and runs off his nerves. The titankin meet them in the middle.

The first kill is Mydei's. He grabs a titankin and rips its head from its shoulders, tossing the body aside as he blocks a blow from the next one, splattering himself with blood. Phainon grits his teeth and stabs one through the chest, kicking it in the abdomen to rip his blade free. Around him, the soldiers and titankin clash. Castorice fights in her own wide bubble, felling them with her scythe, neatly stepping around bodies and dodging blows. It's a wonder she doesn't make a mess of herself. The soldiers give her a wide berth.

He counts. Two, three, five. Golden blood coats his sword, he can hear his blood rushing in his ears, but he’s clear headed. He doesn’t crave cruelty, only sees it for the necessity that it is, and the memory of the way Nikador’s cries corrupted him makes him feel almost monstrous. The titankin aren’t people to be reasoned with, with lives and families at home, otherwise he might feel a bit monstrous now.

He kills another, and one after that. His tally goes up to eight. He doesn’t know what Mydei is at, both of them lost in the sea of bodies. A projectile nicks him in the eyebrow, making him bleed into his eye, gold swirling in his vision. He swings his sword with his body braced for the collision, lifting it again to block a blow, knowing he’s making some kind of noise but unable to hear himself. His teeth grit. He nearly takes a hit from behind before he twists and kicks hard, taking a titankin in the abdomen and slicing it in two with his sword.

Ten, he thinks. A flash of red. Mydei, bloodsoaked and burning. His expression is feral and furious, and Phainon wonders what’s going on in his head. What it feels like, to march toward your fallen god. To be the one to kill them.

He thinks of the way Kremnos reveres Nikador. The way they chant their virtues before battles and dedicate themselves to fighting for love of their god. Are they heartbroken? Or is this another trial, another war to be won? Is it betrayal they feel, or inevitability? Their kings are crowned in the blood of those before them and beloved regardless. Are their gods the same too?

Phainon’s muscles begin to burn, but he’s adept at pushing past that, breathing heavily and continuing to fight. His tally climbs to fifteen, then twenty. He swings his sword, stabs, ducks beneath blades and kicks away grabbing hands. Every body that falls is replaced by another. Sometimes his men are the ones to fall. Still, he presses forward.

It takes a long time to break through the wall of titankin, but he and Mydei do, leaving the men behind as they press further and further into the opposing forces. Phainon finds himself surrounded, but he cuts the titankin down like branches, carving out a path and keeping count. Soon, his tally climbs to fifty. His breath comes in harsh pants, but he fights, because for every monster he kills now, he keeps one of the men from having to fight it instead. 

He stumbles over the rubble of ruined roads and houses, uneven, unkempt fields. He tramples laundry ripped from clotheslines and dead flowers from overturned window boxes. He finds the remains of people’s livelihoods underfoot, and it’s a grievous thing. He knows what it’s like to watch a city burn and crumble at the seams. But this… this is terribly lonely.

Aedes Elysiae had been alight with flames. These neighborhoods of Castrum Kremnos are shrouded in darkness and ground to dust. Perhaps this is what the ashes looked like, after the fires went out.

A hand grabs his wrist, and he startles, lashing out with an elbow before he sees who it is. Mydei catches the blow before it can connect. Phainon relaxes and makes a face at him, pulling free. Mydei makes a face back, then points with his thumb to a clump of shadows in the darkness. Titankin in wait. Phainon squints to see in the dark. They go the opposite direction, Mydei pulling him along and inside of a mostly intact building. It's darker here without so much as the stars to provide light. A tiny flame bursts to life as Mydei strikes a match. Phainon watches him use it to search along the walls until he finds a sconce to steal the candles from. He lights these too, and comes back. The fires flicker on his face. He pulls out one of his earplugs and winces. Phainon hesitates, but he does too. The war cries flood his ears immediately, not as loud as they'd been the last time, but still deafening outside of a fight, still enough to make his limbs itch.

"What's the plan?" he asks, taking one of the candles when Mydei holds it out to him. It flickers rapidly against the breeze of his breath. Wax drips over the backs of his fingers. "We follow the noise," Mydei tells him. "We find Nikador, and we put an end to this." His voice is rough. There's blood on him, but his hair is miraculously clean, if tangled from wind and motion.

"And what about the titankin?" Phainon asks. They're a hindrance at the very least. A genuine threat at worst. "They're everywhere, hiding in the dark. Is this a stealth mission, or are we brute-forcing our way through?"

Mydei's lips quirk. Perhaps the war cries are getting to him, but his expression is wicked. "What's your tally at?"

Phainon smiles back. He can feel the blood in his veins, the way it starts to sing. "Fifty-six," he answers. "Yours?"

"Fifty-nine."

Three more. How had he killed three more? Phainon had been terribly fast. How had Mydei been faster? "Brute forcing, then," he says. "I'll take that as my chance to catch up. I hope you’re not mixing up your numbers."

Mydei scoffs. "I can count just fine, Deliverer. You'll just have to handle watching the gap between us grow."

"Yes," Phainon agrees. "There will be a huge gap by the time we're done with this. One in my favor. Just wait, Mydeimos. You won't be so cocky when I'm the one who wins."

"Show me, then," Mydei tells him. "Follow the noise. Meet me where the god is, and we'll see who’s the real winner."

△

Gradually, Phainon’s eyes adjust to the dark. He isn’t used to it; at first he’s overly cautious as he walks, squinting into the night for fear of things he might stumble over or uneven ground. This wastes precious time, and soon he realizes that there’s little hope of catching up to Mydei if he’s afraid of the dark, so he presses on and keeps an eye out for titankin.

His tally is up to sixty-three before the sound of the cries grows loud enough to leak through his earplugs. It starts by making him anxious. The titankin are sparser here, most of their ranks having made their way to the battlefield, but they still lurk in the darkness. Phainon can’t hear them coming. Fight or flight is a precipice, and he stands right on the edge.

His tally climbs to sixty-seven. The cries get louder. His heart in his ears gets faster. The air feels thin. He has too much energy and not enough to fight to quell it. He takes deep, slow breaths as best as he can. Tries to drown it out, tries to halt his will to fight. Mydei had suggested that as the cause. He said Nikador’s cries only amplify bloodlust, not create it, so maybe if he can make himself relax he can loosen the hold it has on him.

One breath in. He imagines a smiling face and a hand ruffling through his hair. Her laughter, her promises, the sound of her voice when she sang.

A titankin breaks through the shadows. He growls and wrenches his sword up, cleaving it in two. Sixty-eight. Her blood shed. His town on fire. The feeling in his chest is enough to raze a town.

He runs, feet pounding, needing an outlet for the energy, the hopelessness, the fury, the loss. At the racket he makes, he attracts titankin like moths to flame. Six more of them fall to pieces under his sword, and then he’s left, panting and blood splattered in a ring of corpses. Seventy-four. He drops his sword and covers his ears with his hands, hoping to ease the sound, the sensation.

Deep breaths. He’s trembling. The titankin here did not kill his family. Castrum Kremnos is not his home. He rubs his knuckles into his brow and forces himself to calm down.

He can work with this, he thinks. For now, he needs his head, but bloodlust will be good. He’ll need it. He’ll need the drive, the extra strength in his bones.

Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, to be bearer of the Strife coreflame. He breathes. Can’t shake that monstrous feeling. Is that what Strife feels like? Will he have to carry that with him for the rest of his days?

He squeezes his eyes shut. When he opens them again, the gold thread on his finger has manifested, stretching ahead and to the left, glowing just enough to illuminate his path. His breath stills. He stops thinking, and the feeling is gone. Slow, he bends for his sword and follows it.

He doesn’t know what it means. Mydei is… what, thinking about him? In danger? Their string has appeared in proximity, when Phainon wills it to, or when his thoughts turn to Mydei more than in passing, but never like this, and he doesn’t think he’s ever willed Mydei’s side into being.

But their strings turned gold, and Aglaea has yet to reply to him in earnest. It would not be my place to speak on the change, she’d written in her latest letter. It’s between you.

He’d almost taken it for a joke, albeit a bad one, but he’s still left without answers. Maybe the change in color means changes in function too. Maybe… He doesn’t know. He just follows it, using the glow to find his way, focused enough that the cries that leak through his earplugs don’t affect him more than a bad headache.

At the end of it, he finds Mydei covered in gold. His hands to the forearm, his clothes and armor splattered in it. His face, his hair. Their thread winds around his arm to the elbow, leading Phainon to him. He has a boot against a titankin’s chest, his hands on its head as he breaks its neck and kicks the body aside.

He doesn’t notice Phainon until he’s left standing, chest heaving, shoving his hair out of his face. And then he turns to follow the string, finding Phainon standing there. His body makes an aborted motion, and then he stills, fists clenching at his sides.

Nikador is close, Phainon thinks. They can both feel it. As he steps closer, Mydei holds up a hand to stop him. It curls quickly into a fist, lowers as he shakes. In the light from the string, with dark adjusted vision, Phainon watches Mydei’s eyes squeeze shut. He’s afraid of himself again. The things he could do if he listened to the voice in his head. He needs to cut off the will to fight, to make it so there’s nothing for Nikador to amplify, but how?

There’s nothing left to slaughter here. Would gentleness help, or would coming closer only make it all worse?

Trust is a strange thing. Phainon takes a breath to steady his nerves and steps up to Mydei, whose eyes are still closed, unable to see or hear as he approaches. He flinches when Phainon cups his face in his hands, eyes snapping open, glinting with panic in the glow of their string. He tries to pull back, but Phainon follows, shaking his head and miming a big breath. Mydei’s hands land on his waist, gauntlets scraping his plate, gripping him too tight. Shaking. A mirror of that first battle, of them on the ground.

He holds himself back, and he breathes. Phainon gives him a smile as he starts to relax. Slowly, he lets go to remove one of his own earplugs. A bit hesitant, Mydei follows suit. They both wince at the sound.

“You were right,” Phainon tells him. “It only works if there’s something to amplify. You just… need to not want to fight.”

Mydei’s laugh is rough and shaken. He’d really been scared, hadn’t he? It’s that monstrous feeling. The possibility that he might be capable of hurting someone he cares about. He’s lucky he met Phainon for a match.

“Easier said than done,” Mydei says. “I always want to fight you.”

Phainon laughs too. His doesn’t come out quite right either. “I’m at seventy-four,” he says. “What’s your tally?”

A frown. Mydei kicks the body of the broken-necked titankin again. “Seventy-four,” he answers. “We tied.” They share a flinch under Nikador’s next cry. The ground shakes with it. “They’re close,” Mydei murmurs. He’s gravely sober. Phainon studies him in dim gold light.

“Our string,” he says. “Why did it appear?” Now, proximity and attention to it keep it manifested, but earlier? “Were you thinking of me?”

“No,” Mydei says, and frowns. “I thought…” He trails off. He thinks it was Phainon’s doing.

“It wasn’t me,” Phainon says.

Mydei shrugs. “Perhaps it knew that I needed you.”

△

Nikador’s divine body is in a temple, high ceilinged and grand, with stained glass windows and stone spires. It towers over everything amidst the rubble, and if Phainon were the titan gone mad, perhaps he’d hole up here too.

The earth rumbles as they approach, quakes as they pull the wide doors open. The entrance is dark and gaping, and Mydei’s step only falters for a moment before he presses inside. Phainon keeps pace, not stopping to ask if he’s ready, if he’s worried. This has been Mydei’s mission for months, since before they met. He isn’t going to slow him down now. He just stays steady, careful with his footing, using the light of their thread to guide him, following the roars.

He steels himself for the battle ahead, hands curling into fists, the anticipation spiking the bloodlust, letting the cries into his head. It’s all he can do to calm himself. Mydei too. But they need clear heads now more than ever. When the fighting starts, then, the fervor will help. For now, he only hopes to watch Mydei’s back, to save the people. Together, he realizes, they’re going to slay a god.

Mydei’s hands are in fists. He’s wound the thread around the length of his arm for the illumination, a dozen times around his hand so it’s like he’s holding a lamp. Phainon’s head splits from the force of the cries. His heart pounds like nothing else. They push the doors to the main room of the temple open, and Nikador is there amidst broken and upturned pews, an altar cracked down the center, beautiful stained glass windows shattered across the floor.

There are fires lit in sconces along the walls, blazing dangerously bright, white hot at their cores. The contrast in light levels hurts Phainon’s eyes, and as he squints, gripping his sword, Nikador rises, tall enough to match three men standing on each other’s heads even as they stoop, supported by the lance in their hands. They’re long limbed, towering, and faceless, with a body like stone or armor or some kind of carapace. Strife, in the flesh.

Phainon cranes his head to look, ice in his veins. A deep, slow breath. He fixes his footing, hefts his sword. Mydei takes a step forward as Nikador hauls themself up with their lance, voice booming. He glances at Phainon over his shoulder, eyes steely. He nods. Phainon nods back, and together, they charge.

Nikador roars as they approach, brandishing their lance, swinging it when they come close. Mydei rolls under it, keeping his momentum as Phainon is forced to swerve. It means Mydei gets there first, slashing at the titan’s leg before he has to retreat from a kick.

Phainon comes to Nikador’s flank, but he’s met with little success as the titan swings the butt of their lance at him. He dodges and comes back, cutting into Nikador’s leg, drawing ichor before the wound seals right back up.

A careful retreat, a comeback. Seconds pass. Mydei has the same problem; they don’t have the reach that they need, or the power to cause wounds of any significant scale. They’re like ants with toothpicks, poking and prodding. Each time, the titan bats them away and grows angrier, calling weapons from the sky and the earth. Phainon takes a cut to the upper arm. Mydei nearly loses a hand entirely.

They need to get higher. A little bit longer, and an opportunity presents itself.

“Foothold!” Mydei shouts, spinning away from Nikador’s sweeping hand. The ground shakes as Nikador calls their lances up from the earth, the floor groaning as it splits. Phainon dodges the points of two, a third catching his cloak, creating a tear. Phainon hisses as he focuses on getting closer, tucking his sword close to his side as he runs, catching the shaft of one of the lances and using it to change his course, charging the titan.

Mydei encases Nikador’s foot in crystal, distracting them long enough for Phainon to stab his sword into their hip, pushing it in as far as he can. Nikador’s body doesn’t cut like flesh, it cuts like stone. His sword gets stuck, but that’s what he wanted. Gritting his teeth, he uses it to haul himself up, scrabbling for purchase as he gets a foot on the flat of the blade, fingers finding the ridges at the titan’s joints to hold on. He fights a wave of vertigo as the titan tries to shake him off. A colossal hand descends toward him, but Mydei yells and knocks it aside.

Phainon pushes himself up, clinging with sore fingers, and climbs onto Nikador’s back, holding tight with his legs, slipping the knife he keeps at his waist free from its sheath. He slams it into what must be Nikador’s neck savagely and yanks it back out. Ichor spills. Please, he thinks, and does it again. The titan screams, splitting his head from the inside out, blurring his vision as he fights the onset of numbness to carve—

He’s thrown off, knife clattering to the ground, slamming back first into the ground. It knocks the wind from him, stars in his vision, ears ringing. Bruises. He’ll have plenty of those. Fighting the nauseous, dazed feeling, he pushes himself up, wiping a tear from his eye to watch Mydei climb the broken altar and kick Phainon’s sword out of the titan, slicing through it on the way out. The spray of gold reaches all the way to Phainon on the ground, hauling himself up and seizing his knife and sword both.

As he races back into the fight, Nikador’s voice booms and they run their lance through Mydei’s stomach. Mydei barely stumbles back a handful of steps, hands circling the body of the weapon. As Nikador pulls it out, he falls to his knees, bleeding through his fingers over the hole in his abdomen.

He won’t die from it, Phainon knows, but the feeling rips through him like watching his hometown burn all over again. A cry tears from his throat. He throws himself in front of the titan’s next blow, blocking it with his sword as Mydei recovers. The weight is enough to bend him; he falls to one knee and Mydei curses him from behind.

“HKS,” he grits, rough and bloody. The titan presses harder, trying to squash him. Mydei heals, stands up. “I’m fine,” he says, and Phainon barely spares a glance to make sure he’s out of the way before giving under the pressure and throwing himself through the gap between the titan’s legs.

He expects them to turn, but they don’t. They’re uninterested in Phainon, focusing on Mydei, backing him up against the wall. His footing is steady. Nikador advances on him, forgetting Phainon in the moments it takes to corner their prey, lifting their lance. Mydei doesn’t move, freshly healed and standing his ground amidst firelight and cracked pews. He waits, just a little longer. Phainon runs like his life depends on it—and maybe it does, maybe Mydei’s does too — and reaches Nikador’s back.

The lance comes down just as Mydei leaps out of the way, momentum sending him skidding and falling to his knees. The wall crumbles like nothing more than packed dirt and Phainon thrusts his sword into Nikador’s leg, carving like he might hamstring the god. The sound is deafening: the roar Nikador lets out, the crash of rubble, Mydei screaming for Phainon to move.

Heart thundering, sight gone red, entire body thrumming with adrenaline and sheer terror, Phainon yanks his sword free and moves out of the way before the wall or the stumbling titan can crush him under their weight.

A breeze blows in from the hole in the wall where Nikador’s lance tore through it like paper. Fire flickers beneath piles of stone, catching the edges of a pew and setting it alight. Nikador kneels, their leg wounded, dazed by the consequences of their own demolition. Phainon pants for breath. His hands are numb where they grip the hilt of his sword.

Mydei is on the ground, dragging himself up as a wound in his head from a rock hitting him crystallizes and heals. They need to run, Phainon knows. They need to take advantage of the time they’ve bought, of the titan’s brief vulnerability, but his body won’t move, too stubborn, too scared. He curses himself.

And then, under the rubble, there comes the sound of human suffering. Two soldiers, a third crushed under piles of stone that the first two struggle to lift. Where had they come from? Who are they and why are they here? But it doesn’t matter; at that moment, the plan changes. Phainon is closer to them, but Mydei is running, and as he passes he pulls Phainon along too. Nikador struggles to pull their lance free from the destroyed wall, buying them precious seconds.

Together, they lift, but the wounded soldier does not crawl out when given the chance. Breath coming fast, panic and adrenaline seizing his chest, Phainon looks down. Where the rubble had rested is a mutilated, bloody excuse for a back. This man is dead; Mydei realizes it too, because he drops the stone and stumbles back.

“Go!” he shouts to the remaining two soldiers. They’re closer to boys than men, wide eyed and fearful in a way that shows that this is their first run in with a battlefield. One is Kremnoan, the other Okheman, and he wonders what they’d been thinking. Of glory, perhaps. Of helping the Chrysos Heirs in slaying a god and coming home heroes. One’s arm hangs down with a dislocated shoulder. The other appears to have been gouged in the leg. It’s a miracle he can stand at all.

And then Nikador shouts, furious, pulling their lance free with enough momentum to send themself stumbling. And again, Mydei roars, “Go!” But the soldiers are on the ground tearing at their ears and letting out screams like the pressure is enough to split their heads.

Sharp pain in Phainon’s temples. His vision tunnels, and he doesn’t know what to do. Nikador lumbers toward them. These boys are in no position to run. Helpless, he turns to Mydei, whose expression reminds him of the men in Aedes Elysiae, and the sensation he’s flooded with isn’t overwhelming bloodlust but sheer, crippling terror. The cries, it seems, amplify that too.

“Go.” This time Mydei addresses him. “Take them, Deliverer.”

No. A lance through his spine. His head on the ground, hair matting in a pool of liquid gold. Eyes lifeless and empty. You’re going to be a hero. A laugh. Blood on Phainon’s hands. “I can’t,” he says. No. What about you?

“You can,” Mydei insists, furious with him. A blood vessel has popped in his eye, darkening the white. So much screaming. So much fire, blazing on the walls and catching wooden pews and wreckage where the wall coming down sent the torches flying. A city burning down. Phainon is there, and everyone he loves is dying.

Not you too, he thinks, and watches one of the soldiers draw blood as the screaming turns to pained whimpers. Not you too.

A gauntleted hand grabs his face, sharp points digging into his cheeks as Mydei seizes his chin and forces him to look. Behind him, Nikador stumbles and straightens up, leaning heavily on their lance, still roaring.

“Phainon,” Mydei says, and Phainon finally looks. The urgency in his eyes. The fight still there. He isn’t afraid, not of this. “I can’t die. They can. Take them.”

Lives in his hands. His breath comes too fast, too shallowly. “What about you?”

Mydei’s grip softens. Their thread glows hot as he forces a smile. “I’ll be fine.”

Phainon kisses Mydei hard, just once, just enough to cut his lip on teeth before he shoves Mydei away, letting him loose to save them. “I’ll be back!” he shouts as Mydei turns to face the enemy.

One more glance spared over a bare shoulder. Mydei grins and sets his feet. “You’d better,” he responds, and pushes off the ground into a sprint, charging Nikador before they can think to come this way.

Phainon turns away from the fight, crouching to the soldiers, maddened and still clutching their heads. “I’m sorry,” he murmurs, and strikes each in the neck, hard enough to incapacitate but not to kill. He catches their heads before they can fall, and drags each by the armpits to the exit, hauling them each through the first set of double doors and pushing them shut.

The ground shakes beneath them. The clamor of the battle inside is enough for Phainon to choke on. His head pounds with his heart. He can’t lift two men at once, but he forces himself to take turns dragging them down the hall and outside of the temple.

They’ll die if he leaves them here, bleeding out, lost in the black tide, titankin roaming and ready to kill. He’ll have to take them all the way back, but how? This is too slow, and every second he wastes is another Mydei has to fight alone.

With some deliberation, he tears a flag from the window of an abandoned home. It’s thick, sturdy fabric, and he cuts notches into one side with the knife at his waist so he can tie it to a plank he finds somewhere in the rubble.

One of the soldiers stirs as Phainon sets him on the flag. Pained and delirious, he accepts the handful of fabric Phainon stuffs into his hand. “Hold this,” he says, and then gestures at the other soldier, still asleep. “Make sure he doesn’t fall out.”

With that, he lifts the plank, setting it on his shoulders so he can drag both the men at once. It’s back breaking, unideal work, but he can’t find a wagon or a cart in the dark, destroyed neighborhood. Until he spots one, or until the men can walk, this is what he’ll have to work with.

One step at a time. His lungs strain. Sweat drips down his everything. Splinters dig their way into his palms. But without him, these men will die, injured and exhausted and corrupted by the sound of the war cries. Without him, Mydei’s sacrifice will be for nothing.

It rolls over and over in his head. As he stops to fight a group of titankin, it’s all that he can think about. As he picks up the plank again after, it’s all that lets him return to the rhythm of labored steps. Every bit of him burns. Is Mydei in worse pain? He heals in an instant, but Phainon knows he still feels the hurt. He can’t die, but for one spot. He’ll be careful to guard it in Phainon’s absence. Phainon will come back, and he’ll still be fighting as strong as ever, a mess of blood and sweat and dirt, but alive all the same.

Phainon grunts as he presses harder. The ground inclines just slightly, making this a dozen times harder, but he can’t afford to slow down. The soldiers are dead weight. The next time he pauses for a fight, he steps around the corpses of titankin and checks to make sure they’re still breathing.

The one with the dislocated shoulder stares at him with confused, clouded eyes. He’s breathing, but blood leaks out his ears, and he doesn’t respond when Phainon speaks to him. The one with the wounded leg is similar, bleary but alive. He replies in a weak voice. The fistful of fabric Phainon gave to him is still clutched in his white-knuckled hand.

He drags them all the way back to the battlefield, pausing to move the bodies of titankin and men alike out of the way to clear a path. It feels like he’s been pulling them for so long that he can no longer feel the pain in his muscles, just the rubbery, mechanical sensation of strain. One foot after the other. Minutes, seconds, hours pass. He stumbles into the crowd of remaining soldiers. There, he finds Castorice kneeling, skirts tucked under her, hem blotted with blood. She has the head of a boy no more than seventeen in her lap, his body mutilated beyond repair, blooming with purple flowers as she slides her fingers over his closed eyelids. Gaze downturned, she guides the survivors in prayer.

When she’s finished, she looks up from the ash in her lap, tears streaming down her cheeks, and finds Phainon. The men around her kneel, heads bowed to the dead and the dying, and somehow Phainon begins to weep too.

△

Phainon is given water and dried meat and cheese while he explains the situation to Castorice, Krateros, and a group of their highest ranking generals. The soldiers he’d dragged have been carted off to the healers, and as much as Phainon wants to race back now that his task is done, his body won’t let him.

After a chance to rest, he trembles as he walks, legs weak and unsteady, feet blistered and aching, chafed all over from his plate. He can barely lift his sword, let alone swing it, and the headache that splits his head is enough to make his vision swim and his stomach turn.

He’ll be of no use to Mydei like this, he knows. So for now, he nibbles on jerky and tries to be patient with his own recovery. On his finger, the string blazes gold, leading into the distance where he knows Mydei fights. Still alive, still fending off the titan.

“You need help,” Castorice says. Her eyes are swollen and tearstained, hands folded in her lap.

“Ordinary soldiers can’t follow,” Krateros reminds them. “Just look at what happened.”

She wipes her eyes with the back of one gloved hand. A gentle soul. The opposite of Strife. “I’ll go,” she volunteers.

“Lord Phainon is out of commission.”

“I’m not!” Phainon protests, slamming a fist into his thigh. “I can fight. After a bit of rest I’ll be fine. I’m not leaving them to face a god on their own. I promised Mydei I would come back.” Silence stretches. Phainon’s face heats, but he doesn’t know what he has to be embarrassed for. Just the way they look at him.

Krateros laughs softly, but his expression is still sober. “Headstrong boy,” he sighs. “He would choose you.”

“I…”

“Phainon will see the healers and rest a bit longer, and then we will go,” Castorice says, clearing her throat. Leadership is awkward on her shoulders, but she’s trying. A lump forms again in Phainon’s throat; he’s terrified he might cry again.

“Every second we waste here,” he says, “is another that Mydei fights alone.” His hand stretches back for the hilt of his sword, needing to squeeze something, needing— He looks down. What he finds is not his sword, but a coin. Gold, emblazoned with the shape of a cat. “I…”

“It sounds like—” comes a voice. Heeled shoes come next as their owner flips delicately into their circle. She fumbles with Phainon’s sword for a moment, finding it too tall or too heavy, before she chooses to lean on it, long tail flicking, free hand adjusting the hood on her head. Cipher smiles when Phainon looks up, the points of her canine teeth sharp. She bends a little, fingers around the hilt of Phainon’s sword, her other hand folding behind her back. “—You need a messenger.”

Chapter Notes

warning again for violence, gore, and injury

Child of Strife.

The lance catches him in the side, tearing through muscle and flesh, spraying ichor. Mydei catches the shaft and stumbles back. One step, two. The pain is blinding. Nikador rips the weapon free and he falls to his knees, clutching the wound as his body knits itself back together. His head throbs. He only goes through the motions on autopilot.

Fight, fall, force yourself back up. Crystal falls away to reveal untouched skin, pale and clean against the blood and dirt crusted on the rest of him. Nikador waits for him to stand, shaky on overused muscles, on fragile, freshly formed flesh. The pain stays long after the wound does. Mydei is immortal, but he isn’t impervious.

One foot, then the other. He rises, tilts his head up, fixes his stance. Nikador raises their lance, shouts something the splits Mydei’s ears and makes the ground rumble. Rubble falls from cracks in the ceiling. The air smells like smoke from the blazing pews set alight by fallen sconces.

Mydei dodges the titan’s strike, entire body protesting every moment. The pain slows him down, the throb in his head, the way he can barely think. Energy deserts him. The war cries do nothing more than bleed his ears and make him restless. He takes another hit, this one to the thigh, cracking his armor and sending him crashing back to the ground.

Child of Strife, comes the voice again. He looks up. Again, Nikador waits. Maybe that’s their Honor, to not kick an opponent while they’re down. Mydei’s hands curl into fists on the ground. Dirt, ash, splinters. His thigh spasms as it mends itself. Vision swimming, he undoes the straps on the broken piece of plate and pulls it off. Beneath, his pants are torn and stained with gold. Again, he stands. The titan lifts their weapon, and he charges, timing it just right, jumping in time to kick off the hilt of the lance and catch Nikador across the chest, drawing blood with his gauntlets, roaring with some kind of tired satisfaction before the titan shoves him off and sends him flying.

He hits his head on the way down, skin lacerating as he skids on the ground. He’s blinded briefly, robbed of breath. Again, Nikador waits for him to rise.

Why do you fight your destiny?

An image behind his eyelids. A red, crystal throne. When he opens his eyes, it’s gone. He pushes himself up. Charges despite the pain, the exhaustion, and trades a handful of blows with the titan. And again, the lance cuts through him and he falls, bruising his body on rubble, a piece of the wall cracking him straight in the forehead.

Child of Strife, the voice insists. Deep, gravelly. Nikador’s voice, or the voice or whatever is inside of them.

I’m not, he thinks back, and feels them make an inquisitive sound in reply.

Laying there as he heals, he’s almost tempted to stay down. He’s never endured this kind of agony in his life. Not even floating down the icy River of Souls felt like this. But pain is always forgotten with time.

He thinks of the people. The villages Nikador will crush if Mydei isn’t here to distract them. Slowly, he drags himself upright.

So much blood in a body. He watches his torso turn to golden gore. Slams into the wall and slumps, eyes cast down as the mess crystalizes and crumbles to reveal new flesh. He almost doesn’t feel the pain. He’s made of it. A little more is nothing at all.

Chosen of Strife, the voice says this time. You are strong. Why don’t you kill?

I’ve killed plenty, Mydei thinks back. His spear in his father’s chest. His boot against a soldier’s skull. His gauntlets tearing through throat after throat. The path behind him is stained in red and gold alike.

He stumbles as he stands. Nikador strikes him down again. Stands there, looming. A hundred deaths, they seem to say, how many more will it take to make you crumble? The image of a town leveled. Bodies broken, children crying, blood pooling in the streets.

No, Mydei thinks, and catches the titan’s lance before it can connect again, gritting his teeth, screaming his throat raw as he snaps the thing in half, slicing through himself for leverage in the process, falling to his knees and cradling the metal point, laughing as the titan roars and splits the sky to rain him into pulp.

It takes a long time to heal from this. As he waits, he listens to fire crackle, smells the smoke. Realizes he’s burning alive amidst the pews as he smells his own cooked flesh. He drags himself on charred, torn limbs. Lays there and wants nothing more than to never get up. Still, the titan waits.

You fight to protect? The voice asks.

Yes, Mydei thinks.

The image of the throne again. Red crystal, gleaming in firelight. Become stronger, and you can protect anything. The sound of a laugh in his ears, wheezing and contagious, long memorized. A gold thread on his finger, still manifest and furiously glowing when he peels his eyes open to look. His whole body is a scab. His hand twitches, and pain floods him, so he stays down a little longer.

Become stronger, the voice says again. It shows him Kremnos on fire. It shows him the men in the Kremnoan Detachment, throats slit, eyes empty, limbs broken and twisting in ways they shouldn’t. It shows him Krateros with his good eye gouged from his face, choking on his own blood. It shows him the children, it shows them—

Stop, Mydei thinks. “Stop,” he says it aloud, voice like sandpaper, throat sore and destroyed. Crystal flakes from him as he pushes himself to all fours, then to his feet. Everything in him screams with pain. Nikador comes at him bare handed, and he fights. Still, he falls, gurgling as a claw punctures his neck. He can’t breathe as it turns to crystal; the healing is its own kind of agony. He chokes, asphyxiates, tears spilling down his temples as he spasms.

Protect them, the voice demands. More bloodshed. Friends, new and old, crumpled and twisted and mutilated. You’re too weak. How will you protect them?

He gasps for breath as the crystal flakes away and allows him his lungs again. He rolls onto his knees, propped on his forearms as he spits blood and saliva to the earth. Nikador roars at him and pins him back down with one heavy hand as soon as he manages to right himself. Blood leaks out his ears at the noise. He watches his tears mix with dust as cringes away from it.

The weight of the titan fractures both legs and some of his ribs. More of the wall comes crumbling, too far to bury him, but close enough that he’s hit with some of the rubble too. This next death is just as agonizing as the last. Nikador stalks off as he heals, growing bored or restless or tired of him.

Weak, the voice curses. It shows him Phainon next. His smile, and then his body broken beneath the titan’s hands. Protect this one, Chosen, or we will tear him limb from limb.

Why? Mydei thinks. His bones scream, freshly mended, as he stands and throws himself at Nikador again, drawing blood even as he’s knocked down again.

He’s not strong enough yet, the voice tells him. We don’t want him, Chosen. We reject him. He is meant for other things.

Stop calling me that.

The next death, he’s crushed under rubble. He dies three more times digging himself out.

Chosen, the titan says again. He tears their arm from its socket, laughing as they screech and stumble back, finding the broken hilt of their lance and throwing it straight through his chest.

Chosen, they roar as he chokes on his own blood. He will fail our trial, should he take it. We will break him from the inside out. He isn’t strong enough, but you must be.

No, Mydei repeats, over and over. He tears the wood out of his chest, nearly falls on his face as he waits for the wound to heal again. No.

Chosen of Strife, Child of Strife. Son of Gorgo to be crowned in blood, Undying Prince—

A flash of light, enough to blind him and Nikador both, the titan armless and screeching as a girl in a dress adorned with butterflies brushes past Mydei, her shin brushing his elbow, a field of flowers blooming beneath Nikador’s feet, holding them in place for golden threads to bind them, tying them down, pinning them to the earth for a screaming boy with a greatsword to climb onto their shoulders and sever their head.

And then it’s over, and there’s a flash as the coreflame lifts from the dead, divine body, golden threads receding, flowers fading away. The ladies Tribios shut the Gate of Infinity. Castorice lowers her scythe. Aglaea clasps her hands behind her back and steps toward the fallen titan. Her hair curls around her neck. Her shoes clack softly. It’s finally quiet.

Phainon falls off the back of the titan, slipping in ichor and cursing, coreflame in hand, and Mydei… Mydei is crushed with relief. His knees, aching and exhausted from holding steady, give beneath him. He crashes, graceless, and watches the heads that turn his way.

A soft tail brushes his shoulders. A gray haired girl bends to look at him, ears twitching atop her head. “That must’ve hurt,” she says lightly.

Castorice comes next, kneeling close but not nearly close enough to touch him. “Lord Mydeimos,” she says, visibly worried. “Will you be alright?”

The ladies Tribios next. “De!” one exclaims. “We’ll make sure you’re right as rain in no time,” comes the next. “Does it hurt?” asks the last.

Aglaea watches him with careful, calculating eyes.

Behind them all, Phainon struggles to his feet, slips in blood again, and stumbles all the way to where Mydei is kneeling, rambling the whole way until he’s there, crashing to his knees and looking Mydei over with more warmth and worry than he’s ever had directed toward him in his life.

“Kephale above,” he says, and his voice is a horribly shaky thing. He curses, and his eyes are glassy and watering with emotion. “I’m sorry,” he says, fretting. His hands flutter, trying to find somewhere safe to touch like he knows the pain stays even after the wounds are long gone. He’s a mess of blood and sweat and dirt, and his fingertips brush Mydei’s cheek. “I wish I could’ve come sooner, I—”

“I’m fine,” Mydei murmurs. His voice is like broken glass. He tries to address everyone, but his gaze won’t stray from Phainon. So much gold. His cheek is gooey and scabbed. His hair is matted in places and fluffed up in others. So gentle, he brushes Mydei’s bangs from his eyes with the hand tied with the string. Gold, until suddenly it’s shot with red on his end, rapidly spreading.

“Titans,” he breathes. “Are you sure, I…”

Safe, finally, in the aftermath. Mydei’s entire, aching body caves. His head falls against Phainon’s shoulder, too tired to care about their audience, too tired to be strong. “Deliverer,” he says, shutting his eyes. Phainon reeks of blood and sweat. Mydei is no better. “I’m fine.”

He can feel the way Phainon shudders against him. Feel the hand that settles so lightly in his hair, not even carding through it for fear of pulling on knots. “I really wish you wouldn’t call me that,” Phainon says, so softly.

“It’s not a jab,” Mydei tells him. The words hurt, everything hurts. There isn’t a wound on him but he feels like one raw nerve, tortured and abused and beaten again and again. He lost count of how many times he would have died, were he mortal. “Not anymore. It means I believe in you.”

“I—”

“Get me home safe,” Mydei says, the last bits of strength leaving him. Out of adrenaline and exhausted, he gives his weight to Phainon, who catches him. “I’ll kill you if you don’t,” he adds, but there’s no heat behind it. He’s too weak, too…

He loses his train of thought. Forgets everything but the aches and the sensation of being lifted. His head against an armored chest. An arm around his back, another beneath his knees. He might lose consciousness. Stirs to rocking, to the sound of voices.

“You’re exhausted, Phainon.”

Heavy breathing. A thundering heart beneath his ear. When he cracks one tired eye open, a sun engraved into metal. A red and gold string. Glowing firelight. Old, uneven cobblestones, the worn facades of broken buildings. His eyes slip shut again.

“I can do this much,” someone pants. A cheek against Mydei’s bloody hair, a mouth against his forehead. “I have to do this much.”

△

He wakes slowly. A breath first. The sensation of sheets against his skin. The smell of indigo and pine.

The pain is still there, though it’s dull and aching rather than sharp. The memory of each wound still sits, even if the scars do not, and Mydei is long accustomed to hurt, to healing, but he’s never felt fragile like this. His eyes are dry and itchy when he cracks them open, crusted at the corners.

First he sees the ceiling, the window. His room in Castrum Kremnos. His crimson sheets. His gold string, glowing softly under his nose until he moves his hand and turns his head slowly, gingerly for the pain in his neck. It’s a strange gradient now, gold on his end, red on Phainon’s. The glow it emits is warm and bloody. Mydei meets Phainon’s eyes, finding him intense and unsmiling, cheek propped on his arm as he lays on his side beside him.

“Hey,” he murmurs. He has the blankets puddled around his waist, dressed down and soft, hair clean and tousled. Mydei is clean too; he notices this now. He’s dressed in some of his own sleep clothes, hair washed and rebraided. Phainon’s work. Mydei must’ve slept through it.

It’s strange to imagine that. His own helplessness. His equal’s kind hands.

His entire body still aches. “You brought me back,” Mydei croaks. His voice is a frightening thing.

Phainon still stares, not smiling, not doing anything but looking. His gaze flicks between each of Mydei’s eyes in turn, then to his chest, his bare hands, and back up. “Of course I did,” he says. “You asked me to.”

He hadn’t meant it in a way to create this kind of intensity. They could have strapped him to a dromas or tossed him in a cart, but he remembers being carried. Phainon carrying him. Mydei is not small or light, and they were a long way from the healers’ tent. He’s almost embarrassed.

“I took the liberty of washing you too,” Phainon tells him. “I figured you wouldn’t want to wake covered in gore, but… forgive me if I was presumptuous.”

At this, Mydei gives a rough, painful laugh. “I don’t care, Deliverer,” he says. “It’s not like you haven’t seen it all already.”

Phainon’s lips part and close again. His expression is complicated, serious. But even now he looks like some wet dog in the rain. “Still,” he breathes, reaching out to brush away Mydei’s bangs and touch the backs of two fingers to his brow.

“I can’t get sick,” Mydei reminds him. He reaches up to take Phainon’s hand, even as his muscles protest. Red and gold. Phainon’s fingers are long and thin, calloused at the joints and the palms. Mydei’s thicker and shorter, fingernails squared. Strangely, his palms are softer. Phainon seems to notice this too, running his thumb over the lines on the inside of his hand, gaze dipping in that direction.

With his eyes downturned, Mydei sees the emotion in his expression. Guilt.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon whispers. “I wish I could’ve—”

“Shut up,” Mydei cuts him off. Phainon does, gives a weak laugh.

“I should’ve figured you wouldn’t want to hear it,” he says, meeting Mydei’s eyes again, his still big and wet with emotion. “But still, I just… I wish I could’ve come back a little sooner and spared you even a little bit of the pain. My body gave out after I brought those men back to camp. I wanted to go back but I could hardly stand and—”

And yet you carried me all the way home.

“Equal,” Mydei hushes him. “Your body is not immortal. You did everything I asked of you.”

Phainon exhales a shuddery breath. His throat bobs as he swallows, fingers curling tighter around Mydei’s. “Does it still hurt?” he asks.

“Yes,” Mydei answers honestly. “But my people are alive and the titan is not. That’s enough.”

Phainon must see the truth in his face, because he lets this go. “Okay,” he says, and quiets. He pulls Mydei’s hand to his mouth and kisses the back of it, eyes sipping shut. He’s beautiful when he isn’t talking. The light catches his hair, his cheek. The way he’s bruised and scabbed and softened in the aftermath. Mydei’s husband, his equal. His teeth ache. He wants him, but he isn’t sure if his body will hold out.

“Why is it red?” he asks, eyeing the string.

“I don’t know,” Phainon admits. “One minute I was panicking and the next it was like this.”

Mydei grunts. He pulls Phainon’s hand closer, unfolding it so his fingers are spread. Phainon goes quiet and watches, doesn’t speak as Mydei brings his hand to his mouth and bites the place between his thumb and index finger. Not hard; he gets Phainon’s knuckle where he’s hoped to find flesh, but he still leaves the imprint of a tooth or two. 

“Wha—?”

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him, and kisses the side of his hand. Down more, the side of his wrist. Still bony, but he’s able to pull skin away with his teeth, biting and letting go, moving a bit further up and sinking his teeth in again, not enough to bruise but enough to interlock a second ring with the first, then a third a bit further up. He stops there, looking at his handiwork.

“What are you doing?” Phainon asks, seeming at a loss for words. Mydei has chosen an idiot for an equal. He sighs and slides his tired body closer, pulling Phainon’s arm around his back, pressing his face into his throat.

“Mydei?” Phainon says, searching. Tentatively, he settles, arm relaxing and sliding to a more comfortable spot, chin resting on Mydei’s head. His heart beats so fast; Mydei laughs a little, but that hurts too, so he quiets.

“Stop thinking,” he says, and sighs. Relief bows him even now. To fight for so long and wake up safe. Phainon is terribly warm; Mydei slides an arm around him, too exhausted to do anything other than stay. “None of it matters.”

A shaky laugh. Phainon’s palm covers his weak point, breath ruffling his hair. “Mydei,” he says again, “we killed a god. That kind of matters.”

Mydei grunts unhappily. “Shut up.”

“The trial is in three days,” Phainon tells him.

And that gives him pause. He opens his eyes to the sun on Phainon’s throat, the opening in his shirt pulled awkwardly to show his collarbone. The marks from Mydei’s teeth are gone from it. “Are you ready, then?” he asks. “To bear the coreflame of Strife?”

Hesitation. Phainon’s thundering pulse. Mydei breathes him in, pine and exhaustion. We don’t want him, Chosen. He will fail our trial, should he take it. He isn’t strong enough.

Phainon is gentle as much as he is strong. Mydei hasn’t given it much thought. Phainon as the incarnation of Strife. He just pushed that on him without thought for the consequences.

We reject him. We will break him from the inside out.

He’s strong, certainly. But he isn’t vengeful. Strife doesn't fit.

Suddenly, Mydei feels sick.

“I’m ready,” Phainon tells him. An obvious front. His voice wavers. He presses a little firmer on Mydei’s back. “I can do it.”

His stomach flips and turns. He swallows around a painful lump, twists sore fingers into the fabric of Phainon’s shirt. “Do you want to?” Why is this the first time he’s thought to ask?

More hesitation. “I want to save people,” Phainon answers. “I want…” A breath. “To be a hero. If this will help me do that, then yes. I want it. I’ll do it.”

△

They deliver the coreflame together after a day of rest. Phainon carries it, resolute and determined as Aglaea brings them to the Vortex of Genesis to restore it to its place. Mydei is still sore and aching just standing. It’s all the way in his bones, the consequences of regeneration, so he stays back and stays still when he can, not wanting to bare his weakness to the world.

Still, Phainon hovers about him. He frets and offers little things like water and candies, and it’s both amusing and aggravating. Their shoulders brush too often for it to be accidental. In reality, Phainon just stands far too close, inches closer whenever Mydei tries to put a bit of space between them.

Just like an overeager dog, Mydei thinks with both fondness and annoyance. He takes a step back and stretches an arm out to stop Phainon from following. Phainon glances at his hand, his face. Mydei raises an eyebrow, and he scrunches his nose back.

Aglaea stands before the basin with the Ladies Tribios, who pray on the waters together. Mydei turns his attention forward, to the glimmer of the water in the dark, the way the sky lights up, a constellation forming for each coreflame already recovered. The Lance of Fury’s spot is empty. He lets out a breath.

Aglaea steps back. “Come forward,” she says, turning to Phainon. “Return the coreflame.”

Phainon meets his gaze, seeking reassurance or permission or something else, Mydei doesn’t know. All he has to offer is a short nod. Phainon nods back, and then steps up to the basin, feet sending ripples through the shallow water on the floor. He exhales visibly, shoulders setting, and produces the coreflame of Strife in his cupped hands. It seems smaller than it should be. The authority of a god and the cost of Mydei’s country contained easily in two palms. It lifts from Phainon’s hands as he holds it out, hovering slightly until he draws back and it drops into the water with a splash, swallowed up and sucked in. Phainon returns to his side, reaching for his wrist. This time, Mydei lets him.

The sky changes and shifts as they watch, and when the blur calms, a new constellation is lit. Nikador’s voice echoes briefly in the language of the titans, and then all goes still. Aglaea turns to him, gold-green eyes unreadable. “It’s been a successful cooperation, Lord Mydeimos,” she says. “I believe your debt is paid in full.”

She doesn’t ask him again to join their cause, even if his blood runs gold like the rest of them. She turns to Phainon next. “I hope you’ll be ready when the trial opens,” she says. Phainon’s grip tightens around his wrist.

“Believe me,” he says, too lightly, “I will.”

We reject him, Mydei hears in the titan’s voice. He is meant for other things. The perfect vessel for divinity. He would be wasted on Strife. Protect this one, Chosen, or we will tear him limb from limb.

Crimson and gold thread. A fabricated smile. A burden like the one on Kephale’s back. Still, Mydei can’t bring himself to say a thing.

△

The black tide does not recede. Mydei walks through the lost pieces of his city, neighborhoods gone dark, homes reduced to rubble. The war cries have quieted. What titankin are left are few in number, but black tide creatures have begun to replace them instead.

He goes alone, fights alone with a weary, immortal body, and comes to realize that he’d been foolish to hope. Nikador’s madness was a symptom, not the cause, and little by little, Castrum Kremnos will continue to fall until the flame chase is complete and brings with it a new dawn.

Tonight, his people celebrate. They cheer for their salvation, and alone in the rubble of what was once a library, Mydei allows himself to weep for them. For the loss of their livelihoods, their homes, their safety. For their failure of a prince who wants nothing less than the throne.

Later, he picks himself up and dusts himself off. As he returns home, he finds Castorice under a tree.

“Haven’t you gone home yet?” he asks.

She looks up, squinting in the sun that still reaches these parts of the city. Her feet are bare, still blistered, shoes tucked neatly next to a bag filled with fabric and thread and stuffing. She’s sewing another plush, a chimera this time, finished but for the embroidery she does on its face.

“No,” she says softly. “Not yet.” Her eyes are as tired as he feels; perhaps that’s why he decides to sit with her. She makes room for him, tucking her legs beneath her, giving him more space than he needs, but less than she’s likely used to.

He remembers the brush of her shin at the end of the battle. So light it could’ve just been the fabric of her dress, accidental as she came through the Gate of Infinity, but he knows it wasn’t. And yet here he is, alive and breathing.

“What about you, Lord Mydeimos?” she asks.

He’s home, and he’s tired. In the aftermath, what is he meant to do?

He extends a hand. “Lady Castorice,” he says, “during the battle, I’m fairly certain you touched me.”

Her eyes widen. “What? No, I couldn’t have, or you’d be…”

“I can’t die,” he reminds her. He gestures lightly, hand still outstretched. “May I?”

Her expression is intense, cautious. And yet, as the body yearns for comfort, she reaches out. Their fingers brush, just lightly, and she withdraws her hand, waits with bated breath. Flowers don’t bloom across his skin. He doesn’t crumble to ash. “It doesn’t hurt?” she asks. “You don’t feel like… sleeping, or…”

“No,” Mydei tells her. “It’s safe.”

Her lip trembles. She purses them and reaches out again, setting her hand properly in his. Her palm is cold and small, and when nothing happens, when he doesn’t die, she pulls away again. “Pardon,” she says, and her voice is a bit shaky. “I apologize, I…”

Small comforts. Mydei still remembers the first warm touch after dragging himself from the cold of the River of Souls. He’s so tired, still aching. She gets it, he knows. “Would it help if I hugged you?” he asks.

“No,” Castorice says, and again, the calm of her expression wavers. “I don’t think so, but I’d like it if you would anyway.”

She’s terribly small when Mydei wraps his arms around her. The first friend he’s made in a while. Her hands ball into fists at his back, clinging tight, breathing unsteady, and she lets herself weep.

Small comforts. At least Mydei can do this much. He’s a bit unpracticed as he pats her back, but she doesn’t complain.

△

Phainon is there when he comes back. He’s polishing his sword amidst Mydei’s armor stands, a cloth in hand, the blade across his lap. He pauses when Mydei returns, eyeing the way he’s a bit bloodied, but he seems to know better than to comment. As the days go by, he seems to understand Mydei better.

With a sigh, Mydei sits in the chair opposite him and begins removing his armor piece by piece. “Why don’t you return to Okhema?” he asks.

Phainon lifts his eyebrows. “And leave you here until the trial?”

Are you ready? Mydei wonders. Do you want it? Are you strong enough? He feels like a bruise, inside and out. “I’ll be fine,” he says.

Phainon blinks, hesitates. “It’s not like I have anything urgent to attend to there at the moment,” he says. “Unless you’d like me out of sight for the time being?”

He’s terrible at hiding his insecurity. Mydei pulls his gauntlets off. Fiddles with their string in his hands. His end is still only gold.

It means you’re in love, Aglaea told him when he asked, laughing lightly. It doesn’t need to be anything overly complicated.

Why wouldn’t you tell Phainon, if it’s so simple?

She’d smiled at him then, a strange, impartial smile, like everything to her is as it is to an outsider. The consequence of being a little more than human for a long time, perhaps. Because, she’d said. He isn’t the one who’s afraid of it. Not anymore.

Another word the Kremnoan language lacks. Love and fear. It seems they go hand in hand.

What of red, then?

Aglaea’s deft fingers on her embroidery. Her gaze, knowing and sharp. Mydei’s side of the string, still only gold. Gold for love. Gold for fear. Both are wretched words. Red, she’d said, means Mnestia themself recognizes your devotion.

Love. Devotion. Mydei leans his elbows on his knees and feels a little bit nauseous. “No,” he says, sick with the honesty, sick with the lack of it. Two days until the trial. Two days since Phainon’s side of the string turned red. And still, Mydei’s bones are aching. “I’d like it if you stayed.”

The clang of metal as Phainon sets his sword aside. He’s dressed down. Collar open, sleeves rolled up. Still healing, still beautiful in the aftermath. Equal, Mydei thinks, again and again. He could pound his own heart to mush at the look in his eyes. Is this love? Is this what it feels like?

“Alright,” Phainon says, rather softly. “I’ll stay, then. Until you get sick of me.”

chapters.html:
By the time the day before the trial comes, Phainon has hardly slept. It hangs over his head like an executioner's axe, and every time he closes his eyes he’s plagued with that feeling. The sickening, monstrous one. Bloodlust, cruelty, Strife. The mantle he’s meant to take up. The trial he’s meant to pass.

He lays in bed as long as he can stomach, willing some semblance of sleep to come over him, if not to escape the feeling than to at least heal and prepare his body for what lies ahead. He dozes in restless flashes, tosses and turns and lays itching when he can’t, until Mydei grunts, half awakened by his movement, and traps him in his arms to keep him still.

He can’t decide if it’s better or worse like that. Smothered in heat, breathed on, circulation cut off, a dull pain in his back from the bruises. And yet he can hear Mydei’s heartbeat, steady and slow, feel him alive and warm and safe, press a hand over the untouched, unscarred skin over his tenth thoracic vertebra and breathe in time with him.

Entry hour comes. Daylight slips through a crack in the curtains and pools across Mydei’s bare shoulder blades. The muscle, the markings. He lays on his stomach with his face against Phainon’s throat, dead to the world and drooling. And still, Phainon lays awake, sticking to him with sweat, nose against his hair, tracing the markings with tired fingertips. Mydei doesn’t stir when Phainon pulls the sheet down with his foot so it only covers them to the hips, doesn’t stir at the big breath he takes, the exhale ruffling his hair, doesn’t stir when he cards his fingers through it and whispers, “Mydei.”

Phainon stares at the ceiling for a moment, then looks back at Mydei. The red ends of his hair as they slip through his fingers. The sunlight on his back. Tiredly, Phainon counts vertebrae with his free hand. One, two, all the way to ten. The body above him shifts slightly. He taps the spot, earns a soft grunt. Rubs his thumb in the dip of Mydei’s spine and is rewarded with teeth on the junction of his neck.

“HKS,” Mydei grumbles, deep and scratchy, more asleep than awake. His hand comes up to wipe his mouth, but he leaves the wet spot on Phainon’s neck, shifting slightly before settling into sleep again.

Startled, Phainon lets out a breath. His stomach flips and flips and flips. For you, he thinks, struck with the feeling again. One day until the trial. He’s still a bit sore, still aching. Numb where Mydei lays on him. For you, I’ll do it.

The string spirals into being, crimson with the markings on Mydei’s back. Phainon realizes, for the first time since he’s allowed himself to think about it, that he doesn’t want this at all. This coreflame or the power that comes with it. The strength of a vengeful god. But he’ll take it anyway, because Mydei needs him to.

“Mydei,” Phainon whispers again. There’s no reply. What a perfect time it would be to tell Mydei he loves him. While he’s asleep and soft enough not to hold it against him. When he won’t even know Phainon said it at all.

He holds his tongue and swallows it down as his stomach demands breakfast. Already having given up on the prospect of sleep, Phainon tries to shift. Mydei makes no move to help, dead weight as Phainon tries to squirm out from under him. Unhappily, he even mumbles, “Stop moving.”

“I’m famished, Your Highness,” Phainon tells him, squirming some more. “This mortal one needs sustenance.”

Mydei mutters something incomprehensible and rolls off, turning his back. Phainon gives a weak laugh and aches. Pins and needles flood his arm, his leg. A sweat damp spot on his shirt cools in the air.

“Would you care to join me?” he asks. A grunt. This time, all Phainon does is watch him, waiting for enough feeling to return to move. When it does, he ducks to kiss Mydei’s shoulder. “Later, then,” he murmurs. “Sleep well, Mydeimos.” And then he stands, heart beating, limping his way to the closet to dress, slipping from their rooms to find something to eat.

He meets Castorice over a bowl of yogurt, penning something onto a sheet of paper, her cheek in her hand, hair piled in her lap so it won’t brush the floor. He sits across from her at the table and smiles when she looks up. “Writing reports?” he asks. She blinks.

“Ah…” She straightens up and pulls the paper closer to her. “No… Pardon, Lord Phainon, it’s poetry.”

“Poetry?” he asks. “You write?”

She looks embarrassed at the attention. “I do,” she admits. “Just from time to time. It’s not any good…”

“I dabble a bit myself,” Phainon tells her, stirring fruit and honey into his breakfast. “What do you write about?”

“Just… poems.” She places her arm atop the words she’s written to hide them, though Phainon wasn’t planning on snooping. Tentatively, she asks him as well, “What about you?”

He laughs, a bit awkward, embarrassed now that he thinks about it. “Mydei, mostly. It’s, um. It started as a joke and I’m awful at it, actually, but I’m a bit fond of the ones I’ve written.”

Slowly, Castorice nods. Wordless, she takes a blank page from her notepad and slides it with a pen to the middle of the table, then removes her hands. “Would you like to write something now?” she asks.

He wonders if she can see the dark circles under his eyes. Exhausted, afraid, in love, perhaps he’s in exactly the right state to produce a masterpiece. He takes the pen and paper. “Sure,” he says, spooning a bite into his mouth and turning his gaze to the empty white of the page. The possibility of it intimidates him. Every other time he’s written, it’s been tacked on to the end of a letter with the express purpose of serving as an annoyance.

He glances up. Hesitantly, Castorice returns to her own work, writing a couple more words before she pauses and meets his gaze. He can’t read her poem from this angle. She looks like she wants to cover it again anyway, but she doesn’t, and Phainon finds that an olive branch.

“It’s different,” Phainon explains, “if I’m trying to write something that’s actually good.”

Castorice hums, nodding. “Then don’t,” she tells him. “The more you worry about it, the worse it’ll be. Just write whatever.”

Like all things, overthinking doesn’t help, and yet Phainon can’t stop. He takes a breath, exhales a laugh. “You’re right,” he says, turning back to the paper. “I shouldn’t care so much.”

Laughing soldiers pass them, speaking in Kremnoan and dressed down before their training, holding bowls or plates and searching for a place to sit. They salute to him when they see him looking. It gives him an odd feeling. He’s the husband to their crown prince, the successor to their god, and he doesn’t even speak their language.

Back to the page, still blank. Titans, why does he care so much? Another one for Mydei will do, something he’ll love and hate in equal measure. Something he’ll berate Phainon for as he hides a smile. A little cheesy, romantic in a way that will make him gag. He writes a few lines and pauses. Castorice looks at him.

“Did you figure it out?” she asks.

“I suppose,” he tells her, and reads it out. “You’re terribly unfair / with blood in your hair / Gauntlets of gold, a string half red / I’d tell you I love you, but you’d have my head.”

She smiles slightly. “Is it for him then? Lord Mydeimos?” He nods, and she suggests gently, “you might consider not making everything rhyme, just to vary the flow.”

He chuckles, watches another group of soldiers go by. It’s warm in Castrum Kremnos, lit with day and firelight. He isn’t a fan of the smell of indigo, but he’s getting used to it. Settling into this second home. “You know,” he says, rubbing at the ache in his temples. “Mydei said the same thing.”

“Oh…” she says, and doesn’t seem to know what to add.

He taps the pen on the table, sets it down in exchange for his spoon. “I’ll try it,” he tells her. “Maybe rearrange a few things.” A few more lines. What does it matter, why does it matter? He’s tired enough to stop thinking so much, heavy enough with worry for other things to spare room for worry about this.

The next time he reaches for his spoon, all he finds is another gold coin. He sighs and turns it in his fingers as Cipher takes a seat on top of the table, feet on a chair, taking a bite of his yogurt and making a face. She passes the bowl back, and in an instant, the coin is gone.

“Since when do you have a sweet tooth?” she asks, licking her teeth, tucking the coin in her pocket.

“I…” He doesn’t really, but he had made the yogurt overly sweet, hadn’t he?

“Lady Cifera,” Castorice greets her.

Cipher’s tail flicks against the table, setting a rhythm. “So formal,” she says with distaste. “Weren’t you supposed to leave with Aglaea and Tribios?”

“No, I…” Castorice clears her throat. “I was hoping to find you, actually.”

“Little old me?” Cipher’s eyes widen. She sets a hand on the table and leans her weight into it. “And what, pray tell, do you need with me?”

“Passage,” Castorice says. Her gaze flicks hesitantly to Phainon, then back to Cipher. “To Styxia.”

A slight smile. “And why would you want to go there?”

Castorice swallows. “Professor Anaxa has good reason to believe Thanatos rests there,” she answers. It’s the first Phainon has heard of it. His mouth drops open. “It’s the first real lead I’ve had in a century.”

“Very well,” Cipher says. “And what can you offer me in return?”

“I… I have savings. Not much, but I…”

“Deal,” Cipher says, and hops off the table. She walks a lap around, lightly brushing Phainon as she passes, coming to Castorice’s side. “This sounds interesting. Don’t bleed yourself dry for me, how about… ninety percent?”

“Cipher,” Phainon chides. Castorice looks at him helplessly.

Cipher pouts. “Fine, fine. Eighty, then.” At his expression, she sighs. “Sixty, take it or leave it.”

“I…” Castorice hesitates. “I accept.”

“Tomorrow, then?” Cipher asks. “I’m eager to get out of this place. So grand and for what? There’s barely anything to steal.” She twists something in her fingers. A ring, flashing gold. Phainon frowns, slips a hand in his pocket.

“Yes,” Castorice says. “Tomorrow is fine. I’ll… yes.”

Another coin. Phainon pulls it out, and as the cat engraved on it glimmers in the light, his stomach sinks with dread. “Cipher,” he says, standing, a bit shaky.

“Tomorrow,” she says, nodding. Again, she turns the ring over, studying the signet. “Say, where did you find this?” she asks, turning to Phainon. “It looks valuable. Gorgo’s?”

“Give that back,” Phainon says, voice shaking. She smiles, and the dread fills him to the brim.

“I consider myself a bit of an expert on treasures, you know,” she says, slipping the ring onto each of her fingers only to find it too big for all but her thumb. Even then, it’s loose enough to spin. She holds out her hand to study it, and he considers his options. A fight? No, she’s far faster than him, far more clever, imbued with the power of Trickery. She’ll want a price for it, or a game, and Phainon—

“This one, if it is what I think it is, was supposed to be lost to the River of Souls.” She pulls it off her finger, studies it some more, and he’s so nervous he’s sick with it. Castorice stirs uncomfortably. 

“Cipher,” she says gently, “perhaps you should give that back.”

Cipher ignores her, ignores them both. “It’s for him, isn’t it?” she asks. “Did you take a dip just to find it?”

“I went through a lot of trouble,” Phainon says carefully.

“Oh,” she says, and walks another slow lap around the table. “I never did say congratulations, by the way. You seem happy. It’s cute.” She stops in front of him and holds her hand out. When he doesn’t react, she lifts her eyebrows expectantly. “Don’t you want this back?” 

More than half certain it’ll be a trick, Phainon holds out a hand. Cipher drops the ring into it and tucks some hair behind her ear. “Good luck with the trial,” she says. “I’d offer some advice, but I doubt Strife is anything like Trickery.”

Phainon curls his fingers tightly around the ring, runs his thumb over the shape of the Lance of Fury just to be certain. But it’s the real thing, and Cipher had given it back without a price. He studies her, wonders briefly if she cares a little more than she lets on. “Thank you,” he says, swallowing. “For, well. Everything.”

She smiles a little, an earnest one, a real one, and straightens up. “Yeah, yeah,” she says, and turns, tail flicking him lightly. “I’ll see you, maybe. Depends.” As she starts walking, she pauses briefly, glancing at Castorice. “Tomorrow,” she sing-songs. “Action hour. Don’t forget.”

Wordless, Castorice nods.

Phainon walks about after he finishes his breakfast. He pokes around in parts of the palace he’s never seen before; the armory, the library, what might be a ballroom but is more likely an indoor arena. It’s not as bright and lively as Okhema, but the atmosphere is still warm, still welcoming, still easy enough to grow a fondness for.

He gets smiled at, cried at, bowed at, spoken to in broken common tongue and helpless Kremnoan. They call him King, or King’s One, or some Kremnoan word used to refer to the equal of someone they respect. It’s strange because he’s Prince Consort at best, unless the hierarchy here works differently, and Mydei hasn’t even taken the throne yet.

But somehow he’s become beloved to these people. Face after face,  stranger after stranger, loving him for more than just helping them win the war, but something else too, something he can’t put a name to.

The Kremnoans are warm, so much warmer than their reputation suggests. The more of them he talks to, welcoming and human, the less he wants to take the place of their god.

He winds up in the infirmary, though he has no business there himself. His wounds are all on track to healing already, bruises turning green and brown, cuts scabbed over. He’ll have a few new scars, but he heals fast.

Inside he finds healers and patients both. Two young soldiers, one with his arm in a sling, the other with his leg wrapped and bulky, propped on a stack of pillows.

“My Lord,” the one with the hurt leg says, sounding startled as he attempts a bow from his seat. He shakes the other to get his attention, gesturing slightly. The one with the wounded arm blinks, and then recognition blooms in his eyes and he stands up to bow properly, but doesn’t speak.

They’re both thin, Phainon notices. Stinking of healer’s herbs, tired-eyed. Scabs around their ears, bruises on exposed flesh. “I… apologize,” Phainon says. “I never asked your names. Is your recovery coming well?”

The one with the hurt leg rushes to nod. “Yes, Lord. Recovery is coming just fine. I’m called Ermis, and that’s Aeson. Forgive him, he… lost his hearing in the battle.”

Aeson’s hands twitch. He looks between them but doesn’t seem to follow along. Phainon remembers blood leaking from his ears. “Oh,” he says, and curses himself for having nothing better to say. They’re alive, he thinks. At least they’re alive, at least it hadn’t meant nothing to drag them all the way here, to leave Mydei to fight alone. But they seem so tired, so worn and weary, so sad.

It’s like that, though. They lost the other man that got crushed under the rubble. One lost his hearing. They’re both hospital bound for at least another week, and that does things to a man, Phainon knows it does. War is a terrible thing.

After a too long moment, Aeson decides to speak, voice scratchy from disuse, a little bit quiet like he’s afraid deafness will make him speak too loud. “We’re grateful to you, Lord Phainon,” he says. “Sorry too.”

Phainon looks at Ermis, a helpless lump forming in his throat. “We wanted to help,” Ermis says a bit awkwardly, shrugging. “But instead we made things much harder for you and Lord Mydeimos. So we’re sorry.” Bone deep shame in their words, their expressions. Ermis appears Okheman, Aeson Kremnoan. He knows how they speak of victory and loss. Valorous death before glorious return. Phainon doesn’t know if there are words he can say to make it better.

In a way, he is angry with them. Mydei’s suffering could be traced back, blamed on their presence. But it’s pointless, isn’t it? Pointing fingers. In the end, they’re suffering too.

“I’m just glad you survived,” he says, and tries to smile at them both. So much weight. He’s so tired. “It’s okay.”

Outside, he has to sit. Has to breathe, leaning his elbows into his knees and staring at the dirt for a while. Time passes. He takes the folded up poem from before and the pen Castorice let him keep, and writes out the last few lines.

Mydei is gone when he comes back. The bed unmade, the curtains pulled open to spill light on everything. Phainon sits for a while, pulling off his shoes, rubbing his aching feet. One more day of freedom. He wants it to feel like it, but instead he’s already in the process of chaining himself down.

For you, he thinks, turning paper over in his hands, worn after half a day in his pocket, creases soft. That monstrous feeling, will it live inside him? Will he spend the rest of his days with too much power, itching for a fight? He doesn’t know what divinity feels like. He supposes he’ll find out.

After a long while, he stands up, tosses the poem somewhere Mydei might find it, and resigns himself to a long, long bath.

Gauntlets of gold, a string half red

I’d tell you I love you, but you’d have my head

Foolishly brave or maybe I’m

Bravely foolish

Fearing the wrong things

Counting with fingers down your back

Words, language, love I’ve yet to unpack

Strength and weakness are nothing but dust

Blood, sweat, dirt in your hair

The scent of rust

All’s unfair in

This and war
