When he comes out in a towel to dress, Mydei is there, splitting a pomegranate with a knife, peeling back white membrane to pluck the seeds out and into a bowl. “Your back,” he says as Phainon turns away from him to dress.

There’s a landscape of bruises there, Phainon knows, from when he’d fallen from Nikador’s shoulders. He hasn’t seen them, but he’s prodded them with his fingers and felt the discomfort when trying to find a way to lay down at night. “Haven’t you seen them?” he asks. The soft sound as seeds patter into the bowl.

“No,” Mydei says. He doesn’t ask if it hurts, doesn’t say anything else. There’s still daylight. Phainon slips into a pair of trousers and a loose, high-necked, long-sleeved shirt, and goes to sit with him.

Red-stained fingers. The crack as Mydei breaks the shell of the pomegranate to get to a new section of fruit. He pushes the bowl across his desk toward Phainon.

“Thanks,” Phainon says, taking a couple of seeds, cool and damp with juice, crisp and sweet when he passes them into his mouth. He watches Mydei work, peeling away the white bits, using his thumb to unstick a dozen seeds at once. His hand stretches out to empty a palm full of them into the bowl, eyes not lifting, not saying anything. His braid dangles, head tipped down, a section of hair escaping from behind his ear.

“You’re beautiful,” Phainon tells him.

Without a beat, without a reaction, Mydei replies, “You should shut up.”

Phainon laughs and takes a small handful of pomegranate, sliding the bowl back to Mydei, who barely spares it a glance, just depositing more seeds into it. “Impervious to my charms, I see,” Phainon says, smiling a little. The bath helped. His body is tired in a relaxed way, rather than weary. But his heart still throbs, still crawls up his throat and sits under his tongue like it wants to fall out.

“I’m busy,” Mydei tells him, and drops another empty third of the rind to the desk. He’s made a mess there, but he doesn’t bother with it now. Just works on the last section with pink stained hands and squared fingernails, and pushes the bowl back in Phainon’s direction.

Phainon eyes it, breaks the skin of a seed with his teeth. “You haven’t had any,” he notes. Not even a seed or two as he plucks them from the fruit. Just puts them all in this bowl and gives it to Phainon. Mydei grunts. Glances at him briefly. “You’re awfully romantic, you know?”

Now, a glare. “I’m sitting here, telling you to shut up when you call me beautiful. What part of that is romantic?”

Phainon smiles. “You’re opening a pomegranate for me,” he says, and Mydei just looks at him like he doesn’t get it at all. But he does. He’s the one doing it. He’s the one that holds doors open without even realizing.

He plucks the last few seeds and eats them for himself, like that’s spite, like that’s vengeance, and as he cleans up the pieces of rind he’d left on the desk, Phainon watches, and Phainon feels. Titans, he thinks. This really is what love feels like, isn’t it?

“There’s no word for romance in the Kremnoan language,” Mydei tells him, wiping his fingers clean on a cloth as Phainon watches, cheek propped on his fist, pomegranate on his tongue.

“I’ve accepted all of your Kremnoan things,” he finally says. “Isn’t it only fair for you to let me have this much?”

Mydei’s expression is strange, unreadable but only because Phainon hasn’t had the chance to see it like this before. He doesn’t say anything, just pulls the bowl so it sits evenly between them and takes a couple of seeds. A handful of moments pass in silence.

“Deliverer—”

“I want to learn your language,” Phainon begins. “Would you teach me? I don’t know where to start.”

Mydei stares, stares, stares. “It’s not an easy language,” he finally says. “It’s abstract and doesn’t always follow its own rules.”

“Still,” Phainon says. “Please.”

A pause, a beat, a breath. “Okay,” Mydei agrees. “I’ll teach you.”

They ride dromases back to Okhema, though they’re on the same one this time. Phainon feels like a little thing curled inside a too big body. He puts his head on Mydei’s shoulder and finds himself surprised when he’s allowed, when Mydei even winds an arm around his waist to make it more comfortable.

“I read your poem,” he says, and Phainon could shrivel to ash. “That’s what I was going to say earlier.”

“Oh?” Phainon tries, not lifting his head because he doesn’t want to see Mydei’s face, because he doesn’t want to feel real right now. He likes the dying sun on his face, in his lap. He likes the warmth against him, the unpleasant stick of their skin. He knows what he’s marching toward, and he’s resigned himself to it. For you, he thinks, and slides his fingers down Mydei’s inseam to his armored knee, resting his hand there. This piece is new, though it matches the rest. He’d broken the old plate in the fight with Nikador.

“It.” Mydei clears his throat. “It was better than the rest of them, but you still have a lot of room for improvement.”

“I know,” Phainon tells him.

“You were right,” Mydei adds, a bit strained. His gauntleted fingers twitch on Phainon’s waist.

“As I tend to be. But what about?”

“I’ve been unfair to you.”

Now, Phainon tilts his head to looks at him. The tense of his jaw, the flushed tint to the shell of his ear. He sighs and settles again, pressing the pads of his fingers softly into the spikes on Mydei’s knee armor, testing the sharpness. “How so?” he asks.

“You let me call you equal and treat you as a Kremnoan would, but when it comes to other things, your things… I haven’t been quite as accepting.”

Phainon laughs a little. “Is this about that one line… I’d tell you I love you, but you’d have my head?” he asks. Mydei stiffens slightly. “So it is.”

Mydei pulls his hand away from his knee, moving it a little higher up, grumbling something like, “You’re going to cut yourself.” Phainon laughs again, wishes he could just stay in this, on the back of a dromas, laughing, leaning against his husband, his equal. Mydei goes quiet. Finally, when Phainon does too, he asks, “Did you mean it?”

“Mean…?” Phainon prompts, skimming his fingers up the inside of Mydei’s thigh until he’s stopped again, Mydei’s fingers curling around his and staying, trapping his in place.

“Love,” Mydei grunts. “You mentioned it a few times in the poem. Are you…?”

“Am I in love with you, you’re asking.” Phainon hums softly. Briefly pictures Mydei throwing him off the back of the dromas in a fit of rage. Chuckles, and tells perhaps the most unconvincing lie of his life. “Probably.”

“Probably?”

“Didn’t I say I’ve yet to unpack it?” But he has. He’s turned it over in his head again and again. The way it felt to leave Mydei to fight alone. The way it felt to come back to him, to carry him home, to lay with him until he woke up. The way it feels to be trusted enough to trace fingers down his spine, to hold him and bring him pleasure. The way it feels to be called his equal, to fight by his side and pick up the pieces together in the aftermath. That’s love, isn’t it? They just have different names for it.

“Phainon.”

“Oh, the real name,” Phainon says, pretending to shudder. When Mydei hisses, he goes quiet. “You don’t like the word love, do you?”

“I don’t know what it means,” Mydei says. “But if you—”

“I think it’s like being equals,” Phainon tells him. “I still don’t think I’m saying that right, but… from what you’ve said, what you’ve shown me, I think they’re pretty similar. Love is… softer, maybe, but similar.”

“Softer,” Mydei repeats. “So do you…?”

“Love you?” Phainon fills in. He swallows his beating heart. Shapes the dread in his stomach into something steadier. For you, he thinks, a little more okay with it this time, a little readier. That monstrous feeling is nothing next to this. “Yes, I believe I do.”

Silence.

“I don’t mind if you don’t say it back,” Phainon says. Mydei’s hand is still curled around his, strings tangling, red and gold. The world drags by slowly on the way to Okhema. One more night’s rest, and then the trial, and then his destiny. He can do this much. “I know it doesn’t mean the same thing for you as it does for me.”

“I asked Lady Aglaea what it means when the strings change color,” Mydei says slowly.

“And she told you?”

“Shut up and listen,” Mydei chides. He swallows thick enough for Phainon to hear it. “She said that gold means you’re in love. Red is… devotion.”

Phainon looks at the red around his own finger. Red like the blood of mortals. Red like the ends of Mydei’s hair. His stomach flips, flips, flips. I really would do anything for you, and here’s the proof. “So I’m much more invested in this relationship than you are. How embarrassing for me.”

“HKS,” Mydei says, and shakes him off. Phainon laughs weakly. “I’m trying to say that if what she said is true… then I must— I—”

Gold. Mydei’s clenched fist. “You love me.”

Mydei looks at him. Flushed with frustration or embarrassment. “I guess so,” he says, and Phainon can do nothing more than smile.

“One last time before I become a demigod,” Phainon says. Their bed in Okhema. Mydei in the sheets, his hair undone, makeup washed clean. Phainon climbs to straddle him.

“You’re still injured,” Mydei says, kissing it into his mouth, already undoing his shirt. “You need to rest.”

“So?” Phainon asks, smearing his lips down Mydei’s jaw, reaching for his belt. Then, softly, he’s flipped and lowered onto his back, gently to not upset his bruises, Mydei’s arm slipping out from under his waist as he moves to sit astride Phainon instead. He shrugs out of his upper layers and looks at him with warm, lidded eyes.

“So,” he says, rolling their hips together firm and slow, “relax. I’ll do all the work.”

He wakes up alone the next morning. Perhaps Mydei is only getting breakfast or relieving himself, but it feels oddly like a betrayal. Phainon has gotten used to waking up first.

He dresses, eats, stares himself in the mirror for the last moments he can recognize himself as human. Where are you? he wonders. Mydei’s fresh teeth marks in his neck. He leaves new ones every time they’re together. Where did you go?

The string pulses softly. A dim red glow. Devotion. What does that mean, next to love? An endless chant of for you, for you, for you. The broken body of a god. The power of it writhing in his chest, making him sick.

He’ll still be human. He’ll still know love and peace and warmth. An hour until Tribios will bring him to the Vortex of Genesis to become a god. The string on his hand still glows softly. Sighing, he follows it.

It leads him to the Hero’s Bath, the site of their first meeting, their first fight. Mydei isn’t even bathing, just standing, watching the water fall.

“So this is where you disappeared to,” Phainon calls. Mydei doesn’t turn, doesn’t look at him until they’re standing shoulder to shoulder. And even when he does, he’s frowning. “What is it?”

Mydei looks at him for a long while. Too intensely. He finally says, “I need to know. Did you agree to this because you want to do it and it feels right, or because I, and in turn Aglaea, pushed it on you?”

Phainon looks at him, almost dumbfounded. “I… don’t feel pressured,” he says. Not exactly, not quite. There are others who would try in his stead if he refused.

“Phainon,” Mydei presses.

“I want to be a hero,” Phainon says. “I meant it.”

“But are you certain that Strife is the way to achieve that?”

No, Phainon thinks. Not in the slightest. He holds Mydei’s gaze, frowns back. It’s for you, he thinks. I was always going to do this for you. “Someone needs to inherit the coreflame,” he says. “It was your idea for it to be me.”

“And I’m asking you now,” Mydei says, and his voice shakes, “because I didn’t bother to ask you before. Do you want it to be you?”

“I’ll do it.”

“Phainon.” He lifts a hand, curls it into a fist. Sighs and drops it. “Equal,” he says. “Husband, I… love you, and I’m asking if you’re doing this for me, so I can escape my destiny, or if you’re doing it for you.”

For you, Phainon thinks. He’s so stunned he parts his lips and closes them again. Finally, he croaks, “You. I’m doing it for you.”

And Mydei sighs with something like relief and steps closer, cradling the back of Phainon’s head and pulling him in, exhaling close to his ear. “Thank you,” he says, and it’s all Phainon can do to set hands on his waist as he reels in confusion. “But you don’t need to let me be a fool anymore.”

“I don’t get it,” Phainon says. “I don’t get it at all.”

A breathy laugh. “Strife was never meant to be your destiny,” he says. “You’ve another burden. This is the one I’m meant to shoulder. I’ll take it from here.”

The weight, that heavy, monstrous feeling lifts, replaces itself with a flood of incredulity. “The coreflame?” Phainon asks, pulling back. Mydei’s hand falls from his hair, holding his jaw instead, his cheek. “Mydei, you…”

“Your battles are mine,” Mydei says. “That’s what it means to be equals.”

“You’re joining the flame chase?”

“It would seem that way.” Mydei smiles a little, sharp. “Wait for me, Deliverer. Let’s spar when this is all over.”

Phainon can do nothing more than laugh. “It’s a date, Mydeimos.”

△

It’s a long wait for Mydei’s return. Phainon sits against a rough stone wall in the Vortex of Genesis, feeling a wave of things. Worried for Mydei, yet with full faith in him. Relieved that he won’t have to be the one to take up the authority of Strife, yet lost without it. Grateful, and the slightest bit upset.

He knows this was never meant to be his destiny. Strife doesn’t fit. But what, then, does?

He slips a card from his pocket. It was Cyrene’s, painted with his own visage. You’re going to be a hero, she would say, cards spread before her, divining something Phainon never seriously believed in until she was gone. You know how I know?

A small body settles in next to his own. Trianne, sitting cross-legged, extending an eager hand. “Can we see it?” she asks.

Phainon smiles, chuckling a little, and holds the card out. “Just be careful,” he says. And she is, cradling it gently in her hands, turning it over with uncharacteristic reverence. Trianne has always been the mischievous one, but not now. It’s like she knows how important to him this is.

“It’s beautiful,” she says. “Is it you, Snowy?”

“It is,” Phainon answers with a light laugh. “Though I don’t think I look quite that cool in real life.”

She looks up at him and squints, studying him, and then the card, and then him again. “Not much difference,” she says, and passes the card back. “Who made it?”

“An old friend of mine.” Phainon takes the card back when she extends it. Turns it over in his hands to see the back. “Her name was Cyrene. She was from Aedes Elysiae too.”

“Oh,” Trianne says. She blinks, cocks her head. “Where is she now? We’d like to meet her.”

“I’m sure she’d love to meet you too,” Phainon says, and feels a little choked. It isn’t anger that he feels now, now anymore. Just something softer, sadder. Grief. “But she’s… at the end of the west wind, now.”

“Oh,” Trianne repeats, quieter. “Will you see her tomorrow?”

“Yes, Trianne,” Phainon says, voice wavering a little. “I’ll see her tomorrow.”

△

Still, they wait. Aglaea comes next. She offers him a small bunch of grapes and stands beside him where he chooses to sit. “He’ll be fine,” she says by way of a greeting. “I can feel your worry.”

“I know,” Phainon tells her. He plucks a grape from its stem. It’s sweet and crisp, cool on his tongue. “I just… wonder what kind of hardships he must be facing.”

“Nothing he can’t handle.” She looks at him. “Strife was always going to be his destiny.”

“So why didn’t you say anything?”

“It isn’t my place to drag people kicking and screaming toward their fates,” she answers, smiling slightly. “I had faith things would fall into place.”

He pulls off another grape. It leaves a bit of flesh still attached to the stem, transparent green, shiny with juice. He rolls the fruit over in his fingers and asks, “Would I have failed if I took the trial?”

“Yes, Phainon. You would have.”

“I don’t get it,” he says. “All my life… I’m supposed to be this perfect vessel, but…” He cuts himself off with a sigh.

“Your time will come,” Aglaea says patiently. “There’s another weight meant for your shoulders.”

“I feel useless.”

“You’re not,” she says simply. “One day, you’ll be exactly what Amphoreus needs.”

How do you know? he thinks. How does anyone know? He turns his gaze toward the darkened sky, the constellations lit within. The ones still dim.

“Somehow,” Aglaea says, gazing out there too. “I don’t think you’ll be waiting too much longer.”

△

Time passes. Phainon is left alone. He stands to stretch, walks a lap around the damp, cool cave and takes a seat at the ledge beneath the sky, water crashing below. He listens to that. Watches the constellations flicker and blink. Hears a soft splash, a shaky exhale, footsteps.

Mydei sits beside him, graceless like his legs have turned to rubber, the metal of his armor scraping against rock. He smells like blood, and his expression is frenzied when Phainon looks at him.

“You passed the trial, then?”

“What does it look like?” Mydei grumbles, voice rough and low, hands curling into fists in his lap. Restless, bloodlusting energy, just like the war cries all over again. Whatever he’d seen, whatever he’d been asked to do, it probably still flashes behind his eyes.

Phainon chuckles weakly. “And how do you feel?”

“Like I’m going insane,” Mydei answers. “I want—” A shuddering breath. “It hasn’t settled yet. I’ll get used to it.”

Phainon brings a hand to his cheek, angling his head so they look at each other. “You’re a god now,” he says. A muscle in Mydei’s jaw tics. His gaze dips to Phainon’s mouth and back up, pupils blown wide from the dark or the adrenaline or both. Phainon is half convinced he can hear the sound of his heart.

“Don’t,” Mydei grits. He’s ended up closer, with or without meaning to. The blood smell is strong, metallic and heavy. “I’m… dangerous right now.”

“Dangerous?” Phainon laughs. He grips Mydei’s chin, slinking a little closer, edging his face up, smiling. “To me?”

Mydei grabs his wrist, pulling him off and pulling a punch that Phainon dodges by jumping upright and away from the ledge. Mydei is quick to follow, and they exchange a few blows before Phainon is laughing, laughing, laughing, and Mydei is throwing him onto his back and pinning him down, straddling his waist and bringing a hand to his throat. He’s frowning, gaze still blown and intense, one finger slipping beneath the straps of Phainon’s choker to rest at his pulse point.

“Yield,” he says, a little bit lost as a tear slips from the corner of Phainon’s eye from his laughter. He finally quiets, looking up at this new god, old lover. His braid hanging between them, expression shadowed in the dark. Cold stone beneath Phainon’s back. The hand at his throat hardly puts pressure at all. The other, pinning his wrist, is tangled in a thread that glows crimson all the way through. Love to devotion. When did it change?

“You’re beautiful,” Phainon says, airy as he steals his breath back from the wind.

“Yield,” Mydei repeats, pulling the choker taut. An arena, booming with cheers. Dirt and sweat and fire. Deja Vu.

Swiftly, Phainon grabs Mydei’s wrist, bucking to throw him off, to roll them, locking his legs around Mydei’s knees and pinning one hand with each of his. “Not this time,” he pants. Mydei jerks under him, dangerously close to kneeing him in the groin before he shifts slightly and squeezes hard enough that Mydei can’t move at all. “Your turn,” he says. “Yield.”

But Mydei isn’t looking at him. He’s looking at something beside his head that gleams slightly in the dim light and rolls to a stop. “What is that?” he asks. A little further and it could have rolled right back into the sea.

“Yield and I’ll tell you.”

Mydei glares. “HKS.”

“Darling,” Phainon replies. “Sweetheart, angel, honeyca—”

Mydei throws him off and he hits the ground with a hard thump, hissing as he pushes himself up to sit. Mydei snatches the ring off the ground and turns it so he can see the signet. Phainon waits as he studies it, as he sits there and doesn’t speak for a good minute.

“This was my mother’s, wasn’t it?” he asks after a long moment. Phainon hums his assent. “I thought it was lost to the River of Souls.”

“It was,” Phainon agrees. Mydei looks at him.

“You did this?” he asks.

“Chartonus was a great deal of help.” They hold gazes for a long while. Phainon clears his throat. “I was going to give it to you after I passed the trial, but, well. I suppose now is as good a time as any.”

“HKS,” Mydei curses, slipping the ring on his finger and hauling Phainon in by the collar, kissing him like it’s the last time they’ll get to do it, pulling his lips open with a thumb on his chin, licking into his mouth deeply, hotly, wetly. He tastes how he smells, like blood and teeth and the sweat on his upper lip. Phainon falls back, catching himself with a hand on the ground, kind of gasping, kind of shocked, and then Mydei pulls away from his mouth to fall into his neck instead. Kissing softly, scraping his teeth under Phainon’s choker.

Phainon sets a startled hand on the back of his head, carding through his hair. “So dangerous,” he teases, more than a little baffled. “In the Vortex of Genesis of all places? With all the titans watch— Ah!” Mydei nips his throat, yet another mark blooming beneath his teeth as he lets out an unhappy grunt. Phainon laughs. “That hurts, Mydeimos.”

“Good.”

Phainon laughs. Slides his hand back until he can lay flat, Mydei practically on top of him. He stares at the cragged rock above them, the sky, the stars. “How do you feel?” he asks.

“Fine,” Mydei murmurs. “Tired. I don’t want to go back yet.”

“Okay,” Phainon breathes back. He pets through Mydei’s hair. Soft, rhythmic. “We’ll stay here until you’re ready.”

△

They return under the cover of nightfall, taking alleys instead of main streets and ducking behind corners to avoid being spotted. Mydei isn’t ready to be seen quite yet, cheered and lionized as the new God of Strife, so they do this. Hand in hand, Phainon feels a bit like a kid again, hiding from his parents with a giggling Cyrene. An ache of nostalgia. He pulls Mydei behind a tree.

“Race you,” he says, halfway there. “You lose if you get caught.”

Mydei huffs, gives him a half smile. “You’re on, Deliverer,” he says. “Do you need a head start?”

“Not a chance,” Phainon tells him. “On three. One.”

“Two,” Mydei says. They make eye contact, settling into running stances.

“Three.”

They take off, a straightaway in the dark streets. And really, there’s no one out this late to catch them anyway. Phainon runs and runs, and perhaps he has the advantage of slightly longer legs and a more rested body, because he pulls ahead just slightly, Mydei’s footsteps pounding behind him.

“HKS!” he hears, and almost trips on a loose rock. He laughs and loses his breath, heart pounding, panting, running as hard as he can. The gap between them grows as they approach Marmoreal Palace, and as Phainon slips inside he catches a glimpse of someone walking and skids to a stop, pressing himself against the wall. Mydei crashes into him and they fall, tumbling and cursing, right at Tribbie’s feet.

She blinks at them. “Snowy, De?” she asks. “What are you doing? Are you playing some kind of game?”

Phainon bolts upright, smoothing out his robes. He holds a hand out to Mydei, who slaps it aside and gets up without help, huffing. “Lady Tribbie,” Phainon says, sounding like the fool that he is. “What are you doing out so late?”

She opens her mouth, closes it, pursing her lips with a guilty expression. “Trianne was hungry,” she mumbles. “We were… well…”

Phainon laughs. “Tell you what,” he says, bringing a finger to his lips. “We won’t tell anyone we saw you if you won’t tell anyone you saw us. Deal?”

She laughs, high and delighted. “Deal,” she says, and turns to Mydei. “How was the trial, De?” she asks. “How do you feel?”

“I am well, Lady Tribbie,” he says, a little stiff, a little awkward. “Just eager for some rest.”

She nods. “We get it,” she says, and reaches out to take his hand. A big, bright smile. “Rest well, De. We’re so glad you decided to join us.”

“I… Yes, well. Thank you,” Mydei says, and watches as she skips off. He turns to Phainon. “Let’s go. Since someone got us caught.”

“Someone?” Phainon repeats incredulously. “Just who crashed into who now? If it hadn’t been for you—”

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him, without heat. They walk the rest of the way back to their rooms, and he falls straight into the bed.

Phainon watches his back, the shift of his side as he breathes, red markings. “Aren’t you going to bathe?” he asks, sitting on the foot of the bed.

Mydei grunts. “Tomorrow,” he says. “We can change the sheets.”

“Alright,” Phainon agrees with a laugh, and begins the process of winding down, starting with undoing the buckles on his shoes. In his peripheral, he watches Mydei sit up, body bowing over itself. He twists his mother’s signet ring around his finger. A red thread twists on the sheets between them.

“I don’t want to be king,” Mydei says after a while. “Every king of Kremnos has been crowned by killing his own father, and I…” He sighs.

“That much can end with you,” Phainon tries.

“But what about the rest of it?” Mydei asks. He’s still spinning the ring, not looking at Phainon. “The black tide isn’t going away. We beat Nikador, but Kremnos is still crumbling more and more each day. My people are still losing their homes, and I… I have to lead them somewhere.”

What’s left of Castrum Kremnos isn’t going to last much longer, even Phainon knows this. They’d hoped to take back the city but it’s still falling. Slowly, gradually, but it’s inevitable. Phainon kicks off his shoes and crawls over the mattress to Mydei’s side. “You can send them here,” he suggests gently, kissing his bare shoulder. “They won’t like it, but they can take their time, and you… you won’t have to be king forever, if that’s not what you want.”

Sighing, Mydei leans into him, head on his shoulder, hair ticking his chin. “It was prophesied that I would lead Kremnos to its fall,” he says. “This is it, isn’t it?”

“Maybe,” Phainon says, and pulls one of Mydei’s hands into his lap. “Is this why you decided to join the flame chase?”

A halfhearted laugh. Mydei’s palm opens, fingers spreading for Phainon’s to fit between them. “It would look stupid for me to stand around doing nothing while you play hero.”

“I’m with you,” Phainon tells him. “Like you said earlier, your battles are my battles. That’s what it means to be equals. So if you’ll stand by me in the flame chase, I’ll stand by you as you guide Kremnos wherever the west wind takes you.”

“You’re terribly sentimental, Deliverer,” Mydei tells him, warm fingers skimming his knuckles.

“Romantic,” Phainon corrects, playing with the red string connecting their hands. Devotion flowing both ways in equal measure. He thinks of Mydei’s pinched expression in telling Phainon he loves him and laughs. “Just call me romantic.”
